sourceIssues.printed: Assumption 7.1 (p. 46): "For each x ∈ Q, we have x ≡ 1 mod p, and r̄_{𝔪∅} | G_x is a direct sum of four pairwise distinct characters with Frobenius eigenvalues α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x. We assume that the eigenvalues have been labeled so that the plane λ(α_x) ⊕ λ(β_x) is isotropic, and hence α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x." Theorem 7.2 (p. 47): "Let μ and 𝔪∅ be as above, and suppose that Assumption 7.1 holds. Let 𝔪 denote the ideal of T_μ(Q) containing 𝔪∅ together with the elements xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x for each x ∈ Q. Then 𝔪 is maximal and there is an isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i : H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_{𝔪∅} ⥲ H^0(X_0(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_𝔪 ... Here i is the natural inclusion and pr_Q is defined as follows. For x ∈ Q, let R_x denote the Hecke operator R_x = (xU_{x,2} − α'_xγ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − β'_xδ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − γ'_xδ'_x) ∈ T_μ(Q), and let pr_x denote the idempotent pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R'_x)^{n!}. Then the pr_x's commute with one another and pr_Q denotes their product." Theorem 7.3 (p. 47) states the same isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i for W^sub_{μ,K/O} under a vanishing hypothesis.
sourceIssues.correction:
Assumption 7.1 needs a further condition on the labelling: α_xβ_x ≠ γ_xδ_x in k. Since ν(r̄)(Frob_x) = 1 for x ≡ 1 mod p, this is the same as (α_xβ_x)² ≠ 1, and also the same as α_x ≠ −γ_x or β_x ≠ −δ_x. Genestier–Tilouine (the paper's [31], §5.1, p. 212) state this very condition in their definition of Taylor–Wiles primes, as "(ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1".

A good labelling always exists when the four eigenvalues are pairwise distinct:
- the split {α,β}|{γ,δ} clashes exactly when α = −γ;
- the split {α,γ}|{β,δ} clashes exactly when α = −β;
- if both clashed we would get β = γ, which is excluded.

So swapping β_x and γ_x cures a clash. For the application, the labellings chosen in §4 (p. 815) for the primes Q_N of Prop. 4.10 must satisfy the condition, since §6.3–6.4 and §9 reuse them. Assumptions 6.12(2) and 6.16(2) should say the same.

Another fix is to replace the third factor of R_x by (U_{x,1} − γ'_x − δ'_x). U_{x,1} separates {α,β} from {γ,δ}: in the clash case the difference of the sums is 2(α+β) ≠ 0.

Separately, R'_x in the formula for pr_x is undefined and should read R_x. This is a misprint, and arXiv v1 has it too.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this on the rendered p. 846 and p. 847 images and on arXiv v1 p. 35. The text is identical in both, including the undefined R'_x. I redid the computation.

(1) Why R_x can lie in 𝔪. The third factor of R_x can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term is in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra and needs no knowledge of U_{x,2}-eigenvalues.

(2) When αβ = γδ is allowed. Using αδ = βγ = ν, we get γδ = ν²/(αβ). So αβ = γδ iff αβ = ±ν. The case αβ = ν would force α = γ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −ν is equivalent to α = −γ, and also to β = −δ. Assumption 7.1 and Prop. 4.10(3) (which only asks for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues") do not exclude it. Concrete check in F_7 with ν = 1: (α,β,γ,δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4), which is (2, −1/2, −2, 1/2). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = −1 ≠ ν, so the plane is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6. Then R_x mod 𝔪 = (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0. Since x ≡ 1 mod p and ν(r̄) is a power of the cyclotomic character, ν(Frob_x) = 1. For r̄ with image containing Sp4(F_p), Chebotarev gives such primes x.

(3) Why the theorem then fails. On the 𝔪-part, every element of the finite ϖ^n-torsion is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x^{n!} → 0 there, pr_x acts as 0 on the 𝔪-part, and pr_Q ∘ i = 0. But the source H^0(X, ·)_{𝔪∅} is nonzero: T_μ acts faithfully (Def. 5.13) and 𝔪∅ is a maximal ideal. So the claimed isomorphism fails. Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 fail the same way.

(4) The candidate's other claims hold. The first two factors reduce to (αβ−αγ) and (αβ−βδ), which are nonzero since β ≠ γ and α ≠ δ. The swap argument is also right: a clash for the new labelling needs α = −β, and together with α = −γ this gives β = γ, which is excluded.

(5) Where this matters. Theorem 7.2 is used in the patching step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10, and nothing there fixes the labelling. So a stated result is false as printed in an edge case its hypotheses allow. The main theorems survive once the labelling is chosen correctly, which is always possible. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) R_x lies in 𝔪 in the clash case. The third factor can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term lies in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra: it needs no facts about U_{x,2}-eigenvalues and no reading of the undefined R'_x.

(2) The theorem then fails. The target is ϖ-power torsion, and each element is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x is topologically nilpotent on H^0(X_0(Q), ·)_𝔪, and lim R_x^{n!} = 0 there. Hence pr_Q∘i = 0 into the 𝔪-part. If 𝔪 were not proper the target would be 0, which also fails.

The source is nonzero. By Def. 5.13 (with Q = ∅), T_μ acts faithfully on H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}). T_μ is finite over O and so semilocal, and 𝔪∅ is one of its maximal ideals, so the 𝔪∅-part is nonzero. Therefore Theorem 7.2 fails. So do Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6, which assert that pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism with inverse d_Q^{-1}tr.

(3) Assumption 7.1 allows the clash. Here ν = 1, so γ = 1/β and δ = 1/α, and αβ = γδ ⇔ (αβ)² = 1. The case αβ = 1 would force β = δ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −1 means α = −γ, which is not excluded.

Example in F_7: (α, β, γ, δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = 6 ≠ 1, so {α,β} is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6, and R_x ≡ (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0.

A script over p ≤ 23 checked that:
- R_x ≡ 0 mod 𝔪 exactly in the clash case, since the first two factors are always units;
- the two Lagrangian splittings never both clash.

This kind of Frobenius occurs in the paper itself. Example 4.11 (p. 819) builds the element c·(g,h), with eigenvalues ±(xy)^{1/2}, ±(xy)^{−1/2}. That is {s, −s, 1/s, −1/s}, and its labelling (s, −1/s, −s, 1/s) clashes. Prop. 4.10(3) and the §4 labelling rule (p. 815) ask only for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues" and isotropic planes.

(4) The cited source has the missing hypothesis. The proof of Thm 7.3 rests on [31, Prop. 11.1.2]. Genestier–Tilouine define Taylor–Wiles primes (§5.1, p. 212) by: "P_{π,q} a quatre racines distinctes ᾱ_q, β̄_q, γ̄_q = β̄_q^{-1} et δ̄_q = ᾱ_q^{-1} dans k, telles que (ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1". Their injectivity proof (p. 282) inverts (α_qβ_q − α_qγ_q)(α_qβ_q − β_qδ_q)(α_qβ_q − γ_qδ_q), which needs exactly this condition. Calegari–Geraghty dropped it, so the citation does not rescue the statement.

(5) Where it is used. Theorem 7.2 feeds step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10 and 𝔪_N as in Thm 7.2. Nothing in that proof fixes the labelling. Since a non-clashing labelling always exists, the fix is to add the condition and choose labellings accordingly. Only an abstract Hecke-equivariant isomorphism is used in (b), so Thm 9.1 and the main theorems survive.

Both candidates' arguments and corrections check out:
- X-K5-5: "β≠−δ ⇔ αβ≠−ν", "the alternative split fails iff α=−β", and "both ⇒ α=δ" are all right.
- H-h2-1: "α≠−γ" and the swap argument are right.

The printed text matches the candidate exactly; I checked it on page images at 250 and 400 dpi.

(1) In §6.4 the weight is σ = (a,2). Page 44 says "We now let σ = (a,2) ... denote a nonregular weight". Assumption 6.16, T_σ(Q)^{α,β} and Theorem 6.17 all use σ. Those symbols were last bound in §6.3 (p. 841: "Let μ = (a,b) ... with a ≥ b ≥ 3 be a regular weight"), which conflicts with b = 2. The passage was evidently copied from the proof of Theorem 6.13 (pp. 842–843), which uses the same μ, μ', b and I_{μ,m}.

(2) Theorem 8.13, which the proof cites for the injections, has target weight ω(j+k, 2+k) (p. 865, with σ = (j,2)). That confirms 2+t, not b+t.

(3) The italic m under T_μ(Q)^{α,β} should be the maximal ideal 𝔪. The left-hand side and p. 845 both have fraktur 𝔪, and localisation "at the integer m" means nothing here. The same italic-m slip appears in §6.3 on p. 843 ("T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m / I_{μ,m}"), which is outside this locator.

(4) A minor point about the candidate's wording: μ and b are not strictly undefined. They are leftovers from §6.3, where b ≥ 3, so they are incompatible with §6.4 rather than unbound. The more charitable reading, "μ = (a,b) generic as in Remark 6.5, with b = 2", is never stated, and it clashes with the σ notation used in the same proof. The misprint verdict stands either way.

The intended meaning is clear from p. 845 and Theorem 8.13, so the argument is unaffected. The statement of Theorem 6.17 is untouched, and so are its later uses in §9 (text lines 3785 and 3822), which depend only on the statement. arXiv:1907.08691v1 p. 34 has the identical text, including ω(a+t, b+t), μ, μ' and the italic m.

sourceIssues.printed: In order to obtain a representation that also satisfies Definition 4.6(1), we note that ν(r′_m) = χϵ^{−(a−1)}χ_Q, where χ_Q is a finite-order character of p-power order which is unramified outside Q. sourceIssues.reason: The leading χ is defined nowhere in §6.4 or in the proof. Theorem 6.13(1), applied in weight μ′ = (a′,b′) = (a+t, 2+t), gives ν∘r = χ_{μ′,0}ε^{−w′}, where w′ = a′+b′−3 = a+2t−1. sourceIssues.locator: §7.1, Theorem 7.3, p. 847 (the "explicit inverse" sentence and the proof's K to K/O step); also Lemma 7.4 and its proof, p. 848; Lemma 7.5, pp. 849–850; Lemma 7.6, p. 850
sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 7.3 (p. 47): "...is an isomorphism. An explicit inverse is given by the composition H^0(X_0(Q), W^sub_{μ,K/O})_𝔪 ↪ H^0(X_0(Q), W^sub_{μ,K/O})_{𝔪_∅} →[d_Q^{−1}tr] H^0(X, W^sub_{μ,K/O})_{𝔪_∅}, where d_Q = ∏_{x∈Q}[GSp_4(Z_x) : Π(x)] (which is prime to p) and tr is the trace map associated to X_0(Q) → X." The proof says: "Furthermore, if d_Q^{−1}tr is an inverse over K, then the fact that it is defined over O implies immediately that it also gives an inverse over K/O." Lemma 7.4 (p. 48): "In particular, the left-hand vertical maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms." Its proof: "Note that f can be recovered from F via the formula f = d_Q^{−1}tr(F)." Lemma 7.5 (p. 49) and Lemma 7.6 (p. 50): "...is an isomorphism with inverse d_Q^{−1}tr." The proofs of Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6 repeat "with inverse d_Q^{−1}tr" for the auxiliary vertical maps. Each is checked against the page image (display on p. 47 checked at 220 dpi). arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text with the same numbering: Theorem 7.3 on p. 35, Lemmas 7.4 and 7.5 on p. 36, Lemma 7.6 on p. 37.
sourceIssues.correction:
pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism, but d_Q^{−1}tr is not its inverse. Set v_Q := tr∘pr_Q∘i, an endomorphism of H^0(X,·)_{m_∅}. It is a p-adic limit of spherical Hecke operators at the primes of Q, since tr∘[Π g Π]∘i is K-spherical. So v_Q lies in (the completion of) T_{m_∅} and commutes with h, h̃, i, tr, restriction to S and S_0(Q), and the connecting maps.

Under Assumption 7.1 (x ≡ 1 mod p, and α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x distinct, so the parameter is regular mod ϖ), the value mod m_∅ is d_x·c_x ≡ 4·(1/4) = 1. So v_Q ≡ 1 mod m_∅, and v_Q is a unit.

The correct inverse is v_Q^{−1}∘tr = (tr∘pr_Q∘i)^{−1}∘tr, restricted to the m-summand, which is defined over O. In the statements of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6, replace d_Q^{−1}tr by this. In Lemma 7.4, drop "mutually inverse" in favour of "the left-hand pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism", and use f = v_Q^{−1}tr(F) = h^t v_Q^{−1}tr(g) in the proof. The proofs then go through unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason:
Set-up from the paper. K_{x,0} = Π(x) is the Klingen parahoric (§5.2, p. 822). pr_x is "the idempotent" lim(R'_x)^{n!} (p. 847), so pr_Q∘i sends the spherical vector v0 to its component in one U_{x,2}-eigenline of π_x^{Π(x)}. tr∘i = d_Q, so d_Q^{−1}tr is averaging e_K over GSp4(Z_x)/Π(x). The composite therefore acts by c = (e_K-coefficient of that component). The four c's sum to 1 because v0 is the sum of its components, so c = 1 cannot hold in general.

I redid the computation independently, with my own code (bern.py and run*.py in work/agents/v-dQ).

(1) GL2 analogue by q-expansions. With U f_α = α f_α, f_α = f − βVf and tr(Vf) = (a/p)f in weight 2, I get (p+1)^{−1}tr(pr_α f) = (αp−β)/((p+1)(α−β))·f. This equals f only if α = pβ, and it is ≡ 1/2 mod (p−1). The Bernstein-presentation model reproduces this exactly (for example −7/6 and 13/6 at q = 5).

(2) GSp4, principal-series module H⊗_A χ of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra (Bernstein relations), with W_J = ⟨s2⟩ (Klingen) and λ = (0,1,2) ↔ β_{x,2}. The θ's commute and are additive (checked). At q = 7, χ = (2,3,5), the four values are c = −5863/2000, 779/200, −11/1000 and 19/400. They sum to 1 and none equals 1. With the other reader's parameters t = (2,3,5,15/2) my code reproduces their values exactly: 339663/154000, −1083/875, 59/1750, −247/154000. At q = 1 every c = 1/4 = |W_J|/|W|. For (p,q) = (13,53), (11,23), (23,47), (7,29), with θ-eigenvalues distinct mod p, every c ≡ 1/4 mod p and (1+q+q²+q³)c ≡ 1 mod p.

(3) Cross-checks. A Macdonald c-function formula, c_C = Σ_{w∈C}∏_{α>0}(1−q^{−1}χ(wα^∨)^{−1})/(1−χ(wα^∨)^{−1}) / P_W(q^{−1}), gives the same numbers. Using the opposite-chamber operator T_{w0}θ_{w0λ}T_{w0}^{−1} (antidominant β_{x,2}) gives the same set of four values, so the result does not depend on conventions. c also varies with χ, so no rescaling of tr can make d_Q^{−1}tr an inverse.

Consequence: for p ≥ 5 the claimed inverse acts as ≡ 4^{−#Q} ≠ 1 on the nonzero 𝔪_∅-part, and for any p it is ≠ 1 for generic Satake parameters. So the printed "explicit inverse" is false.

Dependence. The proof of Theorem 7.2 (pp. 850–851) and everything after it use only that the pr_Q maps are isomorphisms. Lemma 7.6 follows from the five lemma. Lemma 7.4 and the K to K/O step of Theorem 7.3 need some O-integral inverse that commutes with h, and the corrected one qualifies. So the false claims are stated clauses of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6, and nothing downstream breaks. The other reader's formulas, the congruences and the correction all check out. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAILED.
(a) The paper says tr is "the trace map associated to X_0(Q) → X". The map is finite étale of degree [K:K_0(Q)] = d_Q (the Klingen parahoric Π(x), §5.1), so tr∘i = d_Q. No renormalisation of tr is in play.

(b) A convention-free contradiction. Assumption 7.1 fixes only that λ(α_x)⊕λ(β_x) is isotropic, and four labellings satisfy it: (α,β,γ,δ), (α,γ,β,δ), (β,δ,α,γ) and (γ,δ,α,β). Each preserves α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x. The theorem is stated for each of them. The corresponding pr^{(j)} (p. 847: R_x kills the other three products) project onto the four generalized eigenspaces of xU_{x,2} on the old part, taking the products distinct mod ϖ, which is generic. So Σ_j pr^{(j)}∘i = i. If each d_Q^{−1}tr∘pr^{(j)}∘i were the identity, summing would give d_Q^{−1}tr∘i = 4·id. But d_Q^{−1}tr∘i = id, so 3·id = 0 on H^0(X, W_K)_{m_∅} ≠ 0. Hence the claimed inverse fails for some admissible labelling, for every p: over K, and on ϖ^n-torsion for large n.

(c) A GL2 analogue, redone by hand with tr(Vf) = q^{1−k}a_q f and αβ = q^{k−1}. Here (q+1)^{−1}tr(pr_α f) = (αq−β)/((q+1)(α−β))·f. This is ≡ 1/2 mod (q−1), and the two values sum to 1.

(d) My own Casselman–Macdonald script (work/agents/vB-h2-2/cass.py). It verifies Macdonald's identity Σ_w ∏ c_a(wχ) = Q_W(q^{−1}). At q = 7 and z = (3,5), the four coset values are 1/700, −29/700, −377/700 and 221/140 for W_P = ⟨short⟩. For W_P = ⟨long⟩ they are −8/175, −52/35, −443/700 and 443/140. Each set sums to 1, and no value is 1. For (q,p) = (23,11) and (29,7) with regular parameters, every value is ≡ 1/4 mod p and d·c ≡ 1, for either parabolic. For p ≠ 3 the claim therefore already fails on the nonzero ϖ-torsion. This agrees with the readers' numbers and with the prior verdict.

CONSEQUENCES.
- The explicit inverse is used in the K-to-K/O injectivity step of Theorem 7.3's proof, and in Lemma 7.4's divisibility argument (f = d_Q^{−1}tr(F) = h^t d_Q^{−1}tr(g)).
- Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6 need only that the vertical maps are isomorphisms (the Lemma 7.4 argument, and the five lemma).
- The proof of Theorem 7.2 (pp. 850–851) and its only later use (§9, p. 879: "Combining this with the isomorphism of Theorem 7.2") use only the isomorphism.
- With v_Q^{−1}∘tr as the inverse, every step works: it is O-integral, commutes with h, h̃ and restriction, and is intertwined by h^t across weights. So the isomorphisms in Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 all survive. What is false is the stated "inverse d_Q^{−1}tr" / "mutually inverse" clauses in the statements of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6.

(Aside, not assessed: if αβ ≡ γδ mod ϖ, which is possible when (α,β,γ,δ) = (α,β,−α,−β), then R_x does not separate m from the ideal with U_{x,1} ≡ γ+δ.)

sourceIssues.correction: pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R_x)^{n!}. The prime on R_x should be dropped. The primed letters α'_x, β'_x, γ'_x, δ'_x are already used inside R_x for the lifts to O^× of the Frobenius eigenvalues.
sourceIssues.reason: The page image of p. 847 confirms that the displayed idempotent is printed as lim_{n→∞}(R'_x)^{n!}, while only the unprimed R_x is defined, in the display just above it. I searched the full text of the published version (Siegel.txt) and of arXiv v1 (cg20-v1.txt) for any R'_x or R_x. Each has exactly three hits, all in this passage: the sentence "let R_x denote", the display defining R_x, and the display for pr_x with the prime. So R'_x is never defined. The only sensible reading is R_x itself. The primes in this section mark the lifts α'_x, ..., δ'_x ∈ O^× of α_x, ..., δ_x ∈ k^× (p. 847, first line), and R_x is already built from those lifts. I checked the formula myself. The level K_0(Q) is the Siegel parahoric, m contains xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x, and α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x (Assumption 7.1). The Frobenius-stable Lagrangian planes therefore give the eigenvalues αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ for xU_{x,2}. R_x is the product of the factors for the three eigenvalues other than αβ. lim R_x^{n!} is then the idempotent of the finite Hecke algebra that kills the generalized eigenspaces where R_x is nilpotent and is the identity where R_x is a unit, which is exactly what pr_x is meant to be. No normalization of R_x is needed, because the n! limit is already idempotent. arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 35, prints the same thing (checked on the rendered image): "pr_x = lim_{n→∞}(R'_x)^{n!}", with R_x defined identically just above. Later text uses only pr_Q: Theorem 7.3, its proof (which cites [GT05, Prop. 11.1.2]), and the diagrams in §7 on pp. 848–851. None of it mentions R'_x or depends on a separately defined primed operator, so the proofs and stated results are unaffected.

Its proof is Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 on pp. 847–850, plus the 'Proof of Theorem 7.2' on pp. 850–851. arXiv v1 has the same statement word for word (Theorem 7.2, v1 p. 35). sourceIssues.printed: THEOREM 7.2  Let μ and m_∅ be as above, and suppose that Assumption 7.1 holds. Let m denote the ideal of T_μ(Q) containing m_∅ together with the elements xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x for each x ∈ Q. Then m is maximal and there is an isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i : H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_{m_∅} ⥲ H^0(X_0(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_m which is equivariant for the operators T_{x,i} for each x ∉ S ∪ Q ∪ {p} as well as for the operators T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}.
sourceIssues.correction: There are two ways to repair this. (a) Minimal repair: define m as the maximal ideal of T_μ(Q) that contains m_∅, the listed elements, and ⟨u⟩ − 1 for every u ∈ Δ_Q. Then T_μ(Q)/m is generated over T^an_μ(Q)/m_∅ = k by elements that are scalars modulo m. This uses a small check the candidate omits: the central operator U_{x,0} is fixed by the central character, i.e. it lies in O^×·S_ℓ·⟨Δ_Q⟩ for a suitable prime ℓ given by Dirichlet. So T_μ(Q)/m = k. The diamond operators act trivially on H^0(X_0(Q), ·), and they act unipotently on H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ·) when Δ is a p-group. Hence all the localizations used later are unchanged. (b) Keep the printed definition and add the missing argument. First, a residual step: by [64, Cor. 3], and because r̄ is unramified at x, ⟨u⟩ ≡ 1 modulo every maximal ideal containing m_∅. So T/m is local with residue field k. Second, an integral step: pass to high weight using the surjections T_{μ'}(Q) ↠ T_μ(Q)/I_{μ,m} of Remark 6.5, together with Chevalley's lemma. In high weight, ⟨u⟩ equals the inertia character on the (γ_x, δ_x)-plane of the T^an-valued Galois representation, as in Theorem 9.1(a). That character is ≡ 1 mod m_∅, so ⟨u⟩ − 1 ∈ m_∅T and m is maximal.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 846–851 and 842–843 and checked the definitions on pp. 833–835 and 840–841. By Definition 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) ⊂ End_O H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}) is generated over T^an_μ(Q) by the U_{x,i} and the diamond operators ⟨u⟩, u ∈ Δ_Q. In T_μ(Q), m_∅ denotes the pushforward ideal (§6.3, §7.1), and §6.3 says explicitly that it 'need not be maximal'. Modulo the listed ideal, T^an maps onto k and U_{x,1} and xU_{x,2} become constants. The quotient is therefore a k-algebra generated by the images of the ⟨u⟩, which satisfy ⟨u⟩^{|Δ_Q|} = 1 and nothing more a priori. So maximality needs two things: (a) no nontrivial residual diamond character occurs, and (b) ⟨u⟩ − 1 lies in the ideal, not merely in its radical. Neither the proof of Theorem 7.3 nor Lemmas 7.4–7.6 nor the proof on pp. 850–851 mentions maximality or diamond operators. The only other places the ⟨u⟩ appear are Definition 5.13 and §9, step (a). The assertion is therefore unproved as printed. It is not false: the local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q plus Carayol argument sketched in the correction proves it, using results the paper cites elsewhere. The candidate's side remark that the quotient 'need not be a field (it can be non-reduced)' is therefore not right in this setting. Its classification is right, though: a gap that affects nothing. Under the looser reading of 'the ideal … containing' as 'the maximal ideal containing', the uniqueness implied by 'the' would still need step (a). I confirmed the printed text by rendering p. 834, 846, 847, 851 and 879. By Definition 5.13(2) on p. 834, T_μ(Q) ⊂ End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})) is generated over T^an_μ(Q) by U_{x,i} and by ⟨u⟩ for u ∈ Δ_Q = ∏(Z/x)^×. As an ideal of T_μ(Q), m_∅ is the extension of the maximal ideal of T^an_μ(Q). The paper itself warns on p. 841 that this extension 'need not be maximal'. Modulo the printed ideal I, the images of T^an_μ(Q), U_{x,1} and U_{x,2} are scalars. The quotient T/I is therefore a finite k-algebra generated by the images of the diamond operators (and U_{x,0}). Such a quotient of k[Δ_Q] can be non-local through the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q, and non-reduced through its p-part (x ≡ 1 mod p). The statement and proof of Theorem 7.2 use the word 'maximal' only in the statement itself. Theorem 7.3 relies on [31, Prop. 11.1.2] for the isomorphism, not for maximality. Lemmas 7.4–7.6 and the five-lemma argument only concern H^0(X_0(Q), ·)_m, on which ⟨u⟩ acts trivially. None of them shows ⟨u⟩ − 1 ∈ I.

Defence attempted: the claim is very probably true, but it needs non-formal automorphic input that is not given. Residually, a nontrivial prime-to-p nebentypus at x is ruled out only by local–global compatibility ([64, Cor. 3], used for Definition 4.6(5) on p. 844) combined with r̄ being unramified at x. Integrally, ⟨u⟩ − 1 ∈ I needs a Galois representation with values in the Hecke algebra, with ⟨u⟩ matched to an inertia character (as in Theorem 9.1(a), p. 879). The paper states this only for the α,β-ordinary algebra of Theorem 6.17, not for the full T_μ(Q) of Theorem 7.2. No nearby statement or cited source supplies the step. The attribution to Genestier–Tilouine covers only 'sufficiently high weight', and no argument is given for lowering the weight. A charitable reading in which T_μ(Q) acts on X_0(Q), where the diamonds act trivially, would make maximality immediate. That reading conflicts with Definition 5.13, and with Theorem 9.1, which localizes H^0(X_Δ(Q_N)) at m_N.

Downstream use: Theorem 9.1(4) on p. 879 sets 'm_N = the ideal m ⊂ T(Q_N) of Theorem 7.2' and localizes H_N = H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), …)_{m_N}. It uses the classifying map R_{Q_N} → T(Q)^{α,β}_{m_N} of Theorem 6.17, which needs a maximal ideal containing m_∅. Step (c) applies Theorem 7.11, where p. 851 fixes 'a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal m of T_μ(Q)'. I transcribed the text from renders of pp. 847–850.

(1) "co-Cartesian" is not a misprint. Take the upward square: C = H^0(X,W_μ)_{m∅} → D = H^0(X,W_{μ'})_{m∅} along the bottom, A → B along the top, with vertical maps ψ: C → A and φ: D → B, and φ an isomorphism. In an abelian category this square is a pushout iff ψ is epi, and a pullback iff ψ is an isomorphism. The proof explicitly notes that h^t is injective. With that, commutativity gives ψ injective: if ψ(c) = 0, then φ(h^t c) = h^t ψ(c) = 0, so c = 0. The same inputs give τψ = id, where τ = d_Q^{-1}tr. So co-Cartesian plus the noted injectivity already yields "the left-hand vertical maps are mutually inverse isomorphisms". Once the lemma holds, both vertical maps are isomorphisms, and a square with two parallel isomorphisms is both Cartesian and co-Cartesian, so the printed statement is true. The candidate's claim that "a pushout would not give this" is wrong. What the proof shows ("f is divisible by h^t iff F is") is the pullback description, but that does not make "co-Cartesian" false.

(2) "smooth (and in particular irreducible)" is false in the paper's own setting. In §6.3, K_q (and K_x for x of type H) is the full congruence subgroup, so ν(K_q) = 1 + qZ_q. Then π_0(X_{Q̄}) is at least (Z/q)^×, and X is proper and smooth over O, so X_k is disconnected in general, for example whenever μ_q ⊂ k. The conclusion (h is injective on H^0) is still true by the component-wise argument in the correction.

(3) Lemma 7.5 uses the injectivity of h̃^s without saying so. It is true, as argued in the correction.

I rendered p. 849 and confirmed the printed text. First, smooth does not imply irreducible: a disjoint union of two smooth varieties is smooth. Second, X_k is not irreducible in general under the paper's own setup. In §5.2, p. 821 the paper says K is neat, and "This will be the case if S contains a prime x ≥ 3 where K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x". In that case ν(K) = (1+xZ_x) × ∏_{y≠x} Z_y^×. So π_0(Sh_K ⊗ Q̄) = Q_{>0}\A_f^×/ν(K) = Ẑ^×/ν(K) ≅ (Z/x)^×, which has x−1 ≥ 2 geometric components. Since the level is prime to p, the smooth special fibre has the same component set. Frobenius Frob_q acts on it by multiplication by q, so X_k has (x−1)/ord_x(q) connected components. For example, if q ≡ 1 mod x, X_k has x−1 components. The paper puts no restriction on k (§2: O is the ring of integers of an arbitrary finite extension of Q_p with residue field k). So the parenthetical claim "irreducible over k" is false in general, and the implication behind it is invalid. The same holds for X_0(Q)_k. The conclusion is still true. Each connected component of a smooth k-scheme is integral. The Hasse invariant is nonzero on every component, because prime-to-p Hecke correspondences preserve the ordinary locus and act transitively on components (ν(K_p) = Z_p^×). Multiplying a locally free sheaf by a section of a line bundle that is nonzero on each integral component is injective. So Lemma 7.4 and its proof survive once this one-line justification is replaced. It is a false justifying statement, not a failed step. I call it an error rather than a misprint because the printed word "irreducible" asserts something false, not a typo for something true. It affects nothing. Checked against the p. 849 page image; the printed text matches. The conclusion is right but the reason given is false. Smoothness does not imply irreducibility; it only makes each connected component irreducible. Under the paper's own setup X is not connected in general.

(1) §5.2 (p. 821) requires K to be neat, "the case if S contains a prime x ≥ 3 where K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x". The level used in §7 (§6.3, pp. 840–841, item (7)) takes K_q to be the full congruence subgroup of level q. Y_K is the standard moduli space of principally polarised abelian surfaces with K-level structure, which is a model of Sh_K(GSp4).

(2) Since Sp4 is simply connected, π_0(Sh_K ⊗ Q̄) = Ẑ^×/ν(K). Here ν(K_q) = 1 + qZ_q, so this group surjects onto (Z/q)^×, which has q−1 ≥ 2 elements. X is proper and smooth over O, so X_{k̄} has the same number (≥ 2) of connected components.

(3) Over the finite field k, Frobenius acts on these components through multiplication by |k|. So X_k is reducible whenever |k| does not generate (Z/q)^×, for instance when k contains μ_q. Nothing in the paper excludes this, and k is normally enlarged freely. The same holds for X_0(Q)_k, since ν is surjective on the Klingen parahoric.

The defence fails: no convention in the paper makes X connected, and the word "irreducible" appears nowhere else for X. The best charitable reading, that each connected component is irreducible, still leaves out the fact that is actually needed: h ≠ 0 on every component. That fact is true and standard: the non-ordinary locus has codimension 1 (Koblitz, Norman–Oort), the ordinary locus is dense in every fibre, and Hecke transitivity on π_0 gives the same. W^sub_{μ,k} = ω(a,b)(−∞)_k is locally free, and H^0 is left exact. So multiplication by h^t is injective on H^0, and the argument of Lemma 7.4 goes through as written. The candidate's proposed correction is right. One precision: Lemma 6.2(1) states the injectivity only for X_1(Q) and ω(a,b)_k, so it is better cited as "the well-known injectivity used in the proof of Lemma 6.2".

Later uses: Lemma 7.5 ("same argument as Lemma 7.4"), Lemma 7.6 and the proof of Theorem 7.2 (p. 850) use Lemma 7.4, and the appendix refers back to it. None of them relies on irreducibility, only on the injectivity. One side note, outside this candidate: Lemma 7.5 separately needs h̃^s to be injective on H^0(S, ·). The parenthetical does not cover that either; it holds because S = V(h) is reduced and h̃ vanishes only on the 1-dimensional supersingular locus. Since the conclusion is correct, this affects nothing.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this against the page images (pp. 847–850, 862).

(1) The step really needs injectivity. The proof of Lemma 7.4 turns "f is h^t-divisible iff F is h^t-divisible" into "the left vertical maps are mutually inverse". That only works because the horizontal maps are injective, which the paper states explicitly on p. 849: "(Note that since X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k, multiplication by h is injective on H^0.)". Abstractly, let α = pr_Q∘i and α' = d_Q^{-1}tr. Commutativity gives h̃^s(α'α − 1) = 0 and h̃^s(αα' − 1) = 0. To conclude α'α = 1 and αα' = 1 you need h̃^s injective on H^0(S, W_{μ,k})_{m∅} and on H^0(S_0(Q), W_{μ,k})_m. Surjectivity also needs injectivity on the top-left group. So "the same argument as Lemma 7.4" silently needs injectivity of h̃^s on sections over S and S_0(Q). This is not covered by the Lemma 7.4 remark: S is not smooth (it has quadric-cone singularities at superspecial points), and its scheme structure V(h) is never discussed.

(2) Defence attempted. The paper does contain the geometric input, but not the deduction. On p. 849 it cites Boxer [12] for h̃ extending to the boundary and being Hecke-equivariant. It says, calling this "not relevant here", that h̃ vanishes on the 1-dimensional EO stratum to order 2. The proof of Theorem 8.10 (p. 862) says the supersingular locus is a Cartier divisor in the p-rank 1 stratum (Koblitz). Theorem 8.11 uses the same kind of injectivity implicitly: "0 → H^0(Y, ω(j,2)_k ⊗ ω^{-m}) → H^0(Y, ω(j,2)_k) → ...". So the fact is standard and true, and the other ingredients (tr(h̃G) = h̃ tr(G) because h̃ on S_0(Q) is pulled back; Hecke-equivariance at Q from [12, Thm 4.5.4(3)]) are handled. But nowhere does the paper state or prove injectivity on S or S_0(Q). The authors even call the vanishing-locus information irrelevant, although it is exactly what gives injectivity. So this is a genuine omitted step. It is minor and routine to fill.

(3) The fill (checked). S = V(h) is a hypersurface in a regular scheme, hence CM and pure of dimension 2. The boundary divisor is not contained in S, because h restricted to a boundary component is essentially the elliptic Hasse invariant of the abelian part. So S ∩ boundary has dimension ≤ 1. The supersingular locus has dimension 1. So each generic point of S is an interior point of p-rank 1, where h̃ does not vanish, so h̃ is a unit in the Artinian local ring there. Since the associated points of S are exactly its generic points, h̃ is a nonzerodivisor. The same holds for S_0(Q), which is finite étale over S on the interior because the primes in Q are not p.

Consequences: Lemma 7.5 is used only in Lemma 7.6 (p. 850: "The first three vertical maps are isomorphisms ... by Lemmas 7.4 and 7.5"). Lemma 7.6 is used in the proof of Theorem 7.2 (p. 851). Section 10 (p. 887) mentions Lemmas 7.4–7.5 only as a comparison. Since the lemma is true and the missing step is easy to supply, no stated result is at risk.

For n = 2p−1, Sym^n_k = L(p−1) ⊗ L(1)^{[1]} is irreducible of dimension 2p, so the two O-lattices are homothetic and the isomorphism still holds. sourceIssues.reason:
I confirmed the wording from the rendered pages 851, 853 and 878. The text of arXiv:1907.08691v1 is the same for Assumption 7.7, Lemma 7.9, Theorem 7.11 with its proof, and Theorem 9.1(6); the only difference is "Suppose Assumption 7.7 holds" in Lemma 7.9.

(1) The proof of Theorem 7.11 applies Lemma 7.9 to X_0(Q), which means Δ = 1. Its proof on p. 852 needs H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪 = 0 to make H^1(ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_𝔪 divisible. The proof does need torsion-freeness of H_1(X_0(Q), 𝓛)_𝔪: from (2), dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ ≤ dim_k H_1(X_0)_𝔪/ϖ, and this equals rank ≤ r only if H_1(X_0)_𝔪 has no torsion.

(2) The hypothesis in the theorem is Assumption 7.7 for its fixed Δ, and nothing in the proof uses it. The proof only uses M, the Tor/Hochschild–Serre sequence, Lemma 7.9 at X_0, Lemma 7.10 and char-0 automorphic input on X_0.

(3) The vanishing on X_0 does not follow formally from the vanishing on X_Δ. X_1(Q) → X_0(Q) is finite étale with group Δ_Q (p. 822), so C = RΓ(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪 is perfect over k[Δ] and RΓ(X_0, ·)_𝔪 = C ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k. If H^2(C) = 0, the Tor spectral sequence gives H^2(X_0, ·)_𝔪 ≅ Tor_1^{k[Δ]}(H^3(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_𝔪, k). That group need not vanish. For Δ = Z/p, the perfect complex k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] →N k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] has H^2 = 0, but its coinvariants have H^2 = k. The group H^3(X_Δ, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k) is Serre dual to H^0(X_Δ, ω(1,3−a)_k). Theorem 5.1 does not kill it for a ∈ {2,3}: parts (1) and (3) need a−b ≥ 2 or b ≥ 4. For a ≥ 4 (Remark 7.8) the vanishing holds at every level, so there is no issue there.

So, read literally, the stated hypothesis does not cover what the proof uses, and the paper gives no argument connecting the two. Only a charitable reading of Assumption 7.7 as holding for all Δ, including Δ = 1, closes the gap. The authors plainly intended the X_0 vanishing, since 9.1(6) assumes it for X_0 and X_1. The main result, Theorem 9.1, is not affected, because (6) with i = 0 supplies the needed vanishing. What needs repair is the proof of Theorem 7.11 together with its hypothesis; I label this "the proof", not "nothing". No later result depends on the X_Δ form of the assumption. I checked the rendered p. 822, 826, 828–829, 851–855 and 878, and arXiv v1 pp. 38–40.

(1) The mismatch is real. Lemma 7.9 is stated for the running Δ. The proof of Theorem 7.11 applies it to X_0(Q), i.e. Δ = 1. Its proof (p. 852) reduces torsion-freeness to H^2(X_Δ, F_k)_𝔪 = 0, where F = ω(a,2)(−∞). So the proof needs H^2(X_0(Q), F_k)_𝔪 = 0. Theorem 7.11 fixes a Δ and assumes Assumption 7.7 only for that Δ. This step is essential. Since Tor_1^S(M,O) is a quotient of H_1(X_0)_𝔪, torsion in H_1(X_0)_𝔪 would break the bound dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ ≤ r. Nothing else in the proof uses the X_Δ vanishing: the defect formula, the Hochschild–Serre exact sequence (1)–(2), Lemma 7.10 and the char-0 count all work without it.

(2) Defence attempts. I found no reading of the text that makes Assumption 7.7 refer to X_0.
- "Suppose that Assumption 7.7 holds" comes right after "Let Δ be a quotient…". So it concerns that Δ.
- Reading 7.7 as a standing assumption for every quotient Δ, including Δ = 1, would cover the step. But then §9(c) would have to check it for X_Δ(Q_N) too, and (6) only states it for X_0 and X_1.
- There is no formal implication either. For a perfect k[Δ]-complex C with H^2(C) = 0, one gets H^2(C⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k) ≅ Tor_1^{k[Δ]}(H^3(C), k). For Δ = Z/p this can be nonzero: take the complex k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ] →N k[Δ] →(σ−1) k[Δ].

(3) However, the stated theorem is still true. The paper's own tools close the gap, though the paper does not do so:
(i) Assumption 7.7 and the ϖ-sequence give H^2(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 = 0 (by Nakayama) and H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪[ϖ] = 0.
(ii) In characteristic 0, H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 ⊗ K = 0. The steps:
  - Lemma 7.10, which the paper says "holds in all weights and in all prime-to-p levels", applies at level X_Δ.
  - The inclusion from Theorem 5.2, together with the class (a)–(f) argument of pp. 854–855, shows that every contributing π is tempered at ∞. That argument does not depend on the degree.
  - By Theorem 5.5 with (a−1, 0), this point lies in C_0 and C_1 but not in C_2 or C_3 when a ≥ 2. So nothing contributes in degrees 2 or 3.
(iii) By (i) and (ii), H^3(X_Δ, F)_𝔪 = 0, so H^3(X_Δ, F_k)_𝔪 = 0.
(iv) X_Δ → X_0 is finite étale with group Δ (p. 822). So RΓ(X_Δ, F_k) is perfect over k[Δ], and RΓ(X_0, F_k) ≅ RΓ(X_Δ, F_k) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k. The Tor spectral sequence then gives H^2(X_0, F_k)_𝔪 = 0.
So Theorem 7.11 holds as stated, but its proof as written omits (i)–(iv). That makes this a gap, not an error, and it affects the proof only.

(4) Consequences. Theorem 7.11 is used only in §9 step (c) ("H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11"), and in the Appendix Lemma A.5 ("a consequence of the proof of Theorem 7.11"), which has no bearing on this hypothesis. Theorem 9.1 is unaffected: (6) with i = 0 gives exactly the vanishing on X_0 that the proof uses.

Aside, outside this candidate: §9(c) also never checks the literal hypothesis of 7.11 on X_Δ(Q_N). It follows from (6) with i = 1 by the same argument (i)–(iv). Also, Theorem 7.11 requires p−2 > a, while Theorem 9.1 only requires p−1 > a.

sourceIssues.locator: §7.2, proof of Theorem 7.11, point (2), p. 853. arXiv v1 p. 39 has the same text.
sourceIssues.printed: This spectral sequence tells us that (1) M_Δ ~→ H_0(X_0(Q), 𝓛)_m, and (2) we have a short exact sequence (H_1(X_Δ(Q), 𝓛)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q), 𝓛)_m → Tor_1^S(M, O) → 0.
sourceIssues.correction: '(2) we have an exact sequence (H_1(X_Δ(Q), 𝓛)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q), 𝓛)_m → Tor_1^S(M, O) → 0'. This is the end of the five-term sequence Tor_2^S(M,O) →(d_2) (H_1)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),𝓛)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0.
sourceIssues.reason: Take the Pontryagin dual of the five-term exact sequence 0 → H^1(Δ,H^0) → H^1(X_0) → H^1(X_Δ)^Δ → H^2(Δ,H^0) → H^2(X_0) of the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence, using H^i(Δ,N)^∨ = Tor_i^{O[Δ]}(N^∨,O). This gives Tor_2^S(M,O) → (H_1(X_Δ(Q),𝓛)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),𝓛)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0. The kernel of the first displayed map is the image of d_2 from Tor_2^S(M,O) = H_2(Δ,M), which need not vanish, so injectivity is neither proved nor generally true. The display itself has no 0 on the left, so the intended right-exact sequence is clear. The proof uses only the surjection onto Tor_1^S(M,O), to bound dim_k Tor_1/ϖ by the rank of H_1(X_0(Q),𝓛)_m.

sourceIssues.printed: "Then, by Remark 5.12, the infinitesimal character of π̃_∞ is χ_{(0,0−(a−1),−(a−1))+3/2(1,1,1,1)}. Let χ_π denote the central character of π." (checked on a 1200 dpi crop of p. 54: after the second 0 there is a minus sign and no comma, so the subscript tuple has three entries: 0, 0−(a−1), −(a−1))
sourceIssues.correction: χ_{(0,0,−(a−1),−(a−1))+3/2(1,1,1,1)}, i.e. the infinitesimal character with parameter (3/2, 3/2, 5/2−a, 5/2−a)
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 854 at 110, 600 and 1200 dpi. The subscript reads "(0,0−(a−1),−(a−1))": there is no comma between the second 0 and "−(a−1)". That leaves a 3-tuple, (0, −(a−1), −(a−1)), which cannot be added to 3/2(1,1,1,1) in C^4, so the formula as printed has no meaning. The intended value follows from the paper's own formulas, which I recomputed.

(1) Theorem 5.6(2) on p. 829 gives τ = ((a+b−3−w)/2, (a−b+1−w)/2, (−a+b−1−w)/2, (−a−b+3−w)/2) with w = −(a+b+2c). Remark 5.12 on p. 834 takes μ = (a,b;3−a−b), so c = 3−a−b and w = a+b−6. Substituting gives τ = (3/2, 7/2−b, 5/2−a, 9/2−a−b) = (0, −(b−2), −(a−1), −(a+b−3)) + 3/2(1,1,1,1). This agrees with the display in Remark 5.12.

(2) The proof of Theorem 7.11 works with ω(a,2), where μ = (a,2;1−a) and σ = (−2,−a;4−a) (p. 854). Setting b = 2 gives (0, 0, −(a−1), −(a−1)) + 3/2(1,1,1,1) = (3/2, 3/2, 5/2−a, 5/2−a).

The argument that follows agrees with this value. In case (d), the characters λ|·|^{±1/2} need two parameters that differ by 1, which forces 3/2 − (5/2−a) = a−1 = 1, i.e. a = 2, exactly as the text says. In case (b), the two GL2 pieces must each carry parameters {3/2, 5/2−a}, which differ by a−1, so both are weight-a forms, again as stated. The paper never writes this multiset out; it is what the argument implicitly uses. Theorem 5.6(3) with b = 2 gives λ = (a−1,0;4−a), matching the next paragraph. So the error is a dropped comma, and the correct value is fixed by the explicit "by Remark 5.12".

arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 40, prints the identical string "χ_{(0,0−(a−1),−(a−1))+3/2(1,1,1,1)}" (confirmed on the rendered page).

Side note, not part of this candidate: Remark 5.12 cites "Proposition 5.6" for what the paper labels THEOREM 5.6.

sourceIssues.locator: §7.2, proof of Theorem 7.11, p. 855; arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 41
sourceIssues.printed: "Indeed, since π(λ, C_i) is essentially tempered, the local packet Π_{ψ_∞} (where ψ = π̃ ⊞ 1, in the notation of [3]) is in fact an L-packet by [55, Theorem 2.1]." Checked on a 500-dpi render of p. 55: the symbol is the boxed plus ⊞, not the boxed times ⊠. The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 (p. 41) has the same text: "(where ψ = π̃ ⊞ 1, in the notation of [Art04])".
sourceIssues.correction: ψ = π̃ ⊠ 1. In Arthur's notation for GSp4 this is the general-type (case (a)) parameter μ ⊠ 1 with μ = π̃: the cuspidal symplectic-type representation of GL4 tensored with the trivial 1-dimensional representation of SL2 (written ν(1) or 1).
sourceIssues.reason:
1. The paper never defines ψ; it refers to "the notation of [3]", where [3] is Arthur, "Automorphic representations of GSp(4)". In that notation a global parameter is a formal sum ⊞_i μ_i ⊠ ν_i, with μ_i cuspidal on GL(m_i) and ν_i the irreducible representation of SL2 of dimension n_i, and Σ m_i n_i = 4. The general type is μ ⊠ 1. Brumer–Pacetti–Poor–Tornaría–Voight–Yuen (arXiv:1805.10873v4) use the same convention, citing Schmidt: "type (G) given by the formal tensor µ ⊠ 1, where µ is a cuspidal, self-dual, symplectic, unitary, automorphic representation of GL4(A) and 1 is the trivial representation of SU2(A)".
2. I redid the degree count. π̃ ⊞ 1 is an isobaric sum of the 4-dimensional π̃ with a 1-dimensional character, so it has degree 5. That cannot be a parameter for GSp4, whose dual group GSp4(C) sits inside GL4. It is also not the Sp4/SO5 transfer of a general-type parameter, which would be ∧²π̃ ⊗ χ^{-1}, not π̃ ⊞ 1.
3. The printed version contradicts its own sentence. A sum with two summands would not be case (a) and would have a nontrivial S_ψ, yet the next sentence says "the group S_ψ is trivial in Case (a) of [3]". With ⊠ everything fits: the SL2 factor is trivial, so ψ_∞ is essentially tempered and Π_{ψ_∞} is an L-packet, as the text says.
4. The ⊞ signs in cases (b)–(d) (λ|·|^{1/2} ⊞ λ|·|^{-1/2} ⊞ μ, μ|·|^{1/2} ⊞ μ|·|^{-1/2}, μ1 ⊞ μ2) are correct isobaric sums. They describe the GL4 transfer π̃, not ψ.
5. One correction to the candidate's reason: those case (b)–(d) formulas are on p. 854, not "the same page" p. 855. This does not change the verdict.
6. The appendix (proof of Lemma A.5) and BCGP18 Lemma 2.9.1 reuse the argument of this proof but not this formula. BCGP18 Lemma 2.9.1 uses only cases (b)–(f).

sourceIssues.locator: §8.1, display right before Theorem 8.1, p. 856. arXiv v1 (p. 41) has the identical display.
sourceIssues.printed: There is a q-expansion map  H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → R[[q, q′, ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗_R U.
sourceIssues.correction: The target should be R[ζ, ζ^{−1}][[q, q′]] ⊗_R U: power series in q, q′ whose coefficients are Laurent polynomials in ζ, i.e. formal sums Σ_{Q∈𝒳} a(F,Q) q^Q. For general L, fractional exponents with a bounded power of L in the denominator must also be allowed; the paper suggests pretending L = 1.
sourceIssues.reason: The paper's own expansion (p. 857) is F = Σ_{n,m≥0, r²−4mn≤0} a_F(n,r,m) q^n ζ^r q′^m. For fixed (n,m) the exponent r runs over |r| ≤ 2√(nm), which is finite, so the q^n q′^m coefficient is a Laurent polynomial in ζ. But r is unbounded below over all (n,m), while every element of R[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{−1}] has ζ-exponents ≥ −N for some N. I checked the unipotent argument by hand. With M = (1 k; 0 1) and M.Q = (det M)^{−1} M Q M^T, the form Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n) goes to (m+kr+k²n, (r+2kn)/2; ·, n). Since a(F, M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q) with ρ(M) invertible, and k can be taken in the level of Γ̄ of either sign, any nonconstant F has nonzero coefficients with arbitrarily negative r. So its expansion is not in the printed ring. Concretely, the rank-one forms Q with r = −2t and r² = 4mn carry ζ^{−2t}, and Siegel Eisenstein series have nonzero coefficients there. The intended meaning (the formal q-expansion) is clear, and the later arguments (Lemmas 8.3–8.4 etc.) use only the coefficients a(F,Q). The same verdict covers X-K6-6, whose correction R[ζ,ζ^{−1}][[q,q′]] ⊗_R U is the L = 1 case of the above.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.1, the displayed q-expansion map and Theorem 8.1 with its one-line proof, p. 856. arXiv v1 has the same text (§8.1, Theorem 8.1, v1 PDF p. 41; proof cites "Prop. 3.2 of [Til06]"). Related setup: §5.2, p. 821 (K neat, list of allowed K_x).
sourceIssues.printed: "There is a q-expansion map H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → R[[q, q′, ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗_R U. THEOREM 8.1 The q-expansion map is injective. Proof This is a standard fact (see, e.g., [67, Proposition 3.2])."  (and on p. 57: "Here Γ̄ is the congruence subgroup of SL2(Z) defined in [67, p. 807]; ... (It will do the reader little harm to pretend that Γ̄ is just SL2(Z).)")
sourceIssues.correction: Take a q-expansion at a cusp on each geometric connected component c ∈ π0 = Ẑ^×/ν(K_1(Q)) of Y_1(Q). The coefficients lie in R ⊗_O O′, where O′ = O[ζ_M] and M is the level. Theorem 8.1 should say that the resulting map H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R) → ∏_c (R⊗O′)[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{-1}] ⊗ U is injective. This is [67, Prop. 3.2] applied to each component. This is right and minimal. The formal operators of Lemmas 8.3 and 8.4 must then carry a component label: T = T_{p,1} (similitude p) sends the expansion on component c to one on component p^{-1}·c.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked against the page images (p. 821, 856–861) and against Tilouine [67] itself (Doc. Math. Extra Vol. Coates 2006), fetched from the web archive.

(1) Y_1(Q) is necessarily geometrically disconnected. §5.2 (p. 821) lets each K_x (x ∈ S) be one of S(x), Π(x), K(x), Π(x)^+, I(x), or the full congruence subgroup of level x, and assumes K is neat. The torsion element g = diag(1,−1,−1,1) is in GSp4(Q), with similitude ad = bc = 1 for the paper's antidiagonal form. It lies in the torus of GSp4(Z_x), so it lies in every parahoric S(x), Π(x), I(x) and in the paramodular K(x). It lies in Π(x)^+ because its Klingen-Levi λ-entry is 1. It lies in the level-2 full congruence subgroup because g ≡ I mod 2. It also lies in Π(x), Π^+(x) for x ∈ Q and in GSp4(Z_x) outside S. So neatness forces some x ∈ S with x ≥ 3 and K_x the full congruence subgroup of level x. Then ν(K_x) ⊆ 1+xZ_x, so Ẑ^×/ν(K_1(Q)) maps onto (Z/x)^×, which has order ≥ 2. Hence π_0(Y_1(Q)_C) has at least 2 elements.

(2) The cited proof covers only the connected case. [67, §3.1] says "for simplicity, we restrict our attention to one connected component X corresponding to a discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ Sp4(Z). We assume that X has a geometrically connected model over Z[1/N]." It defines "the arithmetic q-expansion (at the ∞ cusp)". Its Prop. 3.2(1) (q-expansion principle) is proved by "The first point follows from the irreducibility of the modular scheme". Its §2 Remark adds: "All schemes above have geometrically connected generic fibers if and only if ν(K) = Ẑ^×."

(3) Counterexample to the literal statement. Take O with ζ_x ∈ O (for example p ≡ 1 mod x), so Y_1(Q)_O is a disjoint union of at least 2 components. With R = O/ϖ, let F = 1_c·h^N, a power of the Hasse invariant (weight (N(p−1), N(p−1))) supported on a component c that does not contain the chosen cusp. Then F ≠ 0, but its expansion there is 0. So a single-cusp map into one copy of R[[q,q′,ζ]][ζ^{−1}] ⊗ U is not injective on H^0(Y_1(Q), ω(j,k)_R). If ζ_x ∉ O, a cusp is not O-rational and the coefficients would lie in R⊗O[ζ_x], not in R.

(4) The paper cannot be tacitly working on one component. Lemma 8.8 and §§8–9 use T_{p,1} = [K β_{p,1} K] with β_{p,1} = diag(1,1,p,p) (p. 830). This operator moves components by p^{±1} mod x. The paper never mentions components.

The fix is standard and all later arguments work componentwise, so the mathematics is right as intended. The statement as printed, and its cited proof, do not cover the geometrically disconnected Y_1(Q) that the paper actually uses. Minor corroboration of the same conflation: p. 842 (v1 p. 17) says "X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k". Both candidates (C-K5-2 "gap", C-K6-3 "imprecision") describe the same issue, and I confirm it. "gap" is the appropriate protocol kind, with affects = nothing. The defence fails. (1) The level K_1(Q) is not geometrically connected. §6.3(7) takes K_q to be the full congruence subgroup of level q, and §5.2 gets neatness from such a prime x ≥ 3. That subgroup has ν(K_q) = 1+qZ_q, so π0(Y_{K,Q̄}) = Ẑ^×/ν(K) maps onto (Z/q)^×, which has order q−1 ≥ 2. The moduli problem cited, [57, §4.1] (Pilloni), uses "isomorphismes symplectiques à un facteur de similitude près", so the Weil-pairing root of unity varies and the components are indexed by it.

(2) The cited source covers only one component. Tilouine [67, §3.1] says: "we restrict our attention to one connected component X corresponding to a discrete subgroup Γ ⊂ Sp4(Z). We assume that X has a geometrically connected model over Z[1/N]." His Prop. 3.2(1) "follows from the irreducibility of the modular scheme". His own Remark in §2 says: "All schemes above have geometrically connected generic fibers if and only if ν(K) = Ẑ^×". The Γ̄ on p. 807 that CG cite also belongs to this one-component setting.

(3) As printed, the statement is false in cases the paper allows. Take p = 7 and q = 3, which satisfies q ≢ 1 mod p. Then ζ_3 ∈ O, and Y_1(Q) over O is a disjoint union Y′ ⊔ Y″ of at least 2 components defined over O. A nonzero form supported on Y″ has zero expansion at a cusp of Y′. Such forms exist in every weight where H^0 ≠ 0, because GSp4(Z_q) normalises K_q and permutes the components transitively. When ζ_q ∉ O the standard cusp is not even defined over O, so the target ring should be R⊗O[ζ_q], not R.

(4) Consequences: the downstream arguments hold after rewriting them component by component. T_{p,1}, and hence U, Z and V, shift components by p^{-1} mod ν(K), so Lemmas 8.3 and 8.4 relate an expansion on component c to one on component p^{-1}c.
- Theorem 8.22, first step: minimality and the U-relation work on the tuple (F_c). The j > 2 branch uses ρ(pI) = 0, which is independent of the component.
- Theorem 8.22, (2,2) branch: it needs a_{p^{-2}c}(F,Q) = a_c(F,Q). This holds because the central element acts trivially on the m-part (the Nebentypus mod m is trivial). The paper's single-expansion formula "ρ(pI) is the identity" already assumes the same fact.
- Proposition 8.25: the contraction claim holds for every x, so it is independent of the component.
- Theorems 8.10 and 8.11, and the injectivity of multiplication by the Hasse invariant, are geometric and hold on each component.

So Theorem 8.13 and every stated result survive. A related instance of the same suppression is on p. 849, "X_0(Q) and X are smooth (and in particular irreducible) over k". It is harmless because h is nonzero on each component. "gap" is also a defensible kind, since the cited result proves only the connected case. I chose "error" because the printed theorem is literally false in allowed cases.

sourceIssues.printed: where 𝒳 denotes the 2 × 2 positive semidefinite matrices which take on Z[1/L]-integral arguments for integral vectors, or equivalently,  𝒳 = ( m  ½r ; ½r  n ),   m, n, r ∈ Z[1/L].

sourceIssues.reason: The two descriptions called 'equivalent' differ. For Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n), taking Z[1/L]-integral values x^T Q x on all integral x is equivalent to m, n, r ∈ Z[1/L] (m = Q(e1), n = Q(e2), r = Q(e1+e2) − m − n). But the displayed set drops positive semidefiniteness, so read literally it contains, e.g., (−1, 0; 0, 0). The q-expansion on p. 857 sums only over n, m ≥ 0 with r² − 4mn ≤ 0, and the first half of the sentence says 'positive semidefinite', so the intended set is clear. 'Arguments' is also a word slip for 'values'. This is a harmless imprecision in notation.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.2, Remark 8.2, p. 857; arXiv v1 p. 42
sourceIssues.printed: Remark 8.2: "We will assume that either j ≥ 4 or j = k = 2. Since we are most interested in representations with similitude character ν equal to ε^{j+k−3}, the oddness condition forces the congruence j ≡ k mod 2, and so if j > k ≥ 2, then j ≥ 4." (checked on the rendered image of Duke p. 57, published p. 857). arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same exponent in Remark 8.2 on p. 42 (checked on the rendered page): "…with similitude character ν is equal to ε^{j+k−3}, the oddness condition forces the congruence j ≡ k mod 2…" (with a stray "is").
sourceIssues.correction: ν = ε^{−(j+k−3)} = ε^{3−j−k}. For forms with nontrivial Nebentypus this holds up to a finite-order character, as in Theorem 6.13(1): ν∘r = χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}, where w = a+b−3.
sourceIssues.reason:
The sign is wrong under the paper's own conventions.
(i) §2, p. 806 sets the convention: "The Hodge–Tate weight of ε | G_{Q_p} is −1."
(ii) Every other place gives the similitude with a negative exponent:
- p. 802: ε^{1−j} for weight (j,2).
- §4, p. 812: ν(r̄) = ε̄^{−(a−1)}.
- Definition 4.6(1), p. 815: ν(r) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
- Prop. 6.8(1), p. 838: ν∘r_f = λ_f∘χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}, with w = a+b−3.
- Theorem 6.13(1), p. 842: ν∘r = χ_{μ,0} ε^{−w}.
- Proof of Theorem 6.17, p. 846: ν(r′_m) = χ ε^{−(a−1)} χ_Q.
- Theorem 9.1, p. 878: ν(r̄) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
(iii) §8 itself agrees with the corrected sign.
- The weight (j,k) of §8 is the (a,b) of §6: the §8.5 Frobenius eigenvalues on p. 863 are α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1} and α^{−1}p^{k+j−3}. These match Theorem 6.13(3) with a = j and b = k.
- The paired eigenvalues multiply to p^{k+j−3}, and Lemma 8.3 has T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V.
- Since φ acts on D_cris(Q_p(1)) by p^{−1}, a similitude with φ = p^{k+j−3} and Hodge–Tate weight 0 + (j+k−3) is ε^{−(j+k−3)} under the paper's convention.
- ε^{j+k−3} would instead have Hodge–Tate weight −(j+k−3), which cannot pair the nonnegative weights 0, k−2, j−1 and j+k−3.
I redid the parity step: ε(c) = −1, so ε^{±(j+k−3)}(c) = (−1)^{j+k−3}. Oddness (ν(c) = −1) then gives j+k even, i.e. j ≡ k mod 2. So j > k ≥ 2 forces j ≥ k+2 ≥ 4. The deduction holds whichever sign is used.

sourceIssues.printed: a(U_2F, Q) = (−1 + p (det(Q)/p)) a(Q) = (−1 + p ((r^2 − 4mn)/p)) a(Q).   [p. 59, top display, continuing Lemma 8.4 from p. 58 after "If Q ≢ 0 mod p, then". It is followed by "If Q ≡ 0 mod p, then a(U_2F, Q) = (−1 + p^2)a(Q)." Definition 8.5 on the same page reads: "Explicitly, if Q ≢ 0 mod p, then a(X_2F, Q) = a(F, Q) times (D/p), where D is the determinant of the quadratic form associated to Q, and (D/p) is the Legendre symbol."]
sourceIssues.correction: For Q ≢ 0 mod p: a(U_2F,Q) = (−1 + p((r^2 − 4mn)/p)) a(Q) = (−1 + p(−det(Q)/p)) a(Q). So the first expression should use −det(Q), i.e. the discriminant d(Q) = r^2 − 4mn. Definition 8.5 is correct only if "determinant of the quadratic form" is read in Gauss's sense, b^2 − ac = r^2/4 − mn = −det(Q). In §8.8 (p. 874), "D = det(Q)" should likewise read D = d(Q). The same passage also has an unrelated slip: "(D/p)a(F,R)" should be "(D/p)a(F,Q)".
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 859 and confirmed the printed display exactly. The paper's convention is Q = (m, r/2; r/2, n) (p. 856, and again p. 876), and it states on p. 877 that r^2 − 4mn = −4 det(Q). So (det(Q)/p) = (−1/p)((r^2−4mn)/p): the two sides of the printed equality disagree whenever p ≡ 3 mod 4 and d(Q) is prime to p.

I redid the computation. The U_2-part comes from the cosets (pI B; 0 pI) with B symmetric of rank 1 mod p; there are p^2 − 1 of these, which matches the printed Q ≡ 0 value −1 + p^2. It contributes Σ_B e(tr(QB)/p). Writing B = λvv^T with λ ∈ F_p^* and v ∈ P^1(F_p), tr(QB) = λ(mx^2 + rxy + ny^2). The sum is then Σ_v [p·1{Q(v)=0} − 1] = −(p+1) + p·N, where N = 1 + ((r^2−4mn)/p) is the number of projective zeros of a nonzero form. That gives −1 + p((r^2−4mn)/p). A brute-force check over all Q mod p for p = 3, 5, 7, 11 (1822 nonzero Q) matched the discriminant formula every time. The det(Q) formula failed in 1522 cases, all with p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: Q = x^2 + y^2, p = 3 gives −4, not 2.

The second printed expression is right and the first is a sign slip. This is internal to the paper's own conventions: p. 877 fixes det(Q) as the matrix determinant.

Downstream, the argument needs the discriminant. Lemma 8.21 counts F([Q]) by d(Q), and F([Q]) is the set of zeros of Q in P^1(F_p): M^{-1}.Q is p-integral iff Q(v) ≡ 0. §8.8 argues that (D/p) = −1 gives F(Q) = ∅, hence 0 = a(ZF,Q) = (β − β^{-1})a(F,Q), which requires a(X_2F,Q) = −a(F,Q). With det(Q) and p ≡ 3 mod 4 one would get (β + β^{-1}) instead, and the stated hypothesis β^2 ≠ 1 would not suffice. Since the paper defines D in §8.8 as D_Q, the discriminant, the argument goes through. Lemma 8.6 only uses det(Q) ≡ 0, where the sign does not matter.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.3, proof of Lemma 8.6, p. 859; arXiv:1907.08691v1 p. 44, same wording
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We have a(X_2F, Q) = 0 if det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, but a(Z_2F, Q) is a sum over terms of the form a(F, R) with det(R) = 0.
sourceIssues.correction: "... a sum over terms of the form a(X_2F, R) with det(R) ≡ 0 mod p (in fact det(R) = p^2·det(Q))." Here R = M^{-1}.pQ = p·(M^{-1}.Q), and M^{-1}.Q has the same det as Q. So a(X_2F, R) ≡ (det R/p)·a(F, R) = 0 in k, and hence Z_2X_2 = 0 over k.
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 859 and transcribed the proof exactly as printed. It says "det(R) = 0", while the same sentence uses "det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p" for Q. The paper's convention is fixed on the same page: det(Q) = r^2 − 4mn, as in the display for a(U_2F, Q) on p. 859. I recomputed the determinant of every R in the explicit formula for Z_2 on p. 859: for R = (p^2 n, pr, m), det = p^2 r^2 − 4p^2 mn = p^2(r^2 − 4mn). For R = (n+αr+α^2 m, p(r+2mα), p^2 m), det = p^2(r+2mα)^2 − 4p^2 m(n+αr+α^2 m) = p^2(r^2 − 4mn). A random numeric test with 1000 cases also passed. It confirms that the Z-forms M^{-1}.Q keep det(Q), and that M^{-1}.pQ = p·M^{-1}.Q. So det(R) = p^2 det(Q). That is nonzero whenever Q is nondegenerate, e.g. every positive definite index. Read as an integer equation, "det(R) = 0" is false. The argument only needs p | det(R). Then Definition 8.5 gives a(X_2F, R) ≡ (D/p)a(F, R) = 0 mod p, so every term of a(Z_2X_2F, Q) vanishes in k. The candidate's correction and its computation det R = p^2 det Q are both right. One charitable reading exists: since the lemma is "over k", R reduced mod p is a degenerate form over F_p ((0,0,m) or (n+αr+α^2m,0,0)), so its determinant is 0 in k. That is why this is only a notational misprint and not a mathematical error. It is still inconsistent with the explicit "≡ 0 mod p" in the same sentence. arXiv:1907.08691v1 (p. 44, rendered) has word-for-word the same proof, including "det(R) = 0". Downstream, Lemma 8.6 is used only through the identity Z_2X_2 = 0: in the proof on pp. 867–868 (the commutative diagram and Q_2^2F = X_2^2F), on the Siegel.txt text line near 3387 ("because Z_2X_2 = 0"), and at text line 3588. That identity is true and the corrected proof covers it, so no stated result changes.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.4, Theorem 8.10 and its proof, pp. 861–862; arXiv:1907.08691v1 Theorem 8.10, p. 45
sourceIssues.printed: THEOREM 8.10. Let p > 3, let p + 1 ≥ k, and assume that p ∤ k(2k − 1)—so in particular k = 2 and k = p + 1 are admissible values of k. Then the map Θ : H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k+p+1, k+p+1)_{O/ϖ^m}) is injective. In particular, if ΘF = 0, then we must have F = 0. Proof: We may immediately reduce to the case m = 1 and O/ϖ = k. Suppose that F lies in the kernel, so ΘF = 0. After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant. Following [75, Theorem 4.7], it suffices to show that F is not zero on the superspecial locus if it is not divisible by the Hasse invariant. … Hence the restriction to the superspecial points is injective as long has k(p − 1) ≤ p^2 + 1, which holds for k ≤ p + 1. [Checked on the rendered images of pp. 61–62.]
sourceIssues.correction:
The minimal fix is to exclude k = p − 1. The hypotheses become 2 ≤ k ≤ p + 1, k ≠ p − 1 and p ∤ k(2k − 1). Equivalently: 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2 or k = p + 1, with p ∤ k(2k − 1). The bound k ≥ 2 is already implicit, because Prop. 8.9 only defines Θ for k ≥ 2. With this change the printed proof works as it stands.

Either of two alternative fixes also works:
- claim injectivity only on forms not divisible by the Hasse invariant;
- localize at a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal m, which removes the multiples of h. This is the setting where §8.8 actually uses the theorem.
sourceIssues.reason:
Confirmed. k = p − 1 meets every printed hypothesis. p + 1 ≥ p − 1, and k(2k − 1) = (p − 1)(2p − 3) ≡ (−1)(−3) = 3 mod p, so p does not divide it when p > 3.

The spaces H^0(X_1(Q), ω(k,k)) hold all forms, not just cusp forms. §5.2 sets ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b E on the toroidal compactification (the canonical extension; the subcanonical one is written W^sub). Definition 6.1 gives the Hasse invariant h ∈ H^0(X, ω^{p−1}_k), and Lemma 6.2 uses it on X_1(Q).

h has q-expansion 1. Yamauchi [75] v5, Prop. 3.11(2) says so, and the paper relies on it on pp. 865–867: multiplication by A "is the identity on q-expansions".

By Prop. 8.9(1), Θ multiplies each coefficient a_Q by det(Q). Yamauchi's own formula in the proof of his Prop. 3.9 has an extra unit factor (2/3)N^{-2}, which changes nothing. The only coefficient of h sits at Q = 0, and det(0) = 0, so Θh has q-expansion 0. The q-expansion principle (Theorem 8.1) then gives Θh = 0 with h ≠ 0, so Θ is not injective in weight (p − 1, p − 1). For m > 1, ϖ^{m−1}h is a nonzero element of H^0(ω^{p−1}_{O/ϖ^m}), since ω is locally free, and Θ also kills it.

Where the proof fails: the step "after replacing (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1))" turns F = h into F/h = 1, of weight 0. Yamauchi's Theorem 4.7 (v5) does not apply there: it needs k ≥ 2, F nonzero on the superspecial locus and p ∤ k(2k − 1), and p divides 0. His local formula Θ(F)(X) ≡ k(2k − 1)α/9 is 0 at k = 0, matching Θ(1) = 0.

No other value in the range breaks the argument. For 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2, F/h would have negative weight, so no nonzero form is divisible by h. For k = p + 1, the reduction lands in weight 2, which passes. k = p is already excluded by p ∤ k.

arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same Theorem 8.10 (p. 45) with identical hypotheses and proof. Defence attempted and failed. k = p − 1 meets every printed hypothesis:
- p + 1 ≥ p − 1;
- (p − 1)(2p − 3) ≡ (−1)(−3) = 3 mod p, which is nonzero for p > 3;
- Θ is defined in this weight, since Prop. 8.9 needs only k ≥ 2 (take j = k + 2, so j − k = 2 < p − 2 for p ≥ 5).

Two readings that could have rescued the theorem do not apply:
- H^0 means all forms, not cusp forms. Def. 5.3 says ω(a,b) is the canonical extension; cusp forms are written ω(a,b)(−∞).
- The standing weight assumption in Remark 8.2 ("j ≥ 4 or j = k = 2") allows the weight (p − 1, p − 1).

The counterexample:
- Take F = h, the Hasse invariant of Def. 6.1. It lies in H^0(X, ω_k^{p−1}) = H^0(ω(p − 1, p − 1)_k) and pulls back to a nonzero form on X_1(Q).
- Its q-expansion is 1. Yamauchi [75] v5, Prop. 3.11(2), says "H_{p−1}(q) = 1". The paper relies on the same fact on p. 867, where multiplication by a power A of h "is the identity on q-expansions".
- By Prop. 8.9(1), Θh has q-expansion det(0)·1 = 0, so Θh = 0 by Theorem 8.1. For m > 1, ϖ^{m−1}h works the same way.
- This matches the classical picture: Böcherer–Nagaoka give a degree-2 form of weight p − 1 congruent to 1 mod p, and Θ kills it.

Where the proof breaks: the step "replace (k,k) by (k − (p − 1), k − (p − 1))" turns h into the constant 1, of weight 0. There Yamauchi's Thm 4.7 does not apply: it assumes k ≥ 2 and p ∤ k(2k − 1), and p divides 0. His local formula Θ(F)(X) ≡ k(2k − 1)α/9 vanishes at k = 0.

No other value of k in the range fails:
- 2 ≤ k ≤ p − 2: no nonzero form is divisible by h, because the quotient would have negative weight.
- k = p: excluded by p ∤ k.
- k = p + 1: we have Θ(hG) = hΘ(G) on q-expansions, which reduces to weight 2.
- k = 1: Θ is not defined there in the paper.

How far it reaches: the theorem is used only once, in §8.8 on p. 874, where "F − X_2F ∈ M lies in the kernel of Θ … trivial by Theorem 8.10". There M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(2,2)_k)_m (p. 867, with j = 2), so only k = 2 is used, and that case holds. Theorem 8.13 and the main results are therefore unaffected. One detail in the H-h3-0 entry is wrong: k = p + 1 is not used in §8.8. The correction both entries propose (exclude p − 1, keep k ≥ 2) is right and minimal. Theorem 8.10 as stated is still false, so affects = a stated result.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.4, Proposition 8.9(2), p. 861; used in the proof of Proposition 8.25, §8.9, pp. 876–877
sourceIssues.printed: PROPOSITION 8.9. Let p > 3, let j − 2 ≥ k ≥ 2, and let p − 2 > j − k. ... (2) There is a map θ1 : H^0(X1(Q), ω(j,k)_{O/ϖ^m}) → H^0(X1(Q), ω(j + p − 1, k + p + 1)_{O/ϖ^m}) whose action on q-expansions is given by θ1 Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q) con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, where con : Sym^{j−k} ⊗ Sym^2 → Sym^{j−k−2} is the natural SL2(Z)-equivariant projection. Proof: The operator Θ is defined in [75, Proposition 3.9], and the operator θ1 is defined in [75, Proposition 3.12]. [Transcribed from the rendered image of p. 61. Proof of Prop. 8.25, p. 76: "a(θ1 Z^s F, Q) = con(Sym^{j−2}[A]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) + con(Sym^{j−2}[B]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) ... we deduce that β^s a(θ1F,Q) = a(θ1 Z^s F,Q) = 0, and since β ≠ 0, we have a(θ1F,Q) = 0 and θ1F = 0."]
sourceIssues.correction:
Prop. 8.9(2) should read θ1 Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, with no det(Q) factor. Here con is the integral SL2-equivariant projection, which is unique up to a p-adic unit. The target weight (j+p−1, k+p+1) is correct as printed. Deleting det(Q) is the right and minimal correction.

Consequence for the proof of Prop. 8.25. The proof as written only gives a(θ1F,Q) = 0 when (D/p) = 1, through Lemma 8.24. The case (D/p) = −1 is also fine, because there a(F,Q) = β^{-1}a(ZF,Q) = 0. The case p | d(Q) was covered automatically by the printed det(Q), but the correct formula does not cover it, so it needs its own argument.

Fix. Second-transvectant equivariance gives con(ρ(g)x ⊗ gPg^T) = det(g)^2 ρ'(g) con(x ⊗ P). So for det M = p and p-integral P, con(ρ(M)x ⊗ M.P) = p·ρ'(M) con(x ⊗ P) ≡ 0 mod p. By Lemma 8.3, a(θ1ZF,Q) = Σ_S con(ρ(M)a(F,M^{-1}.Q) ⊗ Q) ≡ 0. Hence θ1∘Z ≡ 0 on formal mod-p q-expansions, and θ1F = β^{-1}θ1(ZF) = 0 for every Q at once. With this, Lemma 8.24 and the (D/p) = 1 hypothesis are not needed.

Equivalently, case by case. For p-primitive Q with p | D, F(Q) = {[P]} and βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P), which is killed by the same identity. For Q ≡ 0 mod p, con(· ⊗ Q) ≡ 0.
sourceIssues.reason:
Printed text confirmed on the rendered p. 861. arXiv:1907.08691v1 Prop. 8.9(2) has the identical formula. Its proof of Prop. 8.25 is the same, citing [Yam16] = "ArXiv version from August, 2016", which is Yamauchi 1410.7894v5 (submitted 30 Aug 2016).

(1) The cited source. I downloaded Yamauchi v5. θ_i^k = H_{p−1}·θ̃_i^k, where θ̃_1^k is the projection of KS^{-1}∘∇ onto ω(k1, k2+2) under decomposition (3.31) (see (3.34)). The proof of Prop. 3.12 gives G = H_{p−1}·KS^{-1}∘∇(F) with A_G(T) = Σ_n (1/N)A_{F_n}(T)δ_n ⊗ T. This is linear in T. So the q-expansion of θ1 is pr_1(A_F(T) ⊗ T), with no det(T). Only Θ carries a det(T): "Θ(F)(q) = (2/3)Σ(1/N^2) det(T)A_F(T)q_N^T". The same holds in v8 (Prop. 3.13).

(2) Independent reasons.
(a) θ̃1 involves a single application of ∇, and on the Mumford family d(q^T) contributes one factor of T. So the coefficients are linear in Q, whereas det(Q)·con(a⊗Q) is cubic.
(b) Prop. 8.9(1) and (2) as printed are mutually inconsistent. Yamauchi defines Θ̃ = θ̃_1∘θ̃, and θ has coefficients a_T ⊗ T (his Rem. 3.14). So θ1(θF) = H·ΘF, with coefficients ∝ con(T⊗T)a_T ∝ det(T)a_T. The printed (2), applied in weight (k+p+1, k+p−1), which satisfies the hypotheses, would instead give det(T)^2 a_T.
(c) Weight count. con lands in Sym^{j−k−2}det^{k+2}, and adding the Hasse weight (p−1,p−1) gives the printed target. An extra det(Q) is a shift of (2,2), as Θ shows, and 2 ≢ 0 mod p−1.

(3) The paper's own proof of Prop. 8.25 uses the formula without det(Q): a(θ1Z^sF,Q) = con(Sym^{j−2}[A]a(F,Q) ⊗ Q^∨) + .... Its final "θ1F = 0" silently needs the coefficients with p | D. The printed det(Q) supplies them, but the correct formula does not, so as written the proof has a gap. I checked the repair identity con(Sym[M]x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·Sym[M]con(x⊗P) (second transvectant) by exact rational arithmetic: 900 random trials with p = 5, 7, 11 and det M = p, and it held in every case. I also checked that tv2(Q,Q) = 8det(Q).

Affects: Prop. 8.9(2) is a numbered result and is false as stated. Its only use of the q-expansion formula is the proof of Prop. 8.25. The statement of Prop. 8.25 remains true by the repair, and Thm. 8.11 uses [75, Thm. 3.20], not the formula. Thm. 8.13 and Thm. 9.1 are unaffected. Printed text confirmed on the rendered p. 861 and on arXiv v1 p. 45.

Defence attempts, all of which fail:
(i) Conventions. The paper's weight convention (p. 856: U = Sym^{j−k} ⊗ det^k) and the target weight are exactly those of Yamauchi's θ1, so no reinterpretation is available. The proof simply defers to [75, Prop. 3.12], and [75] is arXiv:1410.7894v5 (ref. list; v1 cites "[Yam16], ArXiv version from August, 2016"). In v5, θ1 = H_{p−1}·θ̃1, where θ̃1 is the projection of KS^{-1}∘∇ onto ω(k1, k2+2) (see (3.34)). The proof of Prop. 3.12 computes A_G(T) := Σ_n (1/N) A_{F_n}(T) δ_n ⊗ T, which is linear in T and has no det(T). The only formula with det(T) is Θ: Θ(F)(q) = (2/3) Σ (1/N^2) det(T) A_F(T) q_N^T.
(ii) Weight count. con(a_Q ⊗ Q) lies in Sym^{j−k−2} det^{k+2}, which is weight (j, k+2). Adding the Hasse weight (p−1, p−1) gives exactly the printed target. A det(Q) factor shifts the weight by (2,2), as Prop. 8.9(1) itself shows ((k,k) → (k+p+1, k+p+1)), and 2 ≢ 0 mod p−1 for p > 3. So the printed q-expansion is that of Θ∘θ1F, not of a form of the stated weight.
(iii) The paper's own computation on p. 876 uses the formula without det(Q), so the authors' actual calculation agrees with the correction.

Hence Prop. 8.9(2) is false as stated. It is not only a typographical slip, because deleting det(Q) opens a hole in a later proof. The only place the q-expansion formula is used is the proof of Prop. 8.25. That proof establishes a(θ1F,Q) = 0 only for (D/p) = 1 (Lemma 8.24), and then concludes "θ1F = 0". With the correct formula, the Q with p | d(Q) are no longer killed by det(Q) ≡ 0, so the proof as written has a gap there.

The gap closes with the GL2-equivariance identity above. That identity also underlies the paper's own claim con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 when AQA^t = p^s Q. I checked it in exact rational arithmetic, using the paper's variance (Q ↦ MQM^T paired with ρ(M), as in a(F,M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q)):

- 1000 SL2 trials confirmed the transformation law.
- tv2(Q,Q) = 8 det Q, as expected.

Other uses: Theorem 8.11 uses θ1 only through [75, Thm 3.20] and restrictions to strata, not through the formula. Prop. 8.9 is never cited by number. The statement of Prop. 8.25 remains true, and Theorem 8.13 and everything downstream are unaffected. Both candidate reports (X-K6-1, H-h3-1) and the prior verdict are confirmed.

sourceIssues.correction: In Proposition 8.9 and Theorems 8.10–8.11, replace the coefficients O/ϖ^m with k = O/ϖ. More generally the results hold over any O-algebra in which p = 0, for example O/ϖ^m with m ≤ e(O/Z_p), by flat base change of Yamauchi's characteristic-p construction. Then drop "We may immediately reduce to the case m = 1" and "It suffices to work over k". When m > e, so that p ≠ 0 in O/ϖ^m (e.g. O = Z_p and m = 2), there is in general no map with weight shift (p+1,p+1) (resp. (p−1,p+1)) acting as stated on q-expansions. A mod-p^m theta operator exists only with a weight shift ≡ 2 mod (p−1)p^{m−1}, which is larger. The candidate's correction (state everything over O/ϖ, i.e. mod p) is right and minimal. Its remark "a larger weight shift would be needed" should be sharpened: the printed statement is false for m > e, not merely unproved.

I confirmed the printed text from the rendered p. 861. The only justification given is the citation of [75], Yamauchi, 'The weight reduction of mod p Siegel modular forms for GSp4'. That source works mod p: its operators involve the Hasse invariant, which exists only in characteristic p. No construction over O/ϖ^m is given for m ≥ 2 with p ≠ 0 in O/ϖ^m, and the claim is false there.

(a) Elliptic analogue. θ does not send forms mod p^2 of weight k to weight k+p+1. Katz's weight congruences show that θf mod p^m has weight ≡ k+2 mod (p−1)p^{m−1} whenever θf ≢ 0 mod p (Chen–Kiming). I checked this for p=5: θE6 is congruent to a form in M_12 = <E4^3, Δ> modulo 5 but not modulo 25.

(b) The Siegel case, computed directly. I coded the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein coefficients from Cohen's H(k−1,N), with checks E4: 13440, 30240; E6: 44352, 166320. Level-1 forms of weight w are spanned by monomials in E4, E6, E10 and E12. I took p=5 and F=E6, which is 5-integral. The hypotheses allow this: Thm 8.10 explicitly admits k=p+1=6, and Prop 8.9 holds with j=8. ΘF is not ≡ 0 mod 5: at T=[[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] the coefficient is (3/4)·44352 = 33264 ≡ 4 mod 5.

For each weight I computed the saturated 5-adic span of the weight-w forms restricted to the 477 matrices T with n,m ≤ 6. Failure of this test is a rigorous obstruction, and a positive control passes. Results:
- ΘE6 ≡ a weight-12 form mod 5, consistent with Böcherer–Nagaoka and Yamauchi.
- ΘE6 is not congruent mod 25 to any 5-integral level-1 form of weight 12, and it also fails in weights 28 and 32.
- It passes mod 25 only in weight 48 = 6+2+2·20. This matches the Chen–Kiming-type shift 2+2p^{m−1}(p−1).
So with O=Z_5 and m=2, the map asserted in Prop 8.9(1) and Thm 8.10 cannot exist at level 1.

At any prime-to-p level, including X_1(Q), a weight-(12,12) form mod 25 with this q-expansion would give a function on the irreducible Igusa tower. Ichikawa/Katz-type weight congruences would then force 12 ≡ 8 (the p-adic weight of ΘE6) mod 20, which is false.

(c) Nothing downstream breaks. The proofs of Thms 8.10 and 8.11 immediately reduce to m=1, and all uses (§8.8, Prop. 8.25 with Thm 8.11) are over k. So the mistake is confined to the stated generality of Prop 8.9 and Thms 8.10–8.11. It is best classed as an error, a false statement for m ≥ 2, rather than a gap. (a) The cited source works only mod p. Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894v5, §3, begins: "In this section we will define various θ-operators on the space of mod p Siegel modular forms". Prop. 3.9 reads: "Recall the Hasse invariant H_{p−1} = det A ∈ H^0(S_{N,p}, ω^{p−1}). Put Θ := H_{p−1}·Θ̃ ... (1) Let F ∈ M_k(Γ(N), F_p) ... (a) Θ(F) ∈ M_{k+p+1}(Γ(N), F_p)". So the construction needs the characteristic-p Hasse invariant and the Frobenius splitting. The other reference, [27] Flander, is also "(mod p)". Nothing in the paper or in its sources builds Θ or θ_1 over O/ϖ^m when p ≠ 0 there.
(b) One partial defence holds. If m ≤ e, then O/ϖ^m = k[ϖ]/(ϖ^m) is flat over F_p, and Yamauchi's maps extend by base change. So the statement is true in that case, but not for general m.
(c) For m > e the statement is false. Example: p ≥ 11, O = Z_p, m = 2, F = the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein series E_4, pulled back to X_1(Q). Take k = 4 and j = 6, which satisfies the hypotheses. Cohen's formula gives a(E_4; n,r,m = 1,1,1) = 13440; my script (vB-X-K6-2/e4.py) also gives 30240 for (1,0,1). So the coefficient of ΘE_4 at Q = [[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] is (3/4)·13440 = 10080 = 2^5·3^2·5·7, a p-unit, and ΘE_4 ≢ 0 mod p.
- Böcherer–Nagaoka (arXiv:1305.0604, Thm 4.1 and Cor. 4.9) show ΘE_4 ≡ F mod p^m with F of weight k+(p−1)p^{m−1} and ρ = det^2. So ΘE_4 is a p-adic Siegel form of weight k+2.
- Suppose G were a mod-p^2 form of weight k+p+1 with the same q-expansion. By the q-expansion principle on the Igusa tower, G and ΘE_4 would agree there, with G transforming by det^{k+p+1} and ΘE_4 by det^{k+2}. Take t a primitive root mod p^2; then t^{p−1} = 1 + p·u with u a unit. This forces p·ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p^2, i.e. ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p, a contradiction.

- A sanity check matches the known mod-p kernel: the coefficients of ΘE_4 above all vanish mod 5 and mod 7, as expected because 4 = p−1 (for p = 5) and 4 = (p+1)/2 (for p = 7).
So the maps in Proposition 8.9 do not exist over O/ϖ^m for m > e. Theorems 8.10 and 8.11 are then ill-posed for such m, since they "reduce to m = 1" a map that does not exist.

- The proof of Theorem 8.13 says (p. 865) "we may work with coefficients over a finite field k = O/ϖ", with M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)_m on p. 867.

- Proposition 8.25 is stated "modulo p" and is combined with Theorem 8.11 on p. 877.
- Remark 8.23 only mentions Θ.
