sourceIssues.printed: Let X = X_1(Q), and denote the rank 1 strata (resp., the supersingular locus, the superspecial locus) by Y, Z, and S, respectively. We are assuming that the restriction of F to Y is nonzero.
sourceIssues.correction:
Read Y as V(h), the closed non-ordinary locus. Then insert: "If F|_Y = 0 then F = hG with G ∈ H^0(X, ω(j−p+1, 3−p)_k), and this group is 0." Also give a reason for "The first term vanishes", which is H^0(X, ω(j−m, 2−m)_k) = 0.

Both follow from one lemma: if a ≥ b and pa − b < 0, then H^0(X, ω(a,b)_k) = 0.

Proof of the lemma, using only what the paper already uses:
1. On each supersingular P^1, ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b with E = O(−1)⊕O(p) and det E = O(p−1). So it is a sum of line bundles of degree at most pa − b < 0, and a section vanishes on Z.
2. Z is cut out in V(h) by s ∈ H^0(ω^m). Dividing by s changes pa − b by −(p−1)m, and dividing by h changes it by −(p−1)^2, so the condition is preserved. By Krull, the section is divisible by every power of s on V(h), and then by every power of h on X, so it is 0.

For (j−p+1, 3−p) we get pa − b = p(j+2−p) − 3 < 0. For (j−m, 2−m) we get pa − b = pj − 2 − (p−1)m < 0.

Both weights also have a < 0. So instead one could restrict to Hecke translates of products of modular curves, where every summand has negative degree on both factors.

(d) Yamauchi (arXiv 1410.7894v8) Thms 4.7 and 4.9 assume f is not identically zero on S(0,0). Nothing there handles forms divisible by h.
(e) Y must be V(h): the second sequence, with twist ω^{−m−(p−1)}, is the sequence for multiplication by h.

TRUTH. With the paper's convention ω(j,k) = Sym^{j−k} ⊗ det^k (p. 856) and the P^1 data it quotes (E = O(−1)⊕O(p), ω = O(p−1)), the top summand degree of ω(a,b) is pa − b. This reproduces the paper's own jp − 2 for weight (j,2). A python check over p ≤ 101 and 4 ≤ j < p−1 confirms pa − b < 0 for both weights. So the lemma above applies. It needs only facts the main argument already uses: Z is a reduced Cartier divisor in V(h) (Koblitz, [70]), and it is the union of P^1s. Theorem 8.11 is therefore true, and the proof is incomplete.

CONSEQUENCES. Theorem 8.11 is used only in the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11"). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17 (p. 845) and then the main Theorem 9.1. None of these is affected once the lemma is supplied. H-h3-11 and X-K6-3 are the same issue; the correction above covers both.

sourceIssues.correction: Replace the appeal to Γ̄ with a change of the local frame (ω1, ω2) of E at the superspecial point X by some g ∈ SL_2(F_p). This is Yamauchi's own device: in the proof of his Theorem 4.9 (arXiv v5; Theorem 3.20 in v1–v3) he uses ρ_r((1 a; 0 1)) with a ∈ F_p. The components F_i are taken in the basis δ_n = ω1^{r−n} ω2^n (ω1∧ω2)^{k2}, so they move by Sym^{j−2} of the frame change. For j − 2 ≤ p − 1 that representation is absolutely irreducible under SL_2(F_p), and F|_X ≠ 0. So some F_p-rational frame gives F_2|_X ≠ 0. Whether θ1(F) vanishes at X does not depend on the frame. The frame change should be F_p-rational, as in Yamauchi, and not an arbitrary element of GL_2(k). Yamauchi's normal form A(X) ≡ (t11 t12; t12 t22) mod m^2 involves a Frobenius twist g^{(p)}, and F_p-rational frame changes keep it. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked against the rendered p. 857 and 861–863 and against Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894 v1–v6. In v5 the cited Theorem 3.20 is Theorem 4.9. It assumes k1 − 3k2 ≢ 0 mod p. The local term of (4.5) at X is −(k1−3k2)/2·t11F0|X − (k1−3k2)/2·t12F1|X − (k1−3)·t22F2|X. In weight (6,2) the first two coefficients vanish and the third is −3, so F_2|_X ≠ 0 is exactly what is needed. The paper's reduction to that case is correct.

Case for the defence. The paper names the right group, SL_2(F_p). The irreducibility argument is correct: if (gv)_2 = 0 for every g, the span of the orbit would be a nonzero invariant subspace inside the hyperplane x_2 = 0. Γ̄ does surject onto SL_2(F_p) because its level is prime to p. Read charitably, "the action of Γ̄" means ρ acting on the coefficients, which mod ϖ factors through SL_2(F_p), and so amounts to a frame change.

Why the justification still fails. On p. 857, Γ̄ is defined only by the q-expansion symmetry a(F, M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q) for M ∈ Γ̄. That symmetry says F is Γ̄-invariant: Γ̄ lies in the level group and acts trivially on X_1(Q) and on F. It gives no action on the fibre of E at a superspecial point in characteristic p. So "applying an element of Γ̄ to F" leaves F_i|_X unchanged in any fixed frame, and the "since the level of Γ̄ is prime to p" clause proves nothing about X. The step actually needed is the frame change. The paper does not state it, but it is standard and appears in the cited source, restricted there to unipotent frame changes. So this is a gap in the exposition, not a false statement. The proposed correction is right and minimal.

Consequences. Theorem 8.11 is used only at the end of the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11, we obtain a contradiction"), and Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 9.1. Weight (6,2) falls inside the range p−1 > j of Theorem 8.13 once p ≥ 11, so the case matters, but the claim F_2|_X ≠ 0 holds with the frame-change argument. Nothing downstream changes.

Side note, a separate citation slip: "[75, Theorem 3.20]" follows the numbering of Yamauchi v1–v3, while "[75, Theorem 4.7]" and the bibliography (v5) follow v4/v5 numbering, where 3.20 is a Lemma and the result is Theorem 4.9.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.5, p. 863. arXiv v1 p. 46 has the same text ("where α and β have non-negative p-adic valuation").
sourceIssues.printed: "We may write the eigenvalues of this polynomial as α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1}, α^{−1}p^{k+j−3}, where α and β have nonnegative p-adic valuation. That means that the coefficient of crystalline Frobenius should have characteristic polynomial X^4 − (α + ···) + (αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}))X^2 + ··· ."
sourceIssues.correction: The expansion 'X^2-coefficient = αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1})' holds when α and β are p-adic units, i.e. in the ordinary case. That is the only case used later, in the 'in particular' of Lemma 8.12. For α, β merely integral, Newton-above-Hodge gives only that the X^2-coefficient has valuation ≥ k−2. That still yields the passage's conclusion that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 863 and confirmed the text.

**The X^2-coefficient.** The polynomial's X^2-coefficient is e_2 = αβp^{k−2} + αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} + 2p^{k+j−3} + α^{−1}βp^{2k+j−5} + α^{−1}β^{−1}p^{k+2j−4}. When α and β are units, every term after the first is O(p^{k−1}), using j ≥ k ≥ 2. So the claim is fine in the ordinary case.

**Counterexample under the printed hypothesis.** Nonnegative valuations do not suffice. Take (j,k) = (4,4), so the Hodge weights are 0, 2, 3, 5, and take p = 5, α = 2·5, β = 3·5^2.
- The Frobenius slopes are {1, 4, 1, 4}. The Newton polygon has vertices (0,1,2,6,10), which lie on or above the Hodge polygon (0,0,2,5,10), and the pairing condition s1+s4 = s2+s3 = 5 holds.
- A python check gives v(e_2) = 2 but v(αβp^2) = 5. So e_2 − αβp^2 has valuation 2, which is less than k−1 = 3.
- The only other labelling with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0 is v(α) = 4, v(β) = 2. It gives v(αβp^2) = 8 and fails in the same way. Labellings with v(β) = −1 are excluded by the printed hypothesis.
- A filtered φ-module with these slopes and Hodge weights exists, since the Newton point lies in B(GSp4, μ).

So the displayed expansion is false in general for non-ordinary forms. The passage's final conclusion, that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral, still holds, because v(e_2) ≥ s1+s2 ≥ k−2.

**Why it affects nothing.** The passage is heuristic ('One expects', 'should'). Lemma 8.12 is proved directly on formal q-expansions. Its 'In particular' is stated only for ordinary forms, where the expansion is correct. The candidate's 'imprecision' is recorded here as an error in a motivational passage. Confidence is medium only on the kind: one could read 'nonnegative valuation' as a slip for 'unit', which would make it a misprint. The mathematics is certain.

sourceIssues.printed: Let m denote the corresponding ideal of the Hecke algebra away from p. Let A denote a nontrivial power of the Hasse invariant of weight k. Then the composite map H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_{O/ϖ^m})^{α,β}_m --A--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})_m --π_β--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})^β_m is injective, where π_β denotes the projection onto the summand where U − β and Q_2 − αβ (equivalently, Z_2 − αβ) are nilpotent.
sourceIssues.correction: 'Let A denote a suitable power of the Hasse invariant of weight k', i.e. a power A^s of the lift A of h^r from Definition 6.1 with p^{m−1} | s, as in Lemma 6.4. Then A has q-expansion ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m and multiplication by A is Hecke-equivariant away from p.
sourceIssues.reason: Definition 6.1 defines h only mod p. A is a noncanonical lift of h^r, and Lemma 6.4 gets Hecke-equivariance of multiplication by A^s on O/ϖ^m-coefficients only when p^{m−1} | s (it cites [32, Thm 6.2.1]). Two things need that equivariance. First, the composite in the theorem is a map between m-localizations. Second, the proof asserts on p. 865 that 'In both results, all of the corresponding maps are equivariant with respect to Hecke operators away from p' to reduce to the socle. For m ≥ 2 and an arbitrary power this equivariance fails: in the GL_2 analogue, multiplication by E_{p−1} mod p^2 does not commute with T_ℓ. The paper's own usage points to the intended hypothesis. The parallel Lemma 8.14 says 'a suitable power'. Theorem 6.17 applies Theorem 8.13 as 'there exists a power A^s of A', with t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), so s = p^{m−1}. So 'nontrivial' is a slip for 'suitable'. Nothing downstream is affected, for three reasons. The application uses s = p^{m−1}. Everything over k = O/ϖ is fine for any power, since h^{rs} has q-expansion 1. And injectivity on O/ϖ^m can in any case be checked on ϖ-torsion, where A acts as h^{rs}.

sourceIssues.printed: Let U denote the action of T on N. Then U satisfies the polynomial U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on the image of M, and so M lies inside the ordinary subspace of N, and so inside N_α ⊕ N_β, where N_γ is the factor of N on which (U − γ) is nilpotent.

sourceIssues.reason: The composition order in 'TU' is wrong, and the correct relation has T applied first. With T = U + ⟨p⟩V on weight-one forms and UV = 1: U(TF) = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩UVF = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩F, so U^2 − UT + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on M. The printed order fails under both possible readings. First, the paper says T acts on N as U, so T(UF) = U^2 F and the relation would give ⟨p⟩F = 0. Second, as formal q-expansion operators, TU = U^2 + ⟨p⟩VU, so U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = ⟨p⟩(1 − VU) ≠ 0. Here VU(Σa_n q^n) = Σ a_{np} q^{np} ≠ F in general. U does not preserve the image of M, so T∘U is not even defined on it. Read as a Hecke polynomial whose coefficient T commutes with U, the intended meaning is clear. The conclusion also holds with the corrected relation: F = ⟨p⟩^{−1}U(TF − UF), so W = M + UM is U-stable with U(W) ⊇ W, hence W is ordinary. This is a notational slip with no effect on the proof.

I checked the page images: the published p. 866 at 110 and 220 dpi, and arXiv v1 p. 48 at 110 dpi. The printed text is as quoted, and arXiv v1 (pp. 48–49) has the same wording.

I redid the computation from the proof's own hypotheses: π_β(F) = (U−α)^m F = 0, so "We are assuming that F = F_α ∈ N_α". U and V are the q-expansion operators, with UV = id and T = U + ⟨p⟩V in weight 1.

(1) Write VF = x_α + x_β in N_α ⊕ N_β. Since U preserves both factors, U(VF) = F ∈ N_α forces Ux_β = 0. U is invertible on N_β because β ≠ 0 (β is an eigenvalue of an invertible matrix). So x_β = 0 and VF ∈ N_α, which is the conclusion the text draws. With "F ∈ N_β" the same step would give VF ∈ N_β instead. So "N_β" must be "N_α".

(2) After the reduction G_α = 0 we have UF = αF. U is injective on N_α and U(VF − α^{-1}F) = F − F = 0, so VF = α^{-1}F. With ⟨p⟩F = αβF this gives ⟨p⟩VF = βF and TF = αF + βF = (α+β)F. That matches the displayed ⟨p⟩VF = αβU^{-1}F_α. The printed VF = βF would force β = α^{-1}, i.e. αβ = 1, since βUF = UVF = F. The reduction explicitly lets ⟨p⟩ act by αβ, which is det ρ̄(Frob_p) and need not be 1. So the ⟨p⟩ has been dropped from the displayed relation.

(3) Write F = Σ a_n q^n. If VF = cF with c ≠ 0, the lowest exponent of VF is p·n0 while that of cF is n0, so n0 = 0 and F is not cuspidal. Comparing constant terms then gives a_0 = c·a_0, so c = 1. With c = α^{-1}, the condition should be "α ≠ 1", not "β ≠ 1".

The candidate's correction is right on all three points. One side remark in its reason is slightly off: VF = βF is compatible with the rest only when αβ = 1, not when α = 1. This does not affect the correction.

The θ argument is unaffected, since θVF = 0 still forces θF = 0. The cusp-form case also still closes. Lemma 8.14 is a warm-up ("a much easier analogue for GL(2)"). The label 8.14 appears nowhere else in the text except at the lemma and its proof heading, and the proof of Theorem 8.13 is separate. So no stated result or later argument changes.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 67: "In the first case, by assumption we know that Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent, and so Q_2 induces an isomorphism of M. On the other hand, the operator Q_2 acts via the formal operator Z_2. In weight τ = (j + k, 2 + k), the corresponding operator Q_2 also acts via Z_2, and so we deduce that Q_2 − αβ acts on M ⊂ N and acts nilpotently. Yet Q_2 only acts invertibly on the ordinary part of N, as can be seen by lifting to characteristic 0." p. 68: "Since the left-hand side is an isomorphism, it follows that Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M, and hence that Z_2 acts invertibly on Z_2 M, and as in the previous argument it follows that Z_2 and hence U is invertible on this space."
sourceIssues.correction: The replacement argument in H-h3-9 is correct, and it is minimal because it uses only identities the paper already states. On M, which has weight (j,2), Lemma 8.3 gives T ≡ U + Z mod p. On N, which has weight τ = (j+t, 2+t), it gives T ≡ U, and Lemma 8.12 gives Q_2 ≡ Z_2. For m ∈ M, Um = T_N m lies in N and Tm lies in M, so Zm = Tm − Um lies in W := Σ_{i≥0} U^i M. This W is a finite-dimensional U-stable subspace of N. The formal identity Z_2 = UZ (p. 859) gives Z_2 M ⊂ UW. Z_2 commutes with U (p. 869; formally, a(Z_2 UF, Q) = a(UZ_2 F, Q), because M^{-1}.pQ is always integral). Hence Z_2 W ⊂ UW, and by induction Z_2^n W ⊂ U^n W. For j > 2, M = Z_2^n M lies in U^n W for every n. For (2,2), Z_2 M = Z_2^{n−1}(Z_2 M) lies in U^n W, using the paper's own equality Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M. In both cases the space lies in ∩_n U^n W, which is the part of W on which U is invertible, and so it lies in N_α ⊕ N_β by Lemma 8.16. The rest of the proof is unchanged, including the injectivity of M → Z_2 M, which uses only (αβ)^2 ≠ 1. The first sentence of the p. 867 passage should therefore be replaced by this argument, and "as in the previous argument" on p. 868 should point to it.
sourceIssues.reason:
This is a genuine gap. The key step, 'Q2 only acts invertibly on the ordinary part of N', is justified only by 'lifting to characteristic 0', and the case (2,2) reuses that step. I redid the computation. For an eigenform of weight (j',k') with Frobenius slopes s1 ≤ … ≤ s4, where s1 + s4 = s2 + s3 = j' + k' − 3, the Hodge weights are 0, k'−2, j'−1, j'+k'−3. The X^2 coefficient is p^{k'−2}·Q2, so Q2 is a unit exactly when s1 + s2 = k'−2. T is a unit exactly when s1 = 0; this uses k' = 2 + t > 2. The slopes (s, k'−2−s, j'−1+s, j'+k'−3−s) with 0 < s ≤ (k'−2)/2 have partial sums s, k'−2, 2k'+j'−3+s and the correct total, so they lie on or above the Hodge polygon. So a Q2-unit eigenform that is not T-ordinary is not excluded by the Galois side. A residual condition does not exclude it locally either. The GL2 analogue: θ^{p−1}f, for f of weight 1 with ρ̄|G_Qp = unr_α ⊕ unr_β, lifts to a non-ordinary crystalline form of weight p², with Hodge–Tate weights {0, (p+1)(p−1)}. Theorem 6.17 uses Hasse powers t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), which can be arbitrarily large. The heuristic in §8.5 (p. 863) does not close the gap. It parametrises the eigenvalues as α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1}, α^{−1}p^{k+j−3} with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0, and writes the X^2 coefficient as αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}). But the term αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} has valuation s1 + s2, which can equal k−2, so 'Q2 unit ⇒ α, β units' does not follow. The obvious formal shortcut also fails. The paper's identity is Z2 = UZ, and Z2 commutes with U, but ZU ≠ UZ formally: a(UF, R) = 0 for non-integral R, so for example the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. So U-nilpotence does not force Z2-nilpotence on N. Likewise 'Z2 and hence U' does not follow, since Z does not act on N. Whether Q2 is invertible only on the ordinary part of all of N remains unproven; the lemma needs only the version on W, which the correction proves. On 'affects', I disagree with the candidate. Under PROTOCOL §18, 'nothing' means the mathematics is right as intended. Here the intended justification fails and the proof needs a new argument, so the right value is 'the proof'. No stated result changes. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true. Its conclusions are used in Lemma 8.17: the statement 'π_β: Z2M → N_β' and M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β (with Lemma 8.16), and on p. 871 'the injectivity of Z2 in Lemma 8.15'. From there they feed Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17, and all of these survive. arXiv v1 has the same passage. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) Charitable reading. "Ordinary part of N" can only mean the U-invertible part. That is how p. 866 uses "ordinary subspace of N" in the GL(2) analogue, and the lemma concludes that U is invertible. The needed claim is therefore: a nonzero generalized Q_2-eigenvalue on N implies U is invertible there.

(2) Lifting to characteristic 0. A lifted eigenform of weight (j+t, 2+t) has Hodge–Tate weights 0, t, j+t−1, j+2t−1. A unit Q_2 means s1 + s2 = t, so the Newton polygon touches the Hodge polygon at vertex 2. Then r|G_Qp has a 2-dimensional crystalline piece V_1 with weights {0, t} and slopes {s, t−s}. Since j−1 ≢ 0 mod p−1, V_1-bar^ss must be unr(α) ⊕ unr(β). U invertible needs s = 0.
- For t = p−1 the defence actually works. Breuil and Berger–Li–Zhu (BLZ) for k = p ≤ p+1 say any positive slope reduces to the irreducible ind(ω_2^{p−1}). The paper supplies none of this.
- But Theorem 8.13 claims every nontrivial Hasse power, and Theorem 6.17 uses t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1), so t can be large.
- For (p²−1) | t and slope s > ⌊(t−1)/(p−1)⌋, BLZ gives V_1-bar = ind(ω_2^t)⊗unr = unr(λ) ⊕ unr(−λ). This is compatible with α = −β, which the hypotheses allow: αβ(α²−1)(β²−1)(α−β)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0 whenever α⁴ ≠ 1.
- Example: p = 5, j = 3, t = 24, α of order 8, β = −α. The slopes are (6, 18, 32, 44) against Hodge (0, 24, 26, 50). The Newton polygon touches at x = 2, so Q_2 is a unit, while v(T) = 6 > 0.

So the Galois side does not rule out Q_2-invertible, non-ordinary eigensystems. Whether they occur globally is still open, and so is the claim for all of N. Hence this is a gap, not an error.

(3) Formal shortcut. Z_2 = UZ, but ZU ≠ UZ. For example, the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. And Z does not preserve N. So "Z_2 and hence U" (p. 868) does not follow by itself.

(4) No nearby statement fills the gap. Lemma 8.16 only gives N = N_0 ⊕ N_α ⊕ N_β. The p. 806 introduction and Remark 8.18 concede that non-ordinary forms do appear.

Consequences. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true (by the correction above), so no stated result changes. Where the lemma is used:
- Lemma 8.17: the map "π_β: Z_2M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β → N_β" (p. 869); "π_β(F) = 0 implies F = F_α ∈ N_α" in the case j > 2; and on p. 871 "the injectivity of Z_2 in Lemma 8.15".
- §8.8 (p. 874 area, "contradicting the injectivity of Z_2: M → N in Lemma 8.15").
- Through these, Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17.
All of them survive. Under PROTOCOL §18 the intended justification fails and a new argument is needed, so 'affects' is "the proof", not "nothing" as H-h3-9 said. C-K6-0 was right to leave the fix open; H-h3-9 supplies it. arXiv v1 has the same text.

sourceIssues.correction: Q_2^3 F = X_2^3 F = X_2 F = Q_2 F, so Q_2F ≠ 0 is an eigenvector of Q_2^2 with eigenvalue 1. Equivalently, since Q_2 is invertible, Q_2^2 F = F. So Q_2^2 − 1 = (Q_2 − 1)(Q_2 + 1) has a nonzero kernel on M, and Q_2 has an eigenvalue λ with λ^2 = 1: F + Q_2F or F − Q_2F is a nonzero ±1-eigenvector. This contradicts αβ being the only generalized eigenvalue, since (αβ)^2 ≠ 1.
sourceIssues.reason: By Definition 8.5, mod p we have a(X_2F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q), so X_2^3 = X_2. By Lemma 8.6, Z_2X_2 = 0. From these, Q_2(Q_2F) = Q_2(X_2F) = X_2^2 F, and Q_2^2 F = F. So Q_2 swaps F and X_2F. Q_2F is a Q_2-eigenvector only if X_2^2F = λX_2F, i.e. only if X_2F = ±F. That fails, for example, when F has nonzero coefficients at forms Q with both signs of (D/p). So as printed the claim is unjustified. The intended conclusion follows at once from what was just computed: Q_2^2 − 1 kills a nonzero vector. The contradiction with (αβ)^2 ≠ 1 therefore stands. The slip is Q_2 in place of Q_2^2 (or 'Q_2 has an eigenvalue'), and the mathematics is right as intended. sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 859, 872, 873 and 874 and checked the text against the page images.

(1) The claim is printed without its key condition. 'There exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p' says nothing about F, and any Q prime to p satisfies it. What the paragraph proves, as its conclusion on p. 874 states, is that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some such Q. The clause 'with a(F,Q) ≠ 0' is missing.

(2) 'In particular' is the wrong connective. Suppose there is a Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and p ∤ det(Q). By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q) ≠ 0, so X₂F ≠ 0 and F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. So the existence claim does not imply F₀ = 0; it contradicts it. F₀ = 0 holds only under the opposite assumption, that every Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 has p | det(Q). In that case every coefficient of X₂F vanishes: either (D/p) = 0 or a(F,Q) = 0, and a(X₂F,Q) = p·a(F,Q) = 0 when Q ≡ 0 mod p. Then X₂F = 0 in characteristic p, so F₀ = 0 because αβ ≠ 0, and ZF = βF + αF₀ = βF.

(3) The same unstated assumption is used again two sentences later. 'By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]' needs (d(Q)/p) = 0 (Lemma 8.21(2), p. 872). That holds for the chosen Q only because of the contrary assumption.

So the printed text states a proof by contradiction without ever stating the contrary assumption, and it misstates what is being proved. Nothing about the conventions makes 'In particular' mean 'suppose not', so the candidate is not a misreading.

On the classification: the missing justification for F₀ = 0 is one line from Definition 8.5 once the assumption is stated. The intended structure is clear from 'we may also assume', from the hint 'F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F', and from the conclusion on p. 874. That fits PROTOCOL §18's definition of a misprint (a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context) better than 'gap'. Classing it as a minor gap would also be defensible.

The mathematics is unaffected once the assumption is restored. Separate problems in the rest of this proof are recorded under other ids: the reversed display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), and the degenerate case d(Q) = 0. Checked on the rendered pages 859 and 872–875 and on arXiv v1 p. 53.

(1) The sentence cannot be read literally. Without "and a(F,Q) ≠ 0", the claim "there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p" is trivial. The words "In particular ... F₀ = 0" also cannot follow from the intended claim. By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p, and we work over k, which has characteristic p. So a Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0 would give X₂F ≠ 0, and hence F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. Read literally, the connective "In particular" states the opposite of what is true.

(2) The defence fails, but the charitable reading works. The phrase "we may also assume" only makes sense as the contrary hypothesis in a proof by contradiction. In weight (2,2), X₂F = 0 is exactly equivalent to "a(F,Q) = 0 for all Q with p ∤ D". The rest of the paragraph uses this hypothesis without saying so, in both weights. "By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]" needs (D/p) = 0 for the minimal Q, which holds only under the contrary hypothesis. Otherwise Lemma 8.21 allows 0, 1 or 2 classes. The paragraph ends in a contradiction: β²a(F,Q) = 0 when j > 2 and β ≠ 0, or β² = 1 in weight (2,2). The authors then state the conclusion on p. 874: "We may therefore assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p." So the intended meaning is clear from context. The only step the reader must supply, contrary hypothesis ⇒ X₂F = 0 ⇒ F₀ = 0, follows at once from Definition 8.5 and αβ ≠ 0. This makes it an expository misprint (a missing clause and the wrong connective), not a substantive gap.

(3) Downstream use. The conclusion of this step is used in §8.9 (Theorem 8.22(1), weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4). There, (D/p) = −1 is excluded and "Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1", which silently needs (D/p) ≠ 0, i.e. p ∤ D, from this step. §8.8 (weight (2,2)) argues on its own through Theorem 8.10 and does not use the conclusion. Theorem 8.22 feeds Theorem 8.13 via Lemma 8.17. Once the passage is read as intended, the mathematics of this step is right, so nothing is affected. The separate issues in the same argument, recorded as other candidates, are not part of this finding: the degenerate or minimal-discriminant case, and the ρ(M_Q) versus ρ(M_P)⁻¹ display.

Since β ≠ 0 and a(F,Q) ≠ 0, it gives a(F,P) ≠ 0. The next sentence then works unchanged: if P = pR, then a(F,P) = a(UF,R) = α·a(F,R), so a(F,R) ≠ 0. So does the rest of the proof. sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the display on the rendered page image; it reads exactly as quoted.

Conventions, from pp. 856–858: M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T. ρ = Sym^{j−k} is extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U). Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P) with M_P.P = Q.

I redid the computation. Normalise Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]] with m a unit, p | r and p | n; this is the case (D/p) = 0, where ℱ(Q) has one element. Then:
- P = M_P^{-1}.Q = [[pm, r/2],[r/2, n/p]], with M_P = diag(1,p).
- When P is p-primitive (v_p(n) = 1), M_Q = diag(p,1) gives M_Q.Q = P.
- So M_Q·M_P = pI, as the paper itself says on p. 874 ("ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) ... zero in higher weight").

With ρ = Sym^{j−2}, the paper's own Z-identity gives ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P). In characteristic p and weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4, this is 0. So the first printed equality, a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), would force a(F,P) = 0. That is exactly the opposite of what the next sentence needs: it uses a(F,P) ≠ 0 to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR. No step in the text justifies that equality. It holds only in weight (2,2), where ρ is trivial and ρ(pI) = 1. Even taken at face value, the printed line would not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 when j ≥ 4, because ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2}(diag(p,1)) is singular mod p.

The corrected line βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) follows directly from the paper's identity. It gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in all weights. The later chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P)a(F,Q) is fine, because both M_P M_Q and M_Q M_P equal pI.

The candidate also says [Q] ∈ ℱ(P) (needed to define M_Q) is only cited afterwards. This is harmless: Lemma 8.20 has no p-primitivity hypothesis. It does not affect the finding.

This is a real but local slip. Theorem 8.22, Theorem 8.13 (via Lemma 8.17) and the reduction to Q with D prime to p in §§8.8–8.9 all hold once the one-line fix is made. No later result depends on the wrong identity. arXiv v1 (p. 53) has the same text. I checked the display on the rendered page images, both the Duke version (p. 873) and arXiv v1 (p. 53). It reads exactly as quoted.

The paper's conventions:
- M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T (p. 857).
- ρ = Sym^{j−k}, extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U) (p. 857).
- Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P), with M_P.P = Q.
- a(F, γ.Q) = ρ(γ)a(F,Q) holds only for γ ∈ Γ̄, not for matrices of determinant p.

Defence attempts. None of them survives.
(a) The identity on p. 872 expresses a(ZF,Q) in terms of a(F,P), not the other way round. Nothing in §8 gives a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q).
(b) One could read the display as a garbled form of the identity at P, namely β·a(F,P) = a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). That needs ℱ(P) = {[Q]}. But this uses P being p-primitive, which the very next sentence derives from the display, so that reading is circular. It also puts β on the other side.
(c) The only other possible source is the Γ̄-equivariance a(F, M_Q.Q) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) applied wrongly to M_Q ∈ 𝒮. That has no Z in it, so it does not produce the display either.

The printed display is false in weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4.
- With ℱ(Q) = {[P]}, the only term in Lemma 8.3 comes from M_P, with P := M_P^{-1}.Q.
- The adjugate pM_P^{-1} is an integral matrix of determinant p, and it sends Q to P. So in the coefficient identity at P we may take M_Q = pM_P^{-1} (writing pM_P^{-1} = s'γ with s' ∈ 𝒮 and γ ∈ Γ̄ gives ρ(s')a(F, s'^{-1}.P) = ρ(pM_P^{-1})a(F,Q)). Then M_Q M_P = M_P M_Q = pI. The paper says the same on p. 874: "ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) is the identity in weight (2,2) and zero in higher weight".
- Hence ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P), which is 0 in characteristic p when j ≥ 3.
- So the first printed equality would force a(F,P) = 0, the opposite of what the next sentence needs (a(F,P) ≠ 0, to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR).
- The printed conclusion a(F,P) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) does not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 either: ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2} of a matrix of determinant p is singular mod p.

In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, and the printed line reduces to the true a(F,P) = a(ZF,Q) = β·a(F,Q). So this looks like the weight-2 line with ρ(M_Q) inserted wrongly. It is a false step, not a mere index slip, so I class it as an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The corrected line gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in every weight, and the rest of the proof survives:
- the minimality argument;
- ℱ(P) = {[Q]}, from Lemma 8.20, which has no primitivity hypothesis, and Lemma 8.21;
- the chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q), which is 0 for j > 2 and a(F,Q) for j = 2. This is fine because both products are pI, even though the printed order ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P) is reversed.

Nothing else in the paper uses the wrong identity. §8.8 and §8.9 start from the output of this proof ("a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p"). Theorem 8.13, which follows via Lemma 8.17, and Theorem 8.22 itself remain true.

On 'affects': X-K7-4's "nothing" understates it, because the printed step actually fails for j ≥ 4. H-h3-7's "the proof" is right: the proof is broken as written, it is repaired locally in one line, and no stated result changes.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.7, proof of Theorem 8.22 (first step, the minimal-discriminant choice), p. 873. Also the statement of Theorem 8.22 on p. 873, and Theorem 8.13 on pp. 864–865
sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 8.22 (p. 73): "Suppose that F = Σ a(F,Q)q^Q is a Siegel modular q-expansion of weight σ = (j,2) in characteristic p, where p − 1 > j. (1) Let σ = (j,2) with j ≥ 4, and suppose that UF = αF and ZF = βF for some α, β with αβ(β^2 − 1) ≠ 0. Then F = 0. (2) Let σ = (2,2), and suppose that F = F_α + F_0, where UF_α = αF_α, X_2F = αβF_0, and ZF = βF + αF_0 for some α, β with αβ(β^2 − 1)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≠ 0. Then F = 0." Proof (p. 73): "… Hence, if F ≠ 0, then there exists a p-primitive form Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0. Without loss of generality, assume that Q is a p-primitive form of minimal discriminant with a(F,Q) ≠ 0. By Lemma 8.21, 𝓕(Q) consists of a single class [P]. It follows that a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). If P is not p-primitive, then P = pR for some R, and then a(F,R) ≠ 0, contradicting the minimality of Q (note that P and Q have the same discriminant). Hence P is also p-primitive."
sourceIssues.correction:
The minimal fix keeps Theorem 8.22 as stated. It is the fix X-K7-5 proposes. Add one line before, or in place of, the minimal-discriminant step:

"If a(F,Q) = 0 for every Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p, then ΘF = 0 in weight (2,2), resp. θ1F = 0 in weight (j,2), since both operators multiply the Q-th coefficient by det(Q). Hence F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 (k = 2, p > 3), resp. Theorem 8.11 (p − 1 > j ≥ 4)."

This makes the descent over p-primitive forms unnecessary, and it also covers the constant-term case. Both theorems are already in the paper, and their hypotheses are exactly those of Theorem 8.22.

Acceptable alternatives:
- Add cuspidality to Theorem 8.22, i.e. a(F,Q) = 0 for degenerate Q. This holds in the application, since §6.4 and Theorem 6.17 use H^0(X1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)).
- Take Q of minimal nonzero |d|, and dispose of an F supported on degenerate Q by the Θ/θ1 argument above.

The α ≠ β route suggested in H-h3-8 is not recommended:
- α ≠ β is not a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22. It comes only from Theorem 8.13.
- For a smaller Γ̄ the Γ̄-classes of degenerate forms can cycle under Z.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has word-for-word the same text (§8.7, Theorem 8.22), and the same undecorated Theorem 8.13.

Where the gap is:
- §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set X to be all positive semidefinite Q, so degenerate Q are included.
- The statement of Theorem 8.22 assumes only "a Siegel modular q-expansion". It does not assume cuspidality, and it does not assume α ≠ β.
- If some degenerate coefficient is nonzero, the minimal |d| is 0. Then R = P/p also has d = 0, and minimality gives no contradiction.

I checked the candidate's example myself. Take S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]} and P = adj(M).Q, with Q = diag(c,0) and p ∤ c.
- Only M = diag(1,p) gives an integral P, namely P = diag(pc,0) = pQ. So R = Q.
- The relations are then β·a(F,Q) = ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,pQ) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q).
- In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, so this gives (β − α)a(F,Q) = 0.
- In weight (j,2), ρ(diag(1,p)) reduces mod p to the projection onto f1^{j−2}. The stabiliser [[1,b],[0,1]] fixes the same line. So if α = β, the relations are consistent and give no contradiction.
- The hypotheses of Theorem 8.22 are αβ(β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (1) and αβ(β^2−1)(α^2β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (2). Neither includes α ≠ β.

The step before this one has the same problem. "If F ≠ 0 there is a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" fails when only a(F,0) ≠ 0, since 0 = p·0. The lemma 8.14 proof on p. 866 handles the analogous constant-term case explicitly ("β ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form"), but Theorem 8.22 does not. The candidate's (−∞) observation is also correct: p. 865 prints the space without (−∞), while pp. 845–846 have it.

Impact: the application is cuspidal, so Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and 9.1 are not affected. The alternative fix above also appears to prove Theorem 8.22 as literally stated for genuine forms. So the result stands, but the written proof has an unhandled case. The affects value "the proof" is right.

A separate slip in the same passage: the display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) is valid only when j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)a(F,P) = 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) = β·a(F,Q) ≠ 0. The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874 and is identical in arXiv v1. The defence fails:

1. Degenerate forms are included. §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set 𝒳 to be all positive semidefinite Q.
2. "Siegel modular q-expansion" occurs only in Theorem 8.22 and is never defined. It must mean the q-expansion of a genuine form, since the proof then uses Theorem 8.10 and Lemma 8.15. Nothing in the statement makes F cuspidal. The spaces M and N (p. 867) and the display of Theorem 8.13 (p. 865) are printed without (−∞).
3. No reading of "minimal discriminant" rescues the step:
   - Minimal |d|: this is 0 whenever some degenerate p-primitive Q has a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
   - Minimal v_p(d), or minimal nonzero |d|: the case where every p-primitive Q in the support is degenerate is still left over.

I checked the failure by exact computation (degen.py in my work directory; S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]}):
- Take p = 5, 7, 11 and Q = c·ℓℓ^T with p ∤ c.
- Exactly one M ∈ S gives an integral P = M^{-1}.Q, as Lemma 8.21 says.
- In every case P = p·R with d(R) = 0 = d(Q). For example, Q = diag(c,0) gives P = pQ.
- So a(F,R) ≠ 0 does not contradict minimality.
- For Q = diag(c,0) the relations reduce to β·a(F,Q) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q). In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0 this reads (β − α)·a(F,Q) = 0. That is no contradiction unless α ≠ β, and α ≠ β is not among the hypotheses of Theorem 8.22.

The Q = 0 subcase (X-K7-5) is also not addressed: "a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" need not exist if only a(F,0) ≠ 0. It is excluded anyway:
- In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0: a(ZF,0) = (p+1)·a(F,0) ≡ a(F,0), so (β − 1)·a(F,0) = 0 and a(F,0) = 0.
- In weight (j,2): a(F,0) is Γ̄-invariant in Sym^{j−2}. That representation is irreducible and nontrivial for SL2(F_p), and Γ̄ surjects onto SL2(F_p) (proof of Theorem 8.11). So a(F,0) = 0.

Consequences. The step's only output is "a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q with p ∤ D" (p. 874).
- §8.8, weight (2,2), does not use it. That argument treats every D directly: (D/p) = −1 is killed by β² ≠ 1, then Θ(F − X2F) = 0, Theorem 8.10 applies, and Lemma 8.15 finishes.
- §8.9 uses it only to meet the hypothesis of Proposition 8.25 (recap on p. 876; "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11", p. 877). If no Q with p ∤ det Q carries a nonzero coefficient, then θ1F = 0 trivially and Theorem 8.11 still gives F = 0.

So Theorem 8.22 holds as stated for genuine forms, and Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and the main results are unaffected. In the application F is in any case cuspidal (§6.4, p. 845). Only the written proof has an unhandled case.

Remark 8.23 says a Θ-kernel argument would need a new theorem in nonparallel weight. Theorem 8.11 is in fact enough, because ΘF = 0 implies θ1F = 0.

A separate slip in the same passage: a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) holds only for j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)·a(F,P) ≡ 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from β·a(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)·a(F,P).

sourceIssues.printed: 8.9. The case σ = (j,2) with j ≥ 4 / We may assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0, where Q is p-primitive and D = d(Q) is nonzero. If (D/p) = −1, then a(ZF,Q) = 0, contradicting the nonvanishing of a(F,Q) and the identity ZF = βZ. Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1.
sourceIssues.correction: "the identity ZF = βZ" should read "the identity ZF = βF". Optionally, "D = d(Q) is nonzero" can be clarified to "D = d(Q) is nonzero mod p (prime to p)". That second change only tidies loose wording; it is not a misprint.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 874 at 130 dpi and read the page image. The candidate's quotation is exact. The phrase 'ZF = βZ' makes no sense as printed: an operator is set equal to a scalar times an operator, applied to nothing. The argument needs the eigen-identity ZF = βF, which is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(1) (p. 873: 'suppose that UF = αF and ZF = βF for some α, β with αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0'). The proof then says 'thus have the equalities UF = αF, ZF = βF.'

I redid the argument. Page 72 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈F(Q)} ρ(M_P) a(F,P). Lemma 8.21(1) says that when Q is p-primitive with (D/p) = −1, F([Q]) is empty, so a(ZF,Q) = 0. With ZF = βF this gives β·a(F,Q) = 0. Since β ≠ 0 (from αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0), we get a(F,Q) = 0, the stated contradiction. So the intended text is certainly βF.

On 'D is nonzero': the argument also has to rule out (D/p) = 0 before 'Hence (D/p) = 1'. That is supplied by the first part of the proof (p. 873: 'there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p') and the recap on p. 874 ('a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p'). In this characteristic-p setting, 'nonzero' is naturally read as nonzero mod p. So this part is imprecise wording rather than a misprint, and the substance of the candidate is the βZ → βF typo.

arXiv:1907.08691v1 (§8.9, p. 54 there) has the identical text: 'D = d(Q) is non-zero … the identity ZF = βZ.'

Effect on results: none. The intended step is correct and immediate from Lemma 8.21(1), the p. 872 identity and the hypothesis ZF = βF with β ≠ 0. Theorem 8.22, and through Lemma 8.17 Theorem 8.13 and the results that depend on it, are unaffected.

sourceIssues.printed: We may assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0, where Q is p-primitive and D = d(Q) is nonzero. [...] Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1. The action of Γ̄ ⊂ SL2(Z) on binary quadratic forms of discriminant D has a finite orbit which may be identified with a ray class group.
sourceIssues.correction: '... has finitely many orbits, and the (finite) set of orbits may be identified with a ray class group.'
sourceIssues.reason: Γ̄ is 'the congruence subgroup of SL2(Z) defined in [67]' (p. 857), so it is infinite. The forms here are positive semidefinite with D = r^2 − 4mn ≠ 0, so they are positive definite. The stabiliser in SL2(Z) of a positive definite form is finite (order at most 6), so every Γ̄-orbit is infinite. What is finite, and carries the class-group structure, is the set of Γ̄-orbits (classes). The next paragraph (p. 875) uses exactly that when it says the ray class group 'is partitioned by this process Q → {P,R} into a finite number of cyclic orbits'. The intended meaning is clear, so this is a wording slip.

sourceIssues.correction: Read "a(X_2F,Q) is equal to (D/p)a(F,Q)" and "has D = d(Q) (the discriminant r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the page images at 130 dpi and the printed text is as quoted above.

(1) a(F,R): nothing called R is defined in §8.8. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) gives a(X_2F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p. The next display also uses a(F,Q) on the right: a(ZF,Q) = βa(F,Q) + β^{-1}(D/p)a(F,Q). So "R" is a plain typo for "Q".

(2) det versus discriminant. By §8.2 (p. 856), Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]], so det(Q) = mn − r^2/4. The paper itself writes "con(Q⊗Q^∨) = r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)" on p. 877, and defines d(Q) as the discriminant on p. 872. That gives (det Q/p) = (−1/p)(D/p), which is wrong for p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: p = 3 and Q = I. Then x^2 + y^2 has no zeros in P^1(F_3), D = −4, (D/3) = −1, but (det Q/3) = +1. The paragraph defines D as the discriminant two lines earlier and relies on Lemma 8.21 (p. 872, stated for d(Q)) to get a(ZF,Q) = 0 when (D/p) = −1. So "D = det(Q)" contradicts its own definition.

I recomputed the Hecke symbol. The rank-one cosets B = λvv^T (λ ∈ F_p^*, v ∈ P^1(F_p)) contribute Σ_v Σ_λ e(λQ[v]/p) = p·#{zeros of Q in P^1(F_p)} − (p+1). This equals −1 + p((r^2−4mn)/p) when Q ≢ 0, and p^2 − 1 when Q ≡ 0. That matches the second expression in Lemma 8.4, so the symbol in X_2 really is the discriminant symbol. This confirms the correction and shows that the paper's first expression (det(Q)/p) is the same slip. One caveat on the candidate's reasoning: Definition 8.5 calls D "the determinant", so the §8.8 wording follows that loose usage. The usage is still wrong against p. 877.

arXiv 1907.08691v1 §8.8 has the same text: "is equal to (D/p)a(F, R), where D = D_Q is the discriminant of Q" and "the only Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 have D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". The only differences are "have" for "has" and "that" for "then". Definition 8.5 and Lemma 8.4 read the same in v1 as well.

sourceIssues.correction:
Replace "F − X₂F ∈ M" by the statement that F − X₂F is (the q-expansion of) a section of weight (p+1, p+1), and apply Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1. The step works as follows.

1. Lemma 8.12 in weight (2,2) gives X₂F = Q₂F − Z₂F. Here Q₂F ∈ M, and Z₂F is the q-expansion of Q₂(hF) ∈ H⁰(X₁(Q), ω(p+1,p+1)_k), where h is the Hasse invariant: in weight (p+1,p+1) ≠ (2,2), Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂, and Lemma 8.8 gives the action.
2. So F − X₂F is the q-expansion of hF − h·Q₂F + Q₂(hF), a section of weight (p+1,p+1). When A = h this is simply "F − X₂F ∈ N".
3. The coefficients of F − X₂F vanish unless det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, so Θ(F − X₂F) = 0.
4. Theorem 8.10 applies with k = p+1, since p ∤ (p+1)(2p+1). It gives F = X₂F. Then Z₂F = Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, which contradicts Lemma 8.15 as printed.
5. The contradiction can also be reached without Lemma 8.15. Formally UX₂ ≡ 0, since a(UX₂F, Q) = p·a(F, pQ). So F = X₂F gives 0 = UF = αF_α, hence F = F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F = (αβ)⁻¹F, which is impossible because αβ ≠ 1.

Replacing M by N alone is not a minimal correction. Theorem 8.13 allows A = h^s for any s ≥ 1, and then N has weight 2 + s(p−1), which is beyond the range of Theorem 8.10 when s ≥ 2. So N has to be taken with A = h, or equivalently one uses the weight-(p+1) section in step 2.

Alternatively, reduce Theorem 8.13 to s = 1. Multiplication by h^{s−1} is injective and is the identity on q-expansions, and it commutes with U, with Q₂ = Z₂ and with the Hecke operators away from p. Hence it commutes with π_β, so π_β∘h^s = h^{s−1}∘(π_β∘h).

Rendered pages checked: p. 874, and for context p. 859, 861, 864, 865, 867 and 868.

1. F ∈ M. The F of Lemma 8.17(2) is obtained inside M by applying Q_2 − αβ and T − α − β. The last sentence of §8.8 uses "injectivity of Z_2 : M → N", which needs F ∈ M.

- Membership: X_2F = Q_2F − Z_2F ∈ N. Lemma 8.12's computation gives Q_2 ≡ p^{j−2}X_2 + Z_2 ≡ Z_2 mod p in weight (p+1, p+1).

- Kernel of Θ: the vanishing of Θ(F − X_2F) holds under the paper's own conventions for (D/p) and det. When p | D we have det ≡ 0, since det = (4mn − r²)/4.
- General powers: the reader's reduction from h^s to h is valid. I also give a direct alternative (b) above. The example Θ(G^p) = 0 in weight (2p, 2p) shows the extra step is needed for s ≥ 2: Theorem 8.10 fails outside k ≤ p+1.

6. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text on p. 53. Theorem 8.10 there also lists k = 2 and k = p+1 as admissible.

Unrelated misprint in the same paragraph: "(D/p)a(F, R)" should be "(D/p)a(F, Q)". Rendered and read: pp. 859–874 and v1 p. 53.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.

(i) X₂ is not an operator on M. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) defines X₂ only as a formal operator on q-expansions. Mod p it is the twist by (D/p) ≡ (−4det Q)^{(p−1)/2}, so it agrees with ±Θ^{(p−1)/2}, which raises the weight. On M only Q₂ = Z₂ + X₂ acts (p. 867: "the operator Q₂ acts on M either as Z₂ or as Z₂ + X₂"). The one place the paper puts X₂F in M is the proof of Lemma 8.15, under the opposite hypothesis Z₂F = 0. In the proof of Lemma 8.17(2) (p. 870) the paper itself writes X₂F = (0, 0, αβF₀) ∈ N₀ ⊂ N, not in M.

(ii) The claim cannot be justified, and the principle it would need is false. Take any F ∈ M.
- If X₂F ∈ M, then Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, so X₂F = 0 by the injectivity of Z₂ on M (Lemma 8.15).
- But at this point the proof has F with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q whose discriminant is prime to p. Since (D/p) = −1 was just excluded, (D/p) = 1, so a(X₂F,Q) = a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- So "F − X₂F ∈ M" is equivalent to the contradiction the proof is looking for. It cannot be obtained without already finishing the proof. (Because this is a proof by contradiction, no concrete false instance exists, but the inference fails.)
- Moreover, X₂(M) ⊂ M would force X₂M = 0. Every F ∈ M would then be supported on det ≡ 0, so ΘF = 0, so F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 with k = 2. Hence X₂ preserves M only when M = 0, and M ≠ 0 here.

(iii) Reading "M" as a slip for "N" (the paper views M ⊂ N "by abuse of notation", p. 867) works only when N has weight ≤ p+1, that is when A = h. Theorem 8.10's remark "so in particular k = 2 and k = p+1 are admissible" fits that intent. But Theorem 8.13 allows any nontrivial power, and Theorem 6.17 (pp. 845–846) invokes it with a power of weight t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1). In weight (2p, 2p), Θ is not injective: Θ(G^p) = 0 for G of weight (2,2), since det(pQ) ≡ 0. So an extra step is needed, and the text is not a pure misprint. Since it is not a slip with a clear intended meaning, I class it as an error (a step that fails) rather than a gap; "gap" would also be defensible.

THE REPAIR, checked step by step.
- Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂ + X₂ in weight (2,2), and Q₂ ≡ Z₂ in weight (p+1,p+1), where the p-power terms vanish mod p.
- a(F − X₂F, Q) = 0 when (D/p) = 1 (the two coefficients cancel) and when (D/p) = −1 (a(F,Q) = 0 was just shown).
- D = −4·det, so (D/p) = 0 exactly when det ≡ 0. Hence Θ(F − X₂F) = 0.
- Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1 gives F = X₂F, and the printed ending then goes through.

WHERE IT IS USED. §8.8 is the only place Theorem 8.10 is used; Remark 8.23 refers only to an analogue of it. Through Lemma 8.17(2), §8.8 gives Theorem 8.13 in weight (2,2). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17, which feeds §9 (the weight (2,2) modularity lifting, including the abelian-surface application). With the repair, every stated result stays true.

Both readers are right. X-K7-8's correction (A = h, reduce A^s to A, F − X₂F ∈ N, Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1) is correct, and so is H-h3-5's.

So Lemma 8.15's injectivity of M → Z_2M applies, and the chain Theorem 8.13 → Theorem 6.17 → main theorems is not affected by this step. (Other steps in the same paragraph have their own candidates, H-h3-5 and X-K7-8.)

(b) Why it is still a gap. Theorem 8.22(2) is stated for any Siegel modular q-expansion with those identities, with α and β chosen afresh subject only to αβ(β²−1)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0. Lemma 8.15 needs α and β "as in Theorem 8.13", which also requires α ≠ β, α² ≠ 1 and the Galois setting, and it needs F in the localized (α,β)-part M, where "the only generalized eigenvalue of Q_2 is αβ" (p. 868). Neither is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(2). The factor α²β² − 1 in 8.22(2) matches the remark on p. 868 that Lemma 8.15 is "the point … which uses (αβ)² ≠ 1". So the authors were relying on Lemma 8.15's argument, but the proof cites the lemma, and the lemma's hypotheses do not hold for a general F.

- Then UF_0 = 0 and Z_2F = αβF_α, which gives (Z_2 + X_2)F = αβF.
- If Z_2F = 0, then F = F_0 and X_2F = αβF, which forces F = 0 since αβ ≠ ±1.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.9, paragraph before Lemma 8.24, p. 875; arXiv v1 p. 54 has the same text ('neighbours')
sourceIssues.printed: on which this operation takes a binary quadratic form to its two nearest neighbors (if the orbit has fewer than two elements, this pair of neighbors may have multiplicity).
sourceIssues.correction: '(if the orbit has at most two elements, this pair of neighbors may have multiplicity)', i.e. 'fewer than three'
sourceIssues.reason: Each class has exactly two neighbours counted with multiplicity (Lemma 8.21(3)), and the relation is symmetric (Lemma 8.20). So each orbit is a cycle, and a class's two neighbours are its two cyclic neighbours. In a cycle of size 1 both neighbours are Q itself; the proof of Lemma 8.21 gives the example of class number 1. In a cycle of size 2, {Q,P}, both neighbours of Q are P. In class-group terms, the neighbours of c are c[𝔭] and c[𝔭]^{-1}, and these coincide when [𝔭] has order 2. So the pair has multiplicity exactly when s ≤ 2. The printed condition 'fewer than two' leaves out s = 2. The printed sentence is not false as it stands (it says 'may'), but its threshold is off by one. The later argument (Lemma 8.24) works for every s, so nothing depends on this.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.9, proof of Proposition 8.25, p. 876, the sentence right after the first display. arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55, has the same text word for word: "Once we have this, we deduce that β^s a(θ1 F, Q) = a(θ1 Z^s F, Q) = 0, and since β ≠ 0, we have a(θ1 F, Q) = 0 and θ1 F = 0." v1 also has the same statement of Prop. 8.25, including the unused hypothesis on a(F,Q).
sourceIssues.printed: We claim that con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 for any x ∈ Sym^{j−2}V, where V = k^2. Once we have this, we deduce that β^s a(θ₁F, Q) = a(θ₁Z^sF, Q) = 0, and since β ≠ 0, we have a(θ₁F, Q) = 0 and θ₁F = 0.
sourceIssues.correction:
Replace "we have a(θ₁F,Q) = 0 and θ₁F = 0" with an argument that covers every Q.

(i) Q with (d(Q)/p) = +1: Lemma 8.24 applies to each such Q, with its own s, A and B, so a(θ₁F,Q) = 0.

(ii) Q with (d(Q)/p) = −1: F(Q) is empty (Lemma 8.21), so βa(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = 0 and a(F,Q) = 0.

(iii) Q with p | d(Q): this case needs an actual argument. The coefficients do NOT vanish because of a det(Q) factor. That factor in Prop. 8.9(2) is itself wrong (H-h3-1): θ₁ has coefficients con(a_Q ⊗ Q). The fix is as follows.
- If Q ≡ 0 mod p, then con(a(F,Q) ⊗ Q) ≡ 0.
- Otherwise F(Q) = {[P]}. Then βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P), where Q = M_P.P = p^{-1}M_P P M_P^T.
- GL₂-equivariance of the contraction gives con(Sym^{j−2}[M]x ⊗ M.P) = det(M)·Sym^{j−4}[M]con(x ⊗ P). This is ≡ 0 mod p because det M = p.

Hence θ₁F = 0.

A shorter fix: the same identity, applied to each term of a(ZF,Q) = Σ_S ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q), shows θ₁∘Z ≡ 0 on mod-p formal q-expansions. So θ₁F = β^{-1}θ₁ZF = 0 at once.

The hypothesis "F has a nonzero coefficient a(F,Q) where (D/p) = 1" is not used. The candidate's step (iii), "a(θ₁F,Q) = det(Q)·con(…) ≡ 0", depends on the wrong det(Q) and has to be replaced as above.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the text against the rendered pages 861 and 874–877.

DEFENCE. Two parts of the missing step are routine.
- The Q in the proof is generic. Lemma 8.24 is stated for any Q with (D/p) = 1, and the proof never uses the Q from the hypothesis. So the step from one Q to all Q with (D/p) = +1 can be read charitably.
- The (D/p) = −1 case is in the recap paragraph just before the proposition: a(ZF,Q) = 0, which with ZF = βF gives a(F,Q) = 0.
- With the paper's own printed Prop. 8.9(2), θ₁ Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q)con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, the p | d(Q) coefficients would also vanish trivially. So under the paper's printed conventions this would be only a terse omission.

WHY THE DEFENCE FAILS. The det(Q) factor is wrong.
- In Yamauchi (1410.7894, the cited [75]; a local copy of v8 is in lit-errata), θ₁ = H_{p−1}·θ̃₁, where θ̃₁ is a projection of KS^{-1}∘∇. The q-expansion there is A_G(T) = (1/N)A_f(T) ⊗ T, which is linear in T. Only Θ carries det(T).
- The weight count agrees: first order gives +(0,2), and the Hasse invariant gives +(p−1,p−1).
- The paper's own display on p. 876 also has no det(Q).
- This is candidate H-h3-1, already confirmed.

With the correct formula, a(θ₁F,Q) = con(a(F,Q) ⊗ Q) does not vanish automatically when p | d(Q). For example, con(Y^{j−2} ⊗ X²) = 2(j−2)(j−3)Y^{j−4}, and d(X²) = 0. Nothing in the paper shows these coefficients vanish.
- Theorem 8.22's opening argument only finds some Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- Even a(F,Q) itself need not vanish for p-primitive Q with p | D, when F(Q) = {[pR]}.

So the final "θ₁F = 0" is asserted without proof for these Q. That is a genuine gap, and it cannot be closed from the printed text.

THE FIX IS SOUND. The identity con(Sym^{j−2}[M]x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·Sym^{j−4}[M]con(x ⊗ P), for det M = p, is equivariance of the second transvectant: Sym^a ⊗ Sym^2 → Sym^{a−2} ⊗ det². I checked it in exact rational arithmetic (check2.py in my work folder): 1500 random trials with p ∈ {5, 7, 11, 13}, 0 mismatches. The contraction reproduces the paper's normalisation (4, −2) ∝ (2, −1). The paper's own claim that con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 when AQA^t = p^sQ is a special case of this identity (it gives a factor p^s).

USE LATER. Prop. 8.25 is used only in the last sentence of §8.9: combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 (injectivity of θ₁), it gives the contradiction that proves Theorem 8.22(1), and so Theorem 8.13. The statement of Prop. 8.25 is still true after the repair, so nothing downstream changes. The proof as written, however, does not establish θ₁F = 0.

This candidate overlaps with the consequence recorded in H-h3-1. It should be cross-referenced or merged with it, and the candidate's step (iii) must not be kept in its present form.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.9, proof of Proposition 8.25, second display on p. 877; arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55
sourceIssues.printed:
Similarly, the contraction mapping on Sym^{j−2} ⊗ Sym^2 for p > j − 2 satisfies
    con(f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0    unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 4.
(Checked on the page image, p. 77 at 300 dpi. arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55, prints the same text: "con(f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 4.")
sourceIssues.correction: "unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2". Equivalently, the image f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k} lies in Sym^{j−4}, so 0 ≤ i+k−2 ≤ j−4. For p > j−2 the contraction is in fact nonzero exactly when 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page fixes the convention just before this display (p. 876 to p. 877). On Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, con sends e_1^2 f_2^2 and e_2^2 f_1^2 to −2, sends e_1 f_1 e_2 f_2 to 1, and kills all other monomials. So e_1 pairs with f_2 and e_2 pairs with f_1.

Contracting e_1^k e_2^{2−k} against f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} therefore uses k copies of f_2 and 2−k copies of f_1, leaving f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k}. This needs i+k ≥ 2 and i+k ≤ j−2. The scalar is a product of falling factorials of i and j−2−i, which is a unit when p > j−2.

I checked this in Python. I used the GL2-equivariant second transvectant φ_xx ψ_yy − 2 φ_xy ψ_xy + φ_yy ψ_xx, with x = f_1, y = f_2 and e_1 ↦ x, e_2 ↦ y in the ψ slot:
- It reproduces the paper's Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2 values (4, 4, −2) ∝ (−2, −2, 1), and con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = 8mn − 2r² ∝ r² − 4mn.
- For j = 4, …, 9 the set of i+k with nonzero contraction is exactly {2, …, j−2}. The printed range {2, …, j−4} is empty for j = 4, 5 and too small for every j.

The printed bound also contradicts the paper's own text in two places:
- For j = 4 it makes con identically zero on Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, against the displayed con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = r² − 4mn = −4 det(Q) just above it.
- In case (1) the paper says "the only monomial which f_1^{j−2} contracts nontrivially with is e_2^2" (i = j−2, k = 0, so i+k = j−2). The printed bound would make that contraction zero.

This is a slip in the upper bound (j−4, the degree of the target Sym, written in place of j−2), so it is a misprint, not an error in the argument.

Effect: none. The proof only needs con(f_1^{j−2} ⊗ e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 for k = 1, 2, because Q^∨ ≡ m e_1^2 + r e_1 e_2 mod p. Here i+k = j−1 or j, both greater than j−2, so the corrected bound gives exactly this. Case (1) also states the needed fact directly and correctly, and case (2) reduces to case (1). Nothing else cites the display: after the proof, Proposition 8.25 is only combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 to finish Theorem 8.13, and it does not rely on this display. The candidate's correction, reasoning and 'affects: nothing' are all right.

sourceIssues.printed: then once again the image of A is generated by f, and the conditions AQA^t = det(A)Q and det(A) = p^s imply once more that n ≡ 0 mod p (multiply out as above but now consider the top left entry), and the proof proceeds as in the previous case.
sourceIssues.correction: '... the image of A is generated by f1, ...'
sourceIssues.reason: At 400 dpi the printed symbol is a bare 'f' with no subscript. For A ≡ [[0,1],[0,0]] mod p, A kills the first basis vector and sends the second to the first, so the image is spanned by f1, just as in case (1), where A = diag(u,0). The rest of the case confirms f1. The top-left entry of AQA^t is n, which gives n ≡ 0 mod p, so Q^∨ ≡ m e1^2 + r e1e2. 'Proceeds as in the previous case' then needs the image of Sym^{j−2}[A] to be f1^{j−2}, which contracts nontrivially only with e2^2, whose coefficient n vanishes. If the image were f2, the relevant coefficient would be m, which need not vanish. So the intended symbol is f1.

The intended meaning is clear and the argument is unaffected.

sourceIssues.printed: (a) The image of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of R_∞ because under the Galois representation r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17, the image of an element σ ∈ I_x, for x a prime in Q_N, is conjugate to a matrix of the form diag(1, 1, ⟨u⟩, ⟨u⟩) where Art_x(u) = σ. This follows from [64, Corollary 3].
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the matrix with the shape for the twisted representation: r_{Q_N}(σ) is conjugate to diag(χ(σ), χ(σ), χ(σ)^{-1}, χ(σ)^{-1}), where χ is the character by which I_x acts on V_1 (Definition 4.6(5)) and χ(σ)^{-2} = ⟨u⟩. Equivalently, the matrix is diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}), with ⟨u⟩^{1/2} = ⟨u^{1/2}⟩ the unique square root in the odd p-group Δ. So ⟨u⟩ = χ(σ)^{-2} still lies in the image of R_{Q_N}, and step (a) goes through. The printed diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) is correct only for the untwisted representation r'_m of Theorem 6.13 and of the proof of Theorem 6.17, before the twist by the inverse square root of ψ_Q̃. The exponent's sign depends on how Art_x and [64] are normalised, but the conclusion does not.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 879, 815, 842, 845 and 846. Theorem 6.17 (p. 845) says r_Q is "a minimal deformation of r̄ outside Q". By Definition 4.6(1) (p. 815) its similitude is ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x ∈ Q_N (x ≠ p). So for σ ∈ I_x, ν(r_{Q_N}(σ)) = 1 and det r_{Q_N}(σ) = ν(σ)^2 = 1. But det diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) = ⟨u⟩^2, and conjugation does not change the determinant. So the printed claim forces ⟨u⟩^2 = 1, and hence ⟨u⟩ = 1 because Δ has odd order. The same thing follows from Definition 4.6(5): inertia acts on V1 by a character and on V2 by its inverse, so the shape diag(1,1,c,c) needs c = 1.

The diamond operators are not trivial in general, and the paper's own results show this. ⟨u⟩ is defined on pp. 833–834 as the deck transformation of X_1(Q) → X_0(Q) and lies in T_σ(Q) (Definition 5.13(2)). Suppose every ⟨u⟩ with u from the inertia at the primes of Q_N were 1. These inertia images generate Δ, so Δ would act trivially on H_N, and H_N ≅ (H_N)_Δ ≅ H ≠ 0. For S = O[Δ] and an S-module M with trivial Δ-action, the base-change five-term sequence gives 0 → M⊗Tor_1^S(O,k) → Tor_1^S(M,k) → Tor_1^O(M,k) → 0, with Tor_1^S(O,k) = I/m_S I ≅ k^q. So d_S(M) ≤ r(1−q), where r = dim_k M/ϖM ≥ 1. That is negative for q ≥ 2 and contradicts Theorem 7.11 (H_N balanced), which step (c) uses.

The paper itself says the untwisted Hecke representation has ramified similitude: Theorem 6.13(1),(4) on p. 842 gives ν∘r = χ_{μ,0}ε^{-w}, and only the twist by √χ_{μ,0} satisfies Definition 4.6(2)–(5). The proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846) twists r'_m by the inverse square root of χ_Q. The [64, Cor. 3] shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩), with similitude ⟨u⟩, is therefore that of the untwisted representation. As printed, the statement is false for r_{Q_N} whenever ⟨u⟩ ≠ 1.

The step's conclusion survives. The universal deformation's inertial scalar χ^univ(σ) on V1 maps to ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, so ⟨u⟩ = (χ^univ(σ))^{-2} is in the image of R_{Q_N}. Also ⟨u⟩−1 = (χ^{-1}−1)(χ^{-1}+1) is in the image of ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min), since minimal deformations are unramified at x. So this is a false intermediate statement with a routine fix; the mathematics as intended is right. It sits on the misprint/error borderline: the paper spells out the twist elsewhere (Theorem 6.13(4), proof of 6.17), but the printed claim about r_{Q_N} is literally false, so I classify it as an error. I tried to defend the printed text and could not.

(1) Theorem 6.17, p. 845, says r_Q is 'a minimal deformation of r̄ outside Q'. Definition 4.6(1), p. 815, fixes the similitude ν∘r = ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x ∈ Q_N (x ≠ p). So ν(r_{Q_N}(σ)) = 1 for σ ∈ I_x.

(2) In the paper's symplectic form, the Siegel Levi is diag(A, λB) with B = S^t A^{-1} S (p. 820). So ⟨e1,e2⟩ and ⟨e3,e4⟩ are dual Lagrangians, and ν(diag(1,1,c,c)) = c. GSp4-conjugation preserves ν, so the printed claim forces ⟨u⟩ = 1. Even if we allow conjugation in GL4, taking determinants gives ⟨u⟩^2 = ν(r(σ))^2 = 1. Since ⟨u⟩ has odd p-power order (Δ ≅ (Z/p^N)^q), again ⟨u⟩ = 1. So the printed claim would make every diamond operator act trivially on H_N.

(3) That is false in the relevant situation. Condition (c), from Theorem 7.11, says H_N is balanced over S_N = O[Δ]. For a nonzero module with trivial Δ-action and q ≥ 2 the defect is negative: for example, M = O has Tor_0 of dimension 1 and Tor_1 of dimension q. So the diamond operators cannot all act trivially.

(4) The paper's own text shows where the printed shape comes from. Theorem 6.13(4), p. 842, says the Hecke-algebra representation satisfies Definition 4.6(2)–(5) only 'after twisting by the unique square-root of χ_{μ,0}'. The proof of Theorem 6.17, p. 846, then twists r'_m by the inverse of a square root of ψ_Q̃, where ν(r'_m) = ε^{-(a-1)}ψ_Q̃. On I_x the central character is the diamond character: the centre z ∈ Z_x^× maps to λ = z under Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× (p. 821, ⟨u⟩ as on p. 833). So the untwisted r'_m(σ) ~ diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩), as [64, Cor. 3] gives. This matches a dual-torus check: a tamely ramified character on the Klingen λ gives inertia eigenvalues 1,1,χ,χ on two Lagrangian planes. Twisting by θ^{-1}, where θ^2 = ψ_Q̃ and θ(σ)^2 = ⟨u⟩, gives r_{Q_N}(σ) ~ diag(θ^{-1},θ^{-1},θ,θ). This satisfies Definition 4.6(5) and has similitude 1. The printed statement drops this twist.

No charitable reading works. ⟨u⟩ is the diamond operator (p. 833). 'r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17' is the twisted, fixed-similitude representation, because the classifying map R_{Q_N} → T is defined from it.

Consequences: step (a) is used only to apply Proposition 3.3 in the proof of Theorem 9.1, and nothing else repeats the claim. With the correction, ⟨u⟩ = χ(σ)^{-2}. Here χ(σ) ∈ R_{Q_N} is the scalar by which σ acts on the canonical summand V_1 of the universal deformation. So the image of S_N still lies in the image of R_∞. The second half of Proposition 3.3(a), which the paper does not address, also holds: χ(σ)^{-2} − 1 maps to 0 in R^min, since minimal deformations are unramified at x. So Theorem 9.1 and everything downstream stand. The candidate's correction is right and minimal.

It is an error rather than a misprint because the printed statement is false and the intended twisted shape is not obvious from the text. I set affects = nothing because the argument as intended survives with a one-line repair. A strict reviewer could argue for 'the proof', since the stated justification of (a) is false as written.

arXiv v1 (p. 57) has the identical text.

I could not download [64] (Sorensen, Doc. Math. 15): the fetch was blocked. The verdict does not depend on it: it follows from the paper's own Definition 4.6(1),(5), Theorem 6.13(4) and the proof of Theorem 6.17.

sourceIssues.locator: §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, item (a), p. 879; hypothesis (a) of Proposition 3.3, p. 812. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text word for word: Prop. 3.3(a) on v1 text ll. 512–513, and item (a) of the proof on ll. 3038–3041, which cites [Sor10, Corollary 3].
sourceIssues.printed: p. 79 (proof of Theorem 9.1), checked on the page image: "We need to check that, given these definitions, the conditions of Proposition 3.3 hold. (a) The image of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of R_∞ because under the Galois representation r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17, the image of an element σ ∈ I_x, for x a prime in Q_N, is conjugate to a matrix of the form diag(1, 1, ⟨u⟩, ⟨u⟩) where Art_x(u) = σ. This follows from [64, Corollary 3]." Then (b) and (c) follow, and after them: "We can thus apply Proposition 3.3, and we deduce that H is a finite free R-module." The hypothesis being checked is Prop. 3.3(a) on p. 12, also checked on the image: "(a) the image of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of R_∞, and moreover, the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N in End_O(H_N) is contained in the image of ker(φ_N);"
sourceIssues.correction: After the first sentence of (a), add the second half of the check. Suggested wording: "Moreover, take x ∈ Q_N. We have x ≡ 1 mod p, and r̄ is unramified at x (Prop. 4.10(3)), so x ∉ S(r̄) ∪ {p}. By Definition 4.6(2) with Q = ∅, every minimal deformation is therefore unramified at x. So for σ ∈ I_x, the entries of r^univ_{Q_N}(σ) − 1 lie in ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min). Their images under the surjection R_{Q_N} ↠ T_σ(Q_N)^{α,β}_{m_N} generate the ideal generated by the entries of r_{Q_N}(σ) − 1. That ideal does not change under conjugation, so by the shape above it contains ⟨u⟩ − 1. Now R_∞ ↠ R_{Q_N} is surjective, ker(φ_N) is the preimage of ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min), and the first half of (a) holds. Hence the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N (generated by the [u] − 1) lies in the image of ker(φ_N)." Both candidates' corrections are right in substance, and this is the minimal fix. One wording fix is needed: the matrix entries of r_{Q_N}(σ) − 1 lie in T, not in R_{Q_N}. The kernel statement belongs to the corresponding entries of the universal representation (or to their ideal). Also, whether one uses the printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) or the shape after the square-root twist in the proof of Thm 6.17, diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2}), the ideal still contains ⟨u⟩ − 1, because ⟨u⟩ − 1 = (⟨u⟩^{1/2} − 1)(⟨u⟩^{1/2} + 1).
sourceIssues.reason:
1. The printed text is confirmed on the rendered pages 812 and 879. Prop. 3.3(a) has two clauses. The second, "and moreover ... augmentation ideal ... image of ker(φ_N)", is needed: in the cited proof ([16, Prop. 2.3] = CG18 Prop. 2.3), it gives ı(𝔞) ⊂ ker(φ_∞) and hence R_∞/ı(𝔞)R_∞ ≅ R. Item (a) of the proof on p. 879 repeats only the first clause, nearly word for word ("The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ because ..."), then moves on to (b). Nowhere in the paper is the second clause verified. A grep shows ker(φ_N) appears only in Prop. 3.3. No statement that R_{Q_N} is an O[Δ_{Q_N}]-algebra with R_{Q_N}/𝔞 = R^min appears in §4 or anywhere else (R_Q is mentioned only on pp. 816–818 and in §9). The analogous proof in CG18 (Thm 3.26, Invent. Math. p. 339–340) does this explicitly: "The second part of condition 5a is a consequence of the following: ... χ_{α_x} ⊕ χ_{β_x} ... we obtain ... a map O[Δ_{Q_N}] → R_{Q_N}. The quotient of R_{Q_N} by the image of the augmentation ideal of O[Δ_{Q_N}] is just R^min." So the omission here is a real missing step, not a convention the authors follow. It fits the protocol's "gap": the proof asserts that the conditions of Prop. 3.3 hold without an argument for part of one.
2. I redid the missing step, and it is routine. Take x ∈ Q_N. Prop. 4.10(3) makes r̄ unramified at x with distinct Frobenius eigenvalues. Def. 4.6(5) gives a canonical splitting V_1 ⊕ V_2 of the universal deformation and a character χ_x : I_x → R_{Q_N}^× on V_1. Def. 4.6(2) with Q = ∅ makes every minimal deformation unramified at x. So χ_x(σ) − 1 ∈ ker(R_{Q_N} → R^min). Its image in End(H_N) generates, together with that of R_∞, the ideal containing ⟨u⟩ − 1. Since ker(φ_N) is an ideal and the first clause holds, the image of the whole augmentation ideal follows.
3. A side point, not the candidate's claim, but it bears on the correction's wording. The printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) has similitude ⟨u⟩, using the pairing 1↔4, 2↔3 of the p-adic shape on p. 812/15. It is the shape of the untwisted r'_m in the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846: "ν(r'_m) = ε^{-(a-1)}χ_Q ... twist r'_m by the inverse of this square root"). The twisted r_{Q_N} of Theorem 6.17 has similitude ε^{-(a-1)}, which is unramified at x, and is conjugate on I_x to diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{-1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}, ⟨u⟩^{1/2}), in line with Def. 4.6(1),(5). Both clauses of (a) still hold, because ⟨u⟩ has p-power order and p is odd. The orchestrator may want to record this as a separate misprint.
4. Scope: the missing clause is true, so Prop. 3.3 applies as the authors intend. Theorem 9.1, Theorem 1.1 and the other results deduced from it, and the appendix's use of them, all stand. Affects: nothing. Defence attempted; it fails. (1) Both halves of Prop. 3.3(a) are confirmed on the page images of p. 812 and 879. Item (a) of the proof restates only the first half ("contained in the image of R_∞ because ...") and goes on to (b). Nothing else in the paper supplies the second half. A grep of the whole text finds "augmentation" only in Prop. 3.3 itself. Nowhere is R_{Q_N} made an O[Δ_{Q_N}]-algebra with R_{Q_N}/a = R^min: not in §4 (Def. 4.6, the text after Rem. 4.7, Prop. 4.10), not in item (4) of the proof, not in Thm 6.17. (2) The second half cannot be dropped. In the patching proof of the cited result ([16, Prop. 2.3] = CG18 Prop. 2.3), it is what gives ı(a) ⊂ ker φ_∞. Without it, the argument only shows that H is free over R_∞/aR_∞. That ring is the faithful quotient of R acting on H, i.e. T. So one would get only "H is free over T" and lose R^min = T, the main assertion of Thm 9.1 (the proof ends "H is a finite free R-module. Since the action of R on H factors through T, the conclusions ... follow"). The second half is also not a formal consequence of the first half together with (b): showing that R^min acts faithfully on H is exactly what is being proved. (3) The authors' own model proof checks it explicitly. CG18, proof of Thm 3.26, item (a): "The second part of condition 5a is a consequence of the following: ... χ_{α_x} ⊕ χ_{β_x} ... we obtain ... a map O[Δ_{Q_N}] → R_{Q_N}. The quotient of R_{Q_N} by the image of the augmentation ideal of O[Δ_{Q_N}] is just R^min." The omission here is therefore a missing step, not a convention of the authors. It fits PROTOCOL §18's "gap". (4) Charitable reading: the "because" clause (the shape of r_{Q_N} on I_x, from [64, Cor. 3]) together with Def. 4.6(2) does give the second half at once, by the argument in the correction. I checked that argument: ker φ_N is the preimage of ker(R_{Q_N}→R^min) under a surjection; the entry ideal is conjugation-invariant and the classifying map R_{Q_N} ↠ T is surjective; x ∈ Q_N lies outside S(r̄) ∪ {p} by Prop. 4.10(3) and x ≡ 1 mod p; and [δδ'] − 1 = [δ]([δ'] − 1) + ([δ] − 1), so the augmentation ideal is generated by the [u] − 1. So the gap is routine and true, but it is not stated. (5) Consequences: the passage is used only to apply Prop. 3.3 in the proof of Thm 9.1. From Thm 9.1 follow R^min = T, H free, and through it Theorem 1.1, its corollaries and the appendix. The missing clause holds, so all of these stand. Separate side issue, not part of this candidate: the printed shape diag(1,1,⟨u⟩,⟨u⟩) is the shape for the untwisted r'_m; after the twist in the proof of Thm 6.17 (p. 846) it becomes diag(⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{-1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2},⟨u⟩^{1/2}). This affects neither half of (a).
