sourceIssues.locator: §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, item (c), p. 880, applying Theorem 7.11, p. 853. H_N is defined on p. 879 and e_{α,β} on p. 845 (§6.4, before Theorem 6.17).
sourceIssues.printed: (c) Finally, H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11.
sourceIssues.correction:
The proof needs its own argument that the (α,β)-summand is balanced, i.e. d_{S_N}(e_{α,β}M) ≥ 0, where M = H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_{m_N}. Theorem 7.11 gives d_{S_N}(M) ≥ 0 only for M itself. There are two possible repairs, and neither is in the paper.
(A) Construct T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}, hence e_{α,β}, integrally on coherent H^1, or on the complex RΓ(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)). They must be compatible with the Δ-action and the Hochschild–Serre sequence, for example via Pilloni [58] (which p. 860 cites as [56]; see the last entry of this list). Then rerun the rank count of Theorem 7.11 on e-parts: e·H_1(X_0(Q_N), L)_{m_N} surjects onto Tor_1^{S_N}(eM, O), and one needs rank e·H^1 ≤ rank e·H^0 in characteristic 0.
(B) Show that e_{α,β} acts as the identity on the characteristic-0 forms H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_K)_{m_∅}. By Theorem 7.2 these are the same as H^0(X_0(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_K)_{m_N}, and Theorem 7.2 is T_{p,1}, Q_{p,2}-equivariant. Then r_e := rank(eM)_Δ = r := rank M_Δ. Tor_1(eM,O) is a direct summand of Tor_1(M,O), which is a quotient of H_1(X_0(Q_N),L)_{m_N} ≅ O^r. So d(eM) = r_e − dim Tor_1(eM,O)/ϖ ≥ r − r = 0. Statement (B) would follow from crystallinity and local–global compatibility at p in weight (a,2), plus Fontaine–Laffaille, but §8.5 says crystallinity is known only in regular weight.
The candidates' wording, "supply a proof that the (α,β)-summand is balanced", is the right minimal correction.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked on the page images of p. 845, 853, 860, 878, 879 and 880.

(1) What Theorem 7.11 covers. Theorem 7.11 (p. 853) states that the O[Δ]-module H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω(1,3−a))_m = H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_m is balanced, for m "a non-Eisenstein ideal of T_μ(Q)". Definition 5.13 generates T_σ(Q) by T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}), U_{x,i} and ⟨u⟩, so it contains no Hecke operators at p. Those operators are in T̃_σ(Q).

(2) What step (c) needs. On p. 879, H_N := H^0(X_Δ(Q_N), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_N}, with m_N the ideal of Theorem 7.2, a maximal ideal of T_σ(Q_N). That is the dual of e_{α,β}·H^0(...)_{m_N}, where e_{α,β} (p. 845) is built from T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. By Lemma 8.8 these commute with the other Hecke operators, including ⟨u⟩. So H_N is an S_N-direct summand of the module in Theorem 7.11. The paper never says it is all of that module. Theorem 6.17 says only that the (α,β)-space "is nonzero after localization at m". Remark 8.18 exhibits nonordinary oldforms. §8.5 says crystallinity at p is known only in regular weight.

(3) Balancedness does not pass to summands. The defect is additive. I redid the reader's example. S = O[(Z/p^N)^2] = O[x,y]/((1+x)^{p^N}−1, (1+y)^{p^N}−1) is a local complete intersection. Its embedding dimension is 3, because the relations lie in m^2 for N ≥ 1, and its codimension is 2. Tate's Poincaré series (1+t)^3/(1−t^2)^2 gives dim Tor_2^S(k,k) = 3 + 2 = 5. So d_S(m_S) = 3 − 5 = −2, d_S(S^2) = 2, and m_S ⊕ S^2 is balanced with defect 0, while its O-free summand m_S is not. (For q = 1 one gets d(m_S) = 0, so the example needs q ≥ 2.)

(4) The proof of Theorem 7.11 does not localize to the summand. It bounds dim Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ by the rank of H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m, through the sequence (H_1(X_Δ(Q),L)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0, and then uses dim H^1 = dim H^0 in characteristic 0. For eM one needs Tor_1(eM,O) to be bounded by the e-part of H_1, since rank(eM)_Δ can be smaller than r. That requires e acting integrally on coherent H^1. Tor_1 is finite torsion, so an action over K does not help. The paper disclaims exactly this on p. 860: "Note that this argument is not sufficient to construct these operators on H^1(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}); however, we have no need to the consider the action of Hecke operators at p on these spaces." The proof defers to [16, Prop. 3.8]. In that weight-one case the patched module is the full m-localization, with no p-idempotent, so that reference does not cover the summand either.

arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text: "(c) Finally, HN is finite and balanced over SN by Theorem 7.11.", and the same Theorem 7.11 for the full localized module, with p − 2 > a.

Nothing shows the conclusion is false, and the fix appears to be available from Pilloni's operators, which the paper cites as acting on higher coherent cohomology. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error. It reaches the proof of Theorem 9.1 (Prop. 3.3(c)), hence the proofs of Theorems 1.2 and 1.1 deduced from it. It also reaches Theorem A.1, which "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889). Checked on the page images of p. 845, 851, 853, 854, 855, 860, 878, 879 and 880, and in the text at the start of §7 and in the appendix.

What the cited theorem covers. Theorem 7.11 (p. 853) reads: "let m be a non-Eisenstein ideal of T_μ(Q) ... Then the O[Δ]-module H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω(1,3−a))_m = H^0(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^∨_m is balanced". There is no (α,β) superscript. On p. 851, m is "a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal of T_μ(Q)". That algebra has no Hecke operators at p. T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} exist only on H^0, through q-expansions (Lemma 8.8). Step (c) applies the theorem to H_N, which is the dual of e_{α,β}H^0(...)_{m_N}. By Lemma 8.8, e commutes with the diamond operators, and the S_N-structure in item (4) already assumes this. So H_N is an S_N-direct summand of the module in Theorem 7.11.

Defences tried, and why each fails.
(1) Read m as a maximal ideal of the larger Hecke algebra that includes T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. The proof of 7.11 bounds Tor_1^S(M,O) through (H_1(X_Δ(Q),L)_m)_Δ → H_1(X_0(Q),L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O) → 0. Localizing that sequence would need the p-operators on H_1, which is dual to coherent H^1. p. 860 says: "this argument is not sufficient to construct these operators on H^1(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}); however, we have no need to the consider the action of Hecke operators at p on these spaces." Nor can an action over K be used: Tor_1 is finite, and e ⊗ K need not preserve the lattice.
(2) Balancedness might pass to direct summands. It does not, because the defect is additive. Over S = O[(Z/p^N)^2] one has d(S) = 1 and d(O) = 1 − q = −1, so S ⊕ O is balanced but O is not. The m_S ⊕ S^2 example in H-h3-18 is also right: the Poincaré series (1+t)^3/(1−t^2)^2 gives Tor_2(k,k) of dimension 5, so d(m_S) = −2.
(3) e might equal 1 on the m_N-part. The paper never says so. On p. 845 it says only that the (α,β)-space "is nonzero after localization at m". Theorem 1.2 calls e "a certain ordinary projection". The image of T_σ(Q)_m in End(M) is local, so it contains no idempotents other than 0 and 1. Hence e cannot be expressed in the operators that do act on H_1 unless e = 1.
(4) The alternative "pd ≤ 1 passes to summands" argument after patching would need the full patched module to be S_∞-torsion. That in turn needs a Galois-side dimension bound for the full m-part, which the paper does not have.
(5) The p. 889 appendix step and Lemma A.5 reuse Theorem 7.11 and do not add the missing point.

The resulting repair (B) is a characteristic-0 statement. It is expected to be true but is not proved in the paper. So the claim in (c) is very likely true and the step is unsupported, not false. That makes this a gap, not an error.

What depends on it. Step (c) is hypothesis (c) of Proposition 3.3 in the proof of Theorem 9.1. Theorem 9.1 gives Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889). The stated results are expected to hold, so affects = the proof.

A separate slip at the same step, not part of this candidate: Theorem 9.1 allows a = p − 2 (p − 1 > a), but Theorem 7.11 as printed requires p − 2 > a, while §7.2 (p. 851) says p > a − 2.

sourceIssues.locator: §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, step (c), p. 880. The root of the problem is the hypothesis of Theorem 7.11 (p. 853), which is Assumption 7.7 (p. 851): "The space H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m is trivial." arXiv v1 has the same text: Assumption 7.7 on p. 38, Theorem 7.11 and its proof on pp. 39–40, hypothesis (6) on p. 56 and step (c) on p. 57.
sourceIssues.printed: (c) Finally, H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11.
sourceIssues.correction: In the proof of Theorem 7.11, Assumption 7.7 is needed only for Δ trivial, i.e. H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m = 0. It enters through Lemma 7.9, which is applied to H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m. The stated hypothesis for X_Δ(Q) is never used. So Theorem 7.11's hypothesis should read "Assumption 7.7 holds for X_0(Q)", and step (c) should add that this is given by hypothesis (6) with i = 0 for Q = Q_N. This works for three reasons. Q_N satisfies Assumption 6.12(2) by Proposition 4.10(2),(3). m_N ⊂ T_σ(Q_N) is maximal, contains m_∅, and contracts to the maximal ideal m_∅ of T^an_σ(Q_N). So localizing the finite-dimensional k-space H^2 at m_N gives a direct summand of its localization at m_∅. Another fix would be to require x ≢ 1 mod p^{N+1} in Proposition 4.10. Then p does not divide deg(X_1(Q_N) → X_Δ(Q_N)), and a trace argument gives the vanishing on X_Δ from (6) with i = 1. The first fix is the smaller one.
sourceIssues.reason:
Pages 51–53 and 78–80 checked as images.

(1) Step (c) cites Theorem 7.11. That theorem assumes Assumption 7.7 for the fixed Δ, i.e. vanishing of H^2 on X_Δ(Q_N) localized at m_N. Hypothesis (6) of Theorem 9.1 only covers X_i(Q), and §5.2 defines K_i(Q) only for i = 0, 1. Vanishing on X_1 gives vanishing on X_Δ by trace only when p does not divide [X_1(Q_N) : X_Δ(Q_N)] = ∏(x−1)/p^N. Proposition 4.10(2) only gives x ≡ 1 mod p^N, so this can fail. Nothing in the paper checks the hypothesis. Remark 7.8 and Theorem 5.1 cover p ≥ a ≥ 4 only, not a = 2 or 3.

(2) Defence: the proof of Theorem 7.11 never uses the X_Δ vanishing. By Definition 3.1, and since Tor^O_p vanishes for p ≥ 2, d_S(M) = rank_O(M_Δ) − dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ for any finite M. This is the formula printed, with r the rank of M_Δ, which is H_0(X_0(Q), L)_m. Hochschild–Serre gives a surjection H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O). So one needs H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m to be torsion-free, which is Lemma 7.9 with Δ trivial and so needs Assumption 7.7 for X_0(Q). The rest is a characteristic-0 argument on X_0(Q) (Lemma 7.10 and Arthur's classification). Hypothesis (6) with i = 0 supplies exactly this, as explained in the correction. So Theorem 9.1 is fully supported by its own hypotheses. The fault is only that Theorem 7.11 states a hypothesis (X_Δ) other than the one its proof uses (X_0), and that step (c) leaves the check implicit.

(3) Is Theorem 7.11 correct as stated? Vanishing on X_Δ does not formally give vanishing on X_0. The Hochschild–Serre terms H^2(Δ, H^0) and H^1(Δ, H^1) with k-coefficients need not vanish for a p-group Δ. So Theorem 7.11 is proved under the X_0 hypothesis, not under the one it states. Its only use is step (c), where the X_0 hypothesis is available.

(4) One detail in the candidate's reason needs care. "Does not descend" should read "the trace argument does not apply"; nobody has shown the vanishing actually fails.

(5) A separate point, not part of this candidate and not assessed here: H_N is the (α,β)-ordinary part, while Theorem 7.11 is stated for the whole m-localized module.

sourceIssues.printed: (2) A is ordinary at p, and if α, β are the unit root eigenvalues of D_cris(V), then (α^2 − 1)(β^2 − 1)(α − β)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≢ 0 mod p. Then H^1_f(Q, asp^0(r) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p) = 0, where asp^0(r) is the 10-dimensional adjoint representation of PGSp(4).
sourceIssues.correction: State that V = V_p(A) (equivalently H^1_et(A_{Q̄}, Q_p)) is the p-adic Galois representation of A, and that r: G_Q → GSp_4(Z_p) is the associated integral representation (Tate module), with mod-p reduction r̄_p as in §A.3.2. asp^0(r) is r composed with the adjoint action on the 10-dimensional Lie algebra of PGSp_4.
sourceIssues.reason: Neither V nor r is introduced in Theorem A.1. Earlier in §A.1, V denotes an arbitrary pure de Rham representation ('for any pure de Rham representation V'), and r denotes 'a p-adic representation r: G_Q → GL_n(O) coming from M' for an automorphic compatible system M. The intended objects (the p-adic realisation of A and its integral model) are clear from Theorem 9.1(1) and from §A.3.2, where r̄_p is 'the corresponding semisimple representation' of the abelian surface A. The ambiguity between H^1 and the Tate module does not matter. Their crystalline Frobenius eigenvalues differ by x ↦ p/x on H^1 versus x ↦ 1/x after the Tate twist, so the unit roots α, β are replaced by 1/α, 1/β. A direct computation gives (α^{-2}−1)(β^{-2}−1)(α^{-1}−β^{-1})(α^{-2}β^{-2}−1) = unit × (α^2−1)(β^2−1)(β−α)(α^2β^2−1), so the non-vanishing condition is the same either way. This is an omitted definition in a theorem statement whose meaning is clear from context.

sourceIssues.locator: §A.1, paragraph after Theorem A.2, parenthetical remark, p. 882. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, p. 3, is identical (with [ACC+18] for [1]).
sourceIssues.printed: (The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)
sourceIssues.correction: '(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for an extension F′/F for which restriction H^1_f(F, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) → H^1_f(F′, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) is injective. This holds, for example, if p ∤ [F′:F], or if (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0 for the Galois closure F″ of F′/F, e.g. F′/F Galois with r̄|G_{F′} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, as for the linearly disjoint CM fields supplied by [1] ...)'. The 'F/F' slip is recorded separately.
sourceIssues.reason: Restriction preserves the Bloch–Kato local conditions, so vanishing over F′ implies vanishing over F exactly when restriction on H^1 is injective. By inflation–restriction, the kernel of H^1(F, M) → H^1(F″, M), with M = ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O and F″ the Galois closure, is H^1(Gal(F″/F), M^{G_{F″}}). The kernel to G_{F′} is contained in it. If p ∤ [F′:F], cor∘res = [F′:F] also gives injectivity. M^{G_{F″}} = 0 iff (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0, since M[λ] = ad^0 r̄. With r̄|G_{F″} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, Schur's lemma gives this. These conditions are not automatic for 'any extension': if p | [F″:F] and ad^0 r̄ acquires G_{F″}-invariants, the kernel can be nonzero, and the remark gives no hypothesis excluding this. In the intended example (symmetric powers of a non-CM E, p large, F′ a Galois CM extension linearly disjoint from F(r̄, ζ_p) as potential-automorphy theorems provide), the condition holds, so nothing downstream is affected. This is an unjustified, over-general reduction in an informal remark, not a false theorem. I could not build an explicit counterexample within the theorem's setting, hence low confidence.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris), §A.1 Introduction, paragraph after Theorem A.2 ("Unlike the case of Theorem A.1, ..."), p. 882. arXiv:1907.08694v1, §1, p. 3 (theorems numbered 1.1/1.2 there).
sourceIssues.printed: "(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)"
sourceIssues.correction: "... is potentially modular over some CM extension F′/F in this case by [1]." That is, F/F should read F′/F, the same auxiliary extension as in the preceding clause.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this against page images: p. 882 at 110 dpi, plus a 300 dpi crop of the passage. The same sentence first has "extension F′/F" with a visible prime. Two lines later it has "CM extension F/F" with no prime. pdftotext gives "F=F" on line 3965, and a grep for "CM extension" finds no other occurrence.

Theorem A.2 (p. 881) fixes F as a CM field. The remark says the theorem's conclusion over F follows from the conclusion over any extension F′/F. It then says symmetric powers of a non-CM elliptic curve E/F are potentially modular by ACC+18 [1], which gives modularity over some CM extension F′/F. Read as F/F, the extension would be trivial. That would make the "potentially" and the preceding base-change clause pointless, and it would claim more than [1] proves. No convention in the paper gives F/F a meaning, so this is a missing prime and not an intended statement.

The arXiv appendix (1907.08694v1) has the same slip. I rendered page 3 and it reads "potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [ACC+18]." Line 109 of the arXiv text shows the same.

Impact: the sentence is a parenthetical in the appendix introduction. It explains which examples Theorem A.2 would apply to. It is not a hypothesis or a step in any proof. Theorem A.2 and its proof in §A.3 (p. 888) do not use it, and neither do Theorem A.1 or the main text.

sourceIssues.printed: If one chooses a prime p, and supposes that ρ has a model over O, then the finiteness of the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is a consequence of the finiteness of the p-class group of Q(ker(ρ)). (The former is a quotient of the latter.)
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the parenthetical by: '(With L = Q(ker ρ), restriction to G_L maps the former, with kernel inside the finite group H^1(Gal(L/Q), ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), which is zero if p ∤ [L:Q], into Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O).)' The finiteness claim itself is correct.
sourceIssues.reason: G_L acts trivially on ad^0(ρ). A Bloch–Kato class restricted to G_L is a homomorphism G_L → ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O that is unramified everywhere. At w | p this holds because H^1_f(L_w, Q_p) = H^1_ur for trivial coefficients. At infinite places nothing is needed since p is odd. So the class factors through Cl(L)[p^∞], and by inflation–restriction the kernel is H^1(Gal(L/Q), M), a finite group since it is |Gal(L/Q)|-torsion and cofinitely generated. This gives finiteness, as the paper says. The parenthetical 'quotient' claim is false as stated. When p ∤ [L:Q] and ρ is unramified at p, the Selmer group equals Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), and enlarging K by degree d raises its order to the d-th power, while Cl(L)[p^∞] does not depend on K. Take any case with a nonzero Selmer group, which the paper itself discusses ('there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(...) is nonzero'). For a large enough coefficient field its order then exceeds |Cl(L)[p^∞]|, so it cannot be a quotient of that group. The accurate relation is an embedding, up to finite kernel, into a Hom group out of the class group; dually, the Pontryagin dual is roughly a quotient. The error is in an informal justification, and the conclusion drawn is unaffected.

sourceIssues.printed: The methods of this paper (following [16]) show that, at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified, the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is detected by congruences between the modular form f and other Katz modular forms of weight 1 which may not lift to characteristic 0. In particular, there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is nonzero.
sourceIssues.correction: "... at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified at p, the reduction ρ̄ is irreducible, and ρ is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ (in the sense of [16, Corollary 1.5(1)]; for example, at all p > 2 with p ∤ N(ρ)·|ρ(G_Q)|, so for all but finitely many p) ...". Adding "ρ̄ irreducible", as the candidate does, is necessary but not sufficient: minimality must also be assumed.
sourceIssues.reason:
Printed text checked on the rendered p. 883; it matches the transcription.

(1) What [16] gives. [16] is CG18, Invent. Math. 211. I read its Theorem 1.4 (p. 303): 'Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... Assume that ρ̄ is unramified at p. ... R^min ⥲ T_m'. The theorem needs ρ̄ irreducible, and it covers only minimal deformations. The Taylor–Wiles patching behind it also needs ρ̄ absolutely irreducible. So the methods cited say nothing at a prime p where ρ̄ is reducible (m Eisenstein), or where ρ is not minimal.

(2) Such primes exist. Let H be the splitting field of x³−x−1 (discriminant −23), and let ρ be the 2-dimensional representation of S_3. It is irreducible and odd, and it is ramified only at 23, so it is unramified at p = 3. In characteristic 3 every irreducible representation of S_3 is 1-dimensional, so ρ̄ is reducible. Both stable lattices check this explicitly: on the sum-zero lattice, b1+2b2 is fixed mod 3. So the sentence covers (ρ, p = 3), but [16] does not apply there. Primes of this kind all divide |ρ(G_Q)|, so the exceptions are finite. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)|, ρ̄ is irreducible and ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v).

(3) The 'iff' can fail in this example. f = η(z)η(23z) satisfies f ≡ E_1(1, χ_{−23}) (mod 3) coefficient by coefficient: the traces are 2, 0, −1 against 1+χ = 2, 0, 2, and a_23 = 1 on both sides. The constant term h/2 = 3/2 ≡ 0, so the two agree as mod-3 Katz forms by the q-expansion principle. On the other side, H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ Q_3/Z_3) = 0:
- h(H) = 1. The Minkowski bound is ≈ 3.51, and the primes of H above 2 and 3 have norms 8 and 27, because they lie over non-principal primes of Q(√−23).
- So a Selmer class dies on G_H, and the group is H^1(S_3, M) ≅ Ĥ^0(C_3, ad^0 L)^{C_2}.
- I computed this for both stable lattices L. In each case N_{C_3}(ad^0 L) = (ad^0 L)^{C_3}, so the group is 0.
- The local conditions at 23 and 3 add nothing: D_23 = C_2, which has no 3-torsion cohomology, and the classes at 3 are unramified.
So if Eisenstein series count as 'other Katz modular forms of weight 1', the 'iff' is false at (ρ, 3). If only cusp forms count (T in [16] acts on H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ), which is dual to cusp forms), I cannot decide the statement at such p. It is simply unproved there. That is why I class this as a gap and not an error.

The authors know these conditions matter: on p. 882 they say they 'do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible' and 'whether r is a minimal deformation'. Nothing in §A.2 assumes either condition. The remark is informal and nothing later uses it. The printed text is confirmed from the rendered p. 883. The claim rests on [16] = Calegari–Geraghty, Invent. Math. 2018, Theorem 1.4: "Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... unramified at p. Let R^min denote the universal minimal unramified-at-p deformation ring of ρ̄ ... R^min ≅ T_m." To read H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ K/O) off R^min = T_m, two things are needed. (i) ρ̄ must be irreducible. (ii) ρ must be a point of R^min, i.e. minimally ramified; this is [16, Cor. 1.5(1)]: "either ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1".

Both conditions can fail at primes p > 2 where ρ is unramified.
(i) Take the S_3 representation cut out by x^3 − x − 1. The discriminant is −23 (computed), and the splitting field is the Hilbert class field of Q(√−23), ramified only at 23. So ρ is odd, irreducible, and unramified at 3. Its reduction mod 3 is reducible: in the reflection representation, (1,1,1) lies in {Σx_i = 0} mod 3 and is S_3-fixed, and Brauer–Nesbitt gives ρ̄^ss = 1 ⊕ ε_{−23}. Here m is Eisenstein, and indeed η(z)η(23z) ≡ E_1(1, ε_{−23}) mod 3. So [16] does not apply.
(ii) Take ρ = Ind_K^Q ψ with K = Q(√−47) (class number 5) and ψ a ring class character of order 15. The order-3 part should have conductor ℓ, with ℓ ≡ 1 mod 3 split in K. Then ρ is unramified at 3, and ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ with ψ̄ of order 5 is irreducible. But ρ|I_ℓ = ω ⊕ ω^{-1} with ω of order 3, while ρ̄|I_ℓ is trivial. So ρ is not minimal and is not a point of R^min.

Defence attempted, without success. No charitable reading restricts p. The paper's own methods also assume residual irreducibility (big image). The authors are aware of both conditions. On p. 882, about Theorem A.2, they write: "we do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible for sufficiently large p. Another is that we do not know whether r is a minimal deformation of r̄ at ramified primes v". §A.2 simply omits these conditions. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)| the reduction of the finite image group is injective and preserves irreducibility, so both conditions hold for all but finitely many p. I cannot show that the "iff" statement is actually false at the excluded p; in the S_3 example both sides are nonzero, since the 3-class group of K gives a Selmer class. The fault is an unsupported claim of scope, so the kind is gap, not error.

Consequences: §A.2 is a discussion remark. Nothing in the paper cites it; grep finds no reference to Section A.2, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 and §A.3 do not use it. So affects = nothing.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix A, §A.3.1, Theorem A.4 and its proof, pp. 885–886; setup of r̄_v on pp. 884–885
sourceIssues.printed: p. 85: "THEOREM A.4 Suppose that H^i(Y, O/ϖ^n)_m = 0 unless i ∈ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0]. Let Q be a finite collection of primes x such that r̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. Then H^i(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^n)_{m_α} = 0 for all i ∉ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0], where" p. 86: "(1) α = {α_x} is a choice of eigenvalues of r̄(Frob_x) for each x dividing Q; (2) the localization takes place with respect to the Hecke algebra T_Q consisting of the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x for all x ∈ Q. In particular, the conclusions of this theorem apply for all sufficiently large p. Proof. We first note that the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄ ensures that the cohomology of the boundary vanishes after localization at m. This is because the cohomology of the boundary may be computed inductively from the cohomology of Levi subgroups and then of GL_{n_i} for n_i < n (see, e.g., Section 3 and in particular Proposition 3.3 of [17]), and so the corresponding Galois representations associated to these classes are reducible. By Poincaré duality (and the discussion above concerning the vanishing of the boundary cohomology localized at m), it suffices to prove the result for i < q_0. Let i be the smallest integer for which the inequality is violated. Then, by the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence, we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. As in [16, Section 9.4] (see also [46, Lemma 6.25(4)]), we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≃ H^i(Y, k)_m. The result then follows by Lemma A.3." Setup, pp. 84–85: "For a prime v of O_E, let r̄_v : G_F → GL_n(k) be the corresponding semisimple Galois representation, and let m denote the corresponding maximal ideal of T." p. 82: "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p."
sourceIssues.correction:
Minimal fix: add one hypothesis to Theorem A.4, or to the §A.3.1 setup: "Suppose moreover that r̄ (= r̄_v) is absolutely irreducible." This is what the proof calls "the assumption", and it matches the parallel coherent Lemma A.6, which does say "Suppose, moreover, that r̄_p is absolutely irreducible." The last sentence then needs a qualifier: "the conclusions apply for all sufficiently large p [for which r̄ is absolutely irreducible]". Lemma A.3 supplies the vanishing hypothesis for large p. It does not supply irreducibility, which p. 882 says is not known.

H-h3-21's extra hypothesis at m^∨ is not needed. Absolute irreducibility of r̄ gives it for r̄^∨ as well, so boundary cohomology vanishes at both m and m^∨. Poincaré duality on Y then turns the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0 into vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0. [16, Remark 9.3] uses the same "by duality, considering both m and m^*".

Alternative fix that keeps the statement as printed: skip the boundary step and run the i < q0 argument on H_c at m_α^∨. Hochschild–Serre and the Taylor–Wiles isomorphism apply to H_c in the same way. Poincaré duality on Y gives H_c^j(Y,k)_{m^∨} = H^{D−j}(Y,k)_m^∨ = 0 for j < q0. Or use the minimal-complex argument over k[Δ_Q]. The application to A.2 still needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)]. That comes from irreducibility, which A.2(1) supplies.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked on the page images (p. 881, 884–886). The core claim holds:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the setup of §A.3.1 assumes r̄ absolutely irreducible. There r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits that irreducibility for large p is unknown.
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m (needed for the Poincaré duality reduction), uses "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄", which the statement does not contain.
- arXiv:1907.08694v1, Theorem 3.2 and its proof, has word-for-word the same text, including "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r".

The candidate's second point is wrong. They say the upper degrees need the hypothesis at m^∨ as well. Given boundary vanishing at m and m^∨ (both follow from absolute irreducibility of r̄), Poincaré duality on Y derives vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0 from the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0. So "suffices to prove i < q0" is legitimate, and the added m^∨ hypothesis is redundant.

Impact: downstream results are fine. Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]"). There, hypothesis (1) (r̄|F(ζp) has enormous image, which includes CHT bigness) forces absolute irreducibility. That application also silently needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)], which the proof of A.4 supplies under this hypothesis.

Minor side slips:
- The proof ends with "follows by Lemma A.3" where the theorem's own hypothesis suffices.
- Theorem A.2 cites "[16, Section 9.2]" for "enormous", but [16] discusses it in §9.4. Checked on the page images (pp. 881–889) and in arXiv v1.

What is missing:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the §A.3.1 setup assumes r̄ is irreducible. r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p".
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m, rests on "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄". The Poincaré-duality reduction to i < q0 uses that step.
- The theorem's last sentence claims the conclusions hold "for all sufficiently large p", which the printed proof does not cover when r̄ is reducible.

Defences tried:
(a) The inherited setting. §A.3.1 works "in [16, Section 9]". In [16] (arXiv 1207.4224v2), §8.5 fixes "a continuous absolutely irreducible representation r̄", and Conjecture B(1)–(5) is stated only for non-Eisenstein m with r̄_m ≅ r̄. A.4 is meant to replace B(4). So the "assumption" is plausibly this imported standing hypothesis. That explains the intent, but it does not make the text correct: §A.3.1 redefines r̄_v for every v as merely semisimple, and the "all sufficiently large p" sentence contradicts p. 882.
(b) The parallel coherent Lemma A.6 (p. 887; v1 Lemma 3.4) states irreducibility explicitly. This confirms the omission in A.4 is a slip.
(c) The conclusion itself is probably true without irreducibility, using the H_c or minimal-complex argument and the same cited inputs. So the statement is not shown false; only the proof's first step relies on the missing hypothesis.

Consequences: Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]") and in the remark on p. 886.
- In A.2, hypothesis (1) is enormous image, which [16] §9.2 defines as "in addition to bigness".
- Bigness gives H^0(r̄(G_{F(ζp)}), ad^0) = 0. With p ∤ n and r̄ semisimple, this forces r̄ to be absolutely irreducible.
- A.2 also assumes the rest of Conjecture B, which is set in the irreducible case.
So A.2 stands. Theorem A.1 does not use A.4; it uses Lemma A.6. The references to "Theorem A.4" on p. 889 that should read A.1 are a separate slip, already filed as X-K8-13.

sourceIssues.correction: 'The result then follows by Lemma A.3' should read 'The result then follows from the hypothesis'. The hypothesis gives H^i(Y, k)_𝔪 = 0 for i < q_0: take n = 1, or use a lowest-degree dévissage along 0 → k → 𝒪/ϖ^n → 𝒪/ϖ^{n−1} → 0, under which H^i(Y,k)_𝔪 injects into H^i(Y,𝒪/ϖ^n)_𝔪 once the lower degrees vanish. Lemma A.3 only shows that the hypothesis holds for all sufficiently large p, which is the 'In particular' clause.
sourceIssues.reason: Theorem A.4 is stated under a vanishing hypothesis for an arbitrary p, and its main conclusion does not assume p is large. The proof reduces to showing H^i(Y, k)_𝔪 = 0 for the smallest offending i < q_0. Lemma A.3 gives this only 'for all sufficiently large v', so citing it literally proves only the final 'In particular' clause. The needed vanishing comes directly from the theorem's own hypothesis, which is word for word the conclusion of Lemma A.3. So the intended meaning is clear and the fix is routine. This is a wrong cross-reference, not a mathematical error or a real gap.

As in [16, Section 9.4] (see also [46, Lemma 6.25(4)]), we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≃ H^i(Y, k)_m." p. 88 (proof of Lemma A.6): "By Hochschild–Serre applied to the map X_1(Q) → X_0(Q), it suffices to show that, if i denotes the smallest integer such that H^i(X_0(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} is nonzero, then H^i(X, ω(−∞))_{m*_Q} is also nonzero."
sourceIssues.correction: Betti case (Theorem A.4). State and prove the theorem for the subcover Y_Δ(Q) → Y_0(Q), where Δ is the maximal p-power quotient of Δ_Q (any p-power quotient also works). The Hochschild–Serre lowest-degree argument then goes through word for word, because a p-group acting on a non-zero k-vector space has non-zero invariants. The alternative is to keep Y_1(Q) and add the missing input: the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q acts trivially on H^*(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α}. That input is local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q, relating diamond operators to inertia, as in [16, Conj. B(2)] and condition (d) of [16, Thm 6.3]. Note that the candidate's first option (going through Y_Δ(Q)) proves the statement for Y_Δ(Q), not for Y_1(Q). Getting back to Y_1(Q) again needs the prime-to-p invariants to be non-zero. Coherent case (Lemma A.6). The statement needs no change, only one missing sentence. By p. 821, Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× through λ mod x, and this map is onto already on the centre Z_x^×. So the diamond operators are central, and for y ∉ S∪Q∪{p} the operator S_y = T_{y,0} (which lies in the localising Hecke algebra) equals y^w⟨y^{-1}⟩_S⟨y^{-1}⟩_Q. Localising at m_α fixes S_y ≡ s̄_y, the same value as at level X. By Dirichlet (CRT on (Z/Q)^× × (Z/N)^×) every prime-to-p character of Δ_Q in H^*(X_1(Q),·)_{m_α} is trivial. Hence the Δ_Q-invariants are non-zero, compare the main text p. 846: "χ_Q is a finite-order character of p-power order which is unramified outside Q".
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 884–889 and checked the printed text above against the images; the arXiv v1 appendix reads the same.

(1) Which cover Y_1(Q) is. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q), Y_0(Q), X_1(Q) or X_0(Q); it relies on [16, §9] and the main text. [16] = CG18, §9.1 sets L_{Q,v} ⊂ K_{Q,v} to be "the normal subgroup with quotient group k_v^×", and §9.5 says "Y_1(Q_N) → Y_0(Q_N) with Galois group Δ := ∏_{x∈Q}(O_F/x)^×". The main text, §5.2 (p. 822) and p. 834, says "X_{K_1(Q)} → X_{K_0(Q)} is then finite étale with Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×". So in both cases the Galois group is the full ∏(O_F/x)^×. That group is essentially never a p-group: N(x)−1 is even whenever N(x) is odd, so for odd p there is always a 2-part. For example, x = 7 and p = 3 give (Z/7)^× ≅ Z/6.

(2) The step. Let i be the least degree with H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} ≅ E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. For a p-group acting on a nonzero k-vector space, the invariants are nonzero. For Δ_Q = Δ'×Δ_p with |Δ'| > 1 prime to p they need not be. Decompose V = ⊕_χ V_χ over characters of Δ'. Then H^a(Δ_Q, V_χ) = 0 for every a whenever χ ≠ 1. Toy check: Z/6 acting on k = F_3 through the quadratic character has V^G = 0 and no group cohomology at all. So the spectral sequence only brings the χ = 1 part down to Y_0(Q). Components with nontrivial prime-to-p nebentypus in degree < q_0 are left untreated.

(3) Localisation does not remove those components. Theorem A.4(2) defines T_Q explicitly as "the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x", so there are no diamond operators, and m_α does not cut out χ = 1. Showing that the χ ≠ 1 components vanish requires local–global compatibility at x for torsion classes (inertia acting through χ, which is nontrivial mod p, would contradict r̄ being unramified at x). The proof never mentions this. Lemma A.6 has the same pattern; its m_α is described only as "any collection of eigenvalues", as in A.4.

(4) Status. The stated results are very probably true, since they follow from local–global compatibility. The p-power subcover version, which is all that [16, §7/§9.5] and Theorem 7.11 need, is proved by the printed argument as it stands. So this is a gap in the proofs of A.4 and A.6 as stated for Y_1/X_1, not a false statement, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 are unaffected.

One minor imprecision in the candidate: the "[16, Conjecture B(2)]" attribution is loose, because the local–global compatibility needed is really the diamond-operator/inertia link. The core claim stands. Lowest-degree Hochschild–Serre: when H^b(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} = 0 for b < i, we get H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} = E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. The argument therefore needs these invariants to be non-zero. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q). It takes Y from [16, §9], says 'As in [16, Section 9.4]', and calls Thm A.4 'a replacement for Conjecture B(4) of [16]'. In [16] (arXiv v2, §9.0.1), Y_1(Q) = Y(L_Q), with K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The Galois group of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q) is Δ̃ = ∏_{x∈Q}(O_F/x)^× ([16] §9.3), and this group is not a p-group. The main text uses the same convention for X_1(Q) (p. 822: Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×; p. 833). An element of prime order ℓ ≠ p acting on k through a non-trivial character has no invariants. So the step is valid only if prime-to-p characters of Δ_Q cannot occur in the m_α-localisation. The localising algebra T_Q in Thm A.4(2) contains no diamond operators. In PGL_n the centre is trivial (T_{α,n} = 1), so no Hecke operator away from Q controls them. With only A.4's hypotheses (vanishing at level Y), ruling them out needs local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q for torsion classes, and A.4 does not assume it. So the Betti step is a real gap. Charitable reading: Khare–Thorne [46], which the proof cites, define U_1(Q) through the maximal p-power quotient (arXiv:1409.7007v1 p. 41: 'U_1(Q)_v is the pre-image ... of the maximal p-power quotient'). With that reading the proof is correct, but the text points to [16]'s full cover. Defence that succeeds for Lemma A.6: in GSp_4 with Klingen level, the Q-diamond operators are central elements, so the S_y in the localising algebra, together with Dirichlet, kill prime-to-p characters (details in the correction). That part of the candidate is only an omitted routine sentence. Consequences: Thm A.4 is used only in the proof of Thm A.2 (pp. 888–889, as a substitute for [16, Conj. B(4)]). The patching in [16] (proof of Thm 9.19) uses only the p-power subcovers Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), for which the corrected argument is complete. Thm A.2 also assumes Conj. B apart from (4), which supplies the missing compatibility. Lemma A.6 feeds Thm A.1 through Assumption 7.7, which concerns X_Δ(Q) with Δ of p-power order (Thm 7.11). Thms A.1 and A.2 are not affected. Only Thm A.4 in the form stated (unconditional, for the full Y_1(Q)) is left without a complete proof.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix, §A.3.2, Lemma A.6 and its proof, pp. 887–888; arXiv:1907.08694v1, §3.2, Lemma 3.4, p. 7
sourceIssues.printed: p. 87: "LEMMA A.6 Suppose that H^2(X, ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_Q} = 0 for any set of auxiliary primes Q, as in the statement of Lemma A.5. Suppose, moreover, that r̄_p is absolutely irreducible. Then, for i ≥ 2, H^i(X_1(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = H^i(X_0(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = 0, where Q is any collection of primes where r̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues, N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and α = {α_x} is any collection of eigenvalues of ρ(Frob_x) for x dividing Q. In particular, the conclusions of this theorem apply for all sufficiently large p." Proof, pp. 87–88: "...we first use Serre duality to reduce the problem to vanishing of H^i(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} for i ≤ 1. ... Equivalently, it suffices to show that, if i denotes the smallest integer such that H^i(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} is nonzero, then H^i(X, ω(−∞))_{m_Q} is also nonzero. ... The result now follows as in the proof of [13, Proposition 7.9.8], which identifies these groups for all i under the Taylor–Wiles hypothesis..." For comparison, Lemma A.5 (p. 87) reads: "H^i(X, ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_Q} = 0 for i = 2 and 3".
sourceIssues.correction: The simplest fix is to assume H^i(X, ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_Q} = 0 for i = 2 and 3, which is exactly what Lemma A.5 gives. Alternatively, keep the H^2 hypothesis and add the missing step: H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0 follows from what is already assumed. The H^2 vanishing kills the ϖ-torsion of H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m, and H^3(X, ω^2_K)_m = 0 for non-Eisenstein m in characteristic 0, by the main text's §5.2 and §7.2 (argued below). The Serre-duality reduction then goes through. Separately, "eigenvalues of ρ(Frob_x)" should read r̄_p(Frob_x), and "this theorem" should read "this lemma".
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 886–888 (and arXiv p. 7) and checked them. The transcription above is exact. In the arXiv appendix v1, Lemma 3.4 on p. 7 has the same text, including 'H^2' alone and 'ρ(Frob_x)'.

1. Serre duality. The main text (§7.3) says ω^3(−∞) is the dualizing sheaf. So H^i(X, ω^2)^∨ ≅ H^{3−i}(X, ω(−∞)), and the case i ≥ 2 becomes degrees 3−i ∈ {0, 1}, as the proof says.

2. The written proof needs more than it assumes. It takes the smallest i0 with H^{i0}(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*} ≠ 0 and deduces H^{i0}(X, ω(−∞))_{m*} ≠ 0. A contradiction needs H^0 and H^1 of ω(−∞) at level X to vanish after localizing. These are dual to H^3 and H^2 of ω^2. The lemma assumes only H^2. If i0 = 0, the argument says nothing, not even about the i = 2 conclusion for X_1(Q).

3. The statement is affected too. The proof uses the identification H^i(X_0(Q), ·)_{mα} ≅ H^i(X, ·)_m 'for all i' ([13, Prop. 7.9.8]). So the i = 3 conclusion for X_0(Q) is equivalent to H^3(X, ω^2_k)_m = 0, which is not assumed. The stated hypotheses do not force it. From 0 → H^2(O)/ϖ^n → H^2(O/ϖ^n) → H^3(O)[ϖ^n] → 0, H^2 vanishing for all n only makes H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m torsion-free. H^3(X, ω^2_k)_m = H^3(O)_m ⊗ k is still nonzero whenever there is a characteristic-0 class in H^3(X, ω^2_K)_m. That is a weight-1 cusp eigensystem congruent to m. The paper rules this out only for sufficiently large p, in Lemma A.5, which is why that lemma states 'i = 2 and 3'. The Betti analogue, Theorem A.4, likewise assumes vanishing in every degree outside [q0, q0+l0]. The intended hypothesis ('as in the statement of Lemma A.5') is clearly both degrees.

4. A nuance. The i = 2 conclusion can in fact be recovered from the H^2 hypothesis alone by a different argument. For X_0(Q) use the identification. For X_1(Q), the Tor spectral sequence for RΓ(X_1(Q)) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k in degrees at most 3 forces H^3(X_1(Q)) to be free over k[Δ] and then H^2(X_1(Q)) = 0. The paper's proof does not do this, and the stated i = 3 case still needs H^3.

Downstream: Theorem A.1 (p. 889) uses Lemma A.6 only for sufficiently large p, where Lemma A.5 supplies both H^2 and H^3. So no later result is affected; the defect is confined to the lemma as stated. The ρ → r̄_p fix is a notational misprint. I rendered pp. 824–830, 886–888 and p. 7 of the arXiv appendix; the quoted text is exact.

1. The gap is real. Serre duality with dualizing sheaf ω^3(−∞) gives H^i(ω^2)^∨ ≅ H^{3−i}(ω(−∞)). The proof says it is "equivalent" to show that the least nonzero degree i ≤ 1 for X_1(Q) is also nonzero for X. That only produces a contradiction if both H^0 and H^1 of ω(−∞)_k at level X vanish after localization. Those are dual to H^3 and H^2 of ω^2_k. The lemma assumes only H^2, and the appendix never proves H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0. The case i = 0 is left open, and the i = 3 conclusion for X_0(Q) needs this vanishing outright. The proof identifies H^i(X_0(Q))_{m_α} with H^i(X)_m for all i, via [13, Prop. 7.9.8].

2. Defence: the stated lemma is still true. The missing H^3 vanishing follows from the stated hypotheses and results the paper itself proves.
(a) X is proper over O of relative dimension 3, so H^3(X, ω^2_k) = H^3(X, ω^2_O)/ϖ. There is an exact sequence 0 → H^2(O)/ϖ → H^2(k) → H^3(O)[ϖ] → 0, so H^2(X, ω^2_k)_m = 0 makes H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m torsion-free.
(b) Assuming r̄_p absolutely irreducible makes m non-Eisenstein (definition on p. 844). In characteristic 0, H^3(X, ω(2,2)_K)_m = 0:
- Lemma 7.10 (boundary cohomology vanishes after localizing at m) shows the localized cohomology equals interior cohomology.
- By Theorem 5.2(2), that interior cohomology comes from A_(2)(G).
- The classification argument in the proof of Theorem 7.11 (pp. 854–855) excludes classes (b)–(f), because they have reducible Galois representations. By Clozel's purity lemma the remaining class (a) is essentially tempered at infinity.
- Theorem 5.6(3) and Theorem 5.5 then leave only degrees i with (a−1, b−2) = (1, 0) ∈ C_i, that is i = 0 or 1. p. 830 states H^i(X(C), ω(a,2))_{(2),temp} = 0 for i = 2, 3.
(c) By (a) and (b), H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m is torsion-free and zero after tensoring with K, so it is 0, and H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0. With both degrees in hand, the paper's least-degree argument works as written. (The i = 2 conclusion alone can also be obtained from the Tor spectral sequence for RΓ(X_1(Q)) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k: H^2(X_0(Q)) = 0 forces H^3(X_1(Q)) to be free over k[Δ] and then H^2(X_1(Q)) = 0.)

So the prior verdict's claim, that the hypotheses do not force H^3 vanishing and that the paper rules it out only for large p, is wrong. Large p is needed in Lemma A.5 only to control torsion affecting H^2.

3. Consequences. The only downstream use is on p. 889: "Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above, where the vanishing result of Lemma A.6 replaces the vanishing results of Lan and Suh". The main text needs only H^2 vanishing: Assumption 7.7 is used in Lemma 7.9 and Theorem 7.11, and §1.2 says "The only point ... is to deduce that H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) = 0". Theorem A.1 in any case assumes p sufficiently large, where Lemma A.5 supplies both degrees.

Conclusion: this is a genuine but fillable omission in the proof. The lemma as stated is correct. Both proposed corrections (adding H^3 to the hypothesis) are right, minimal and harmless, but the paper does not need the stronger hypothesis. The ρ misprint is notational only.

sourceIssues.correction: Delete 'ordinary': '(2) Betti case: R is the minimal deformation ring corresponding to the following conditions:'. The conditions are (a) R^1_v of [16, §8.5.1] at primes of bad reduction and (b) Fontaine–Laffaille of weight [0,1,...,n−1] at v | p. 'Ordinary' is correct only in the coherent case (1).
sourceIssues.reason: Checked against the rendered p. 888. Item (2) lists its local conditions itself: (a) at bad v the ring R^1_v, and (b) 'If v | p and p is sufficiently large ... then we take deformations which are Fontaine–Laffaille of weight [0,1,...,n−1].' No ordinarity condition appears anywhere. The Betti case serves Theorem A.2 (p. 881): π is a weight-0 regular algebraic cuspidal representation of GL(n)/F with no ordinarity hypothesis, so r_λ(π) is in general not ordinary at p. That would make an 'ordinary' deformation ring the wrong ring. In item (1), 'minimal ordinary deformation ring R^min = R_∅' is correct, because Theorem A.1 assumes A is ordinary at p. So in (2) the word 'ordinary' was carried over from (1) by mistake. The intended ring is clear from (a) and (b), and the argument that follows (formal smoothness of the local rings via [20, Cor. 2.4.3, Lemma 2.4.19], R ≃ T) uses the ring those conditions define. sourceIssues.printed: "(1) Coherent case: R is the minimal ordinary deformation ring denoted by R^min = R_∅ in [16, Section 4]." (checked on the p. 88 image. [16] is F. Calegari and D. Geraghty, Modularity lifting beyond the Taylor–Wiles method, Invent. Math. 211 (2018), 297–433; this is the bibliography on p. 91 onward, and the entry's back-references include p. 88.)
sourceIssues.correction: "… denoted by R^min = R_∅ in Section 4 above" (Definition 4.6 with Q = ∅; p. 816 says "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min"; Theorem 9.1 on p. 878 uses the same R^min). In the arXiv appendix the reference should be [CG] (the main paper), not [CG18].
sourceIssues.reason: The citation is wrong. The coherent case of the appendix is Theorem A.1, about a semistable modular abelian surface with a GSp4-valued r and the ordinary condition at p. The deformation ring meant is the one in §4 of this paper. On p. 815, Definition 4.6 defines deformations that are "minimal outside Q", and item (6) is the ordinary condition at p. On p. 816 the paper says "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min". Theorem 9.1 (p. 878) uses "R^min … in the sense of Definition 4.6 (with Q taken to be empty)". In the cited paper [16], §4 is "Complements", made up of 4.1 "Multiplicity two" (canonical modules, and a GL2 ordinary ring R_φ for multiplicity in Jacobians) and 4.2 "Finiteness of deformation rings" (Lemma 4.14). It has no R_∅ or R^min and nothing about GSp4. Where [16] does write "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min", that is in §3.1 (weight-one GL2, unramified at p) and in §5.1 (imaginary quadratic fields), not in §4. The other [16] citations in the same paragraph are correct: §8.5.1 of [16] defines R_v^1, and Theorem 5.16 and Theorem 6.4 exist there. So this is one isolated slip. It comes from the arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, which was a separate preprint citing the main paper as [CG] and the Invent. paper as [CG18]. There, §4 item (1) reads "Coherent Case: R is the minimal ordinary deformation ring denoted by Rmin = R∅ in §4 of [CG18]", and [CG18] is the Invent. paper. So the arXiv version has the same slip; "§4 of [CG]" was intended. It changes nothing: the ring is clear from context. On p. 889, Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above", which uses this paper's R^min, and no later result depends on the wrong pointer.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix §A.4, proof of Theorem A.1, p. 889. Related: §A.3.2 and Lemma A.6 with its proof, pp. 886–888; Theorem 9.1(6), p. 878; Assumption 7.7, p. 851; Theorem 5.1, p. 822; Lemma 7.10, pp. 852–853.
sourceIssues.printed: Equally, Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above, where the vanishing result of Lemma A.6 replaces the vanishing results of Lan and Suh [53] for other low-weight local systems.
sourceIssues.correction:
Weight a = 2 needs the vanishing for the subcanonical sheaf: H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(2,2)(−∞)_k)_m = 0 (Assumption 7.7 / Theorem 9.1(6)), at the level and localization used there. Lemma A.6 gives this for the canonical ω^2 instead.

The minimal fix is to state and prove Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞); both arguments carry over.
- Lemma A.5: the characteristic-0 class then lies in H^i(X, ω^2(−∞)_C). Since the eigensystem of π is non-Eisenstein, the boundary argument of Lemma 7.10 identifies this group with the canonical H^i. That is L²/tempered cohomology, which vanishes in degrees 2 and 3 (see p. 830).
- Lemma A.6: the Serre dual of ω^2(−∞) is the canonical ω, not ω(−∞). The Khare–Thorne/BCGP descent from X_1(Q) to X_0(Q) to X applies unchanged.

The alternative is a mod-p statement that the paper does not contain: H^1(D, ω^2|_D ⊗ k)_m = 0 on the toroidal boundary D, which makes the canonical and subcanonical H^2 agree. The results to follow are Theorem 9.1 with a = 2, whose hypothesis p − 1 > a ≥ 2 allows it; "as in Theorem 1.2" (j ≥ 4) is only loose wording.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked on the rendered pages (pp. 886–889, 878, 851, 804, 822). The text of §A.3.2 is "by abuse of notation, also let ω denote the canonical extension of ω to X". Lemma A.6 states that H^i(X_1(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = H^i(X_0(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = 0 for i ≥ 2. Its proof "use[s] Serre duality to reduce the problem to vanishing of H^i(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} for i ≤ 1".

I redid the duality. By §5.2, ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b E, so ω(2,2) = ω^2. The dualizing sheaf is ω^3(−∞) (§7.2). So the dual of canonical ω^2 is ω^{−2} ⊗ ω^3(−∞) = ω(−∞), which confirms that Lemma A.6 concerns the canonical ω(2,2).

What the main argument needs is different. Theorem 9.1(6) requires H^2(X_i(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_{m_∅} = {0}. Assumption 7.7 requires H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m trivial, and it is used in Lemma 7.9 to make H^1(ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m divisible, which Theorem 7.11's balancedness needs. The Lan–Suh input that Lemma A.6 is meant to replace, Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.8, is also stated for ω(a,b)(−∞)_k. So the substitution swaps a canonical-extension statement for a subcanonical one without argument. The dual form of the needed statement is H^1 of the canonical ω, while Lemma A.6's proof treats ω(−∞).

The two differ by boundary cohomology: H^1(D, ω^2|_D) → H^2(ω^2(−D)) → H^2(ω^2). The paper kills the localized boundary cohomology only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10, statement p. 852). There is no mod-p boundary result anywhere in the text.

Strongest counterargument: §1.2 (p. 804) says one "need[s] only the weaker result that the image of H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^can) in H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) is zero" after localization. If that meant the interior H^2, Lemma A.6 would imply it. But that reduction is only asserted, never proved; the literal map can → sub does not exist; and Section 7 (Lemma 7.9) uses the full subcanonical H^2(·_k)_m = 0. In the same passage the authors call the H^2 vanishing unresolved and say only that one "should be able to" handle weight (2,2) by Khare–Thorne.

Verdict: a genuine gap. It is probably fixable by rerunning Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞), but that argument is not in the paper. The candidate's remark about Theorem 1.2 is also right: it assumes p − 1 > j ≥ 4, so the operative statement is Theorem 9.1 with a = 2. The candidate's suggested boundary vanishing is a sufficient condition; it is correct, but it is one of the two routes.

arXiv: appendix v1 (1907.08694v1) has the same text, with its §3.2 using the same canonical convention and its Lemma 3.4 being Lemma A.6. Its §4 reads "Equally, Theorem 1.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 of [CG], where the vanishing result of Lemma 3.4 replaces the vanishing results of Lan–Suh [LS13] for other low weight local systems used in [CG]." In main-text v1 (1907.08691v1), Theorem 9.1(6) and Assumption 7.7 are identical to the published text.

Scope: Theorem A.1 is the appendix's main result and nothing later in the paper depends on it. It is not shown to be false, so the defect is in the proof only. Checked on the rendered p. 803, 804, 822, 823, 830, 851–853, 878–889.

(1) The appendix's ω^2 is the canonical extension. §A.3.2 says so explicitly. The main text also writes ω(a,b) = W^can_μ (p. 823), with ω(a,b)(−∞) for the subcanonical sheaf. Serre duality confirms it: the dualizing sheaf is ω^3(−∞) (p. 851), so the dual of the canonical ω^2 is ω(−∞), exactly as in the proof of Lemma A.6. For the subcanonical ω^2(−∞) the dual would have been the canonical ω. Two independent passages agree, so a charitable misprint reading (appendix ω meaning subcanonical) is not available.

(2) The main argument needs the subcanonical sheaf. Theorem 9.1(6) reads "H^2(X_i(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_{m_∅} = {0}", and Assumption 7.7 reads "H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m is trivial". The proof of Theorem 9.1 uses these only through Theorem 7.11 ("H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11", p. 880). Theorem 7.11 uses Lemma 7.9: H^1(ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m is divisible, which is equivalent to H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_O)_m being torsion-free. The Lan–Suh input being replaced (Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.8) is also stated for ω(a,b)(−∞)_k.

(3) Canonical vanishing does not give the subcanonical statement. Take a = 2 and 0 → ω^2(−D) → ω^2 → ω^2|_D → 0. Lemma A.6 plus Lemma 7.10 (⊗K) make H^2(sub_O)_m torsion, equal to coker(H^1(can_O)_m → H^1(D, ω^2|_D)_m). Lemma 7.9 needs this cokernel to vanish. That is a mod-p boundary statement, and the paper proves boundary vanishing only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10).

Defences tried:
(a) §1.2 (p. 804) says one needs "only the weaker result that the image of H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^can) in H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) is zero after localization". The printed direction is reversed, since the natural map goes sub→can. Read as interior H^2, it would follow from Lemma A.6. But this is only asserted: the same paragraph says "we were not able to prove it". Also, by (3), interior vanishing is automatic once the canonical H^2_m = 0, yet it does not give Lemma 7.9.
(b) Could the patching be rerun with canonical sheaves? Then Section 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 (which use W^sub) and the H^0 comparison would need mod-p boundary input, which is also not in the paper.
(c) Cited sources: [13, Prop. 7.9.8] is invoked only for the level-lowering step, not for any comparison between canonical and subcanonical cohomology.

So this is a genuine gap, but a routine one. Rerunning Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞) works, with Lemma 7.10's characteristic-0 boundary argument added in Lemma A.5. There is also a minor mismatch in level and localization: Lemma A.6 uses X_0(Q)/X_1(Q) at m_α, while Assumption 7.7 uses X_Δ(Q) at m. The earlier verdict's two routes and its remark about Theorem 1.2 are confirmed.

Consequences: Lemma A.6 is used only in this sentence, to prove Theorem A.1. Theorem A.2 goes through Theorem A.4 (Betti cohomology) and is unaffected, and nothing after Theorem A.1 depends on it. Theorem A.1 is not shown to be false, and the fix is expected to work, so only its proof is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix, §A.4, proof of Lemma A.8, p. 890, lines 1–2 of the proof
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. From such an equality, we can build two finite-dimensional representations A_ℓ and B_ℓ built out of copies of ∧²V_ℓ, Q_p, Q_p(1), V_ℓ, and V_ℓ ⊗ V_ℓ, respectively, which have equal trace on Frob_p for infinitely many p. (Checked on a 400 dpi render of p. 90: both constituents have bold Q with subscript p, the same italic p as in Frob_p, not ℓ.)
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "Q_p, Q_p(1)" with "Q_ℓ, Q_ℓ(1)". On p. 889 the paper defines V_ℓ = H^1(A, Q̄_ℓ), so the matching form is Q̄_ℓ and Q̄_ℓ(1). These are the ℓ-adic trivial and cyclotomic characters of G_Q, whose Frob_p-traces are 1 and p. A pedantic point: with V_ℓ = H^1 and geometric Frobenius (the normalisation that gives the printed characteristic polynomial, whose roots have absolute value √p), the Tate twist with trace p is Q_ℓ(−1). With arithmetic Frobenius on the Tate module it is Q_ℓ(1). This is a convention question. What matters is the subscript: it should be ℓ, not p.
sourceIssues.reason: Rendered pp. 889–890. Lemma A.8 (p. 889) says there is no fixed linear relation between 1, p, b_p, a_p and a_p^2 holding for p in a set S of positive density. The proof moves the terms with positive coefficients to one side and those with negative coefficients to the other, then realises each side as the Frob_p-trace of a single G_Q-representation. The term 2p + b_p comes from ∧²V_ℓ, ±a_p from V_ℓ and a_p^2 from V_ℓ⊗V_ℓ. The constants 1 and p need 1-dimensional representations whose Frob_p-trace is 1 and p for every p. These are the trivial and cyclotomic characters with coefficients in Q_ℓ (or Q̄_ℓ). They are summed with the ℓ-adic V_ℓ into A_ℓ and B_ℓ, the argument then uses the image of G_Q on V_ℓ being GSp_4(Z_ℓ) together with Chebotarev, and so every summand must be ℓ-adic. "Q_p" has no sensible meaning here: p is the prime that varies over S, so Q_p and Q_p(1) are not fixed representations. A p-adic Q_p(1) would also be ramified at p, so it has no Frob_p-trace, and it cannot be combined with ℓ-adic representations. No convention in the paper makes Q_p denote an ℓ-adic coefficient field. The same Q_p appears in arXiv:1907.08694v1 (appendix), Lemma 4.2 proof, p. 8, where I checked the render: "built out of copies of ∧²V_ℓ, Q_p, Q_p(1), V_ℓ, and V_ℓ ⊗ V_ℓ respectively". The main arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 does not contain the passage. Effect: nothing depends on it. The evident intended reading, ℓ-adic trivial and cyclotomic characters, is what the rest of the proof uses. Lemma A.8 is used only for Lemma A.7(2), and through it for the density-1 claim of Theorem A.4. Neither statement changes. Aside, not part of this item: the proof of Lemma A.8 is sketchy in other places, e.g. it says "for infinitely many p" where it means the positive-density set S. The candidate's claim is exactly this misprint.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix, §A.4 (Proofs), proof of Lemma A.7(2), case (3), p. 890. The characteristic polynomial is on p. 889. In the arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1 it is the proof of Lemma 4.1, case (3), p. 9.
sourceIssues.printed: (3) Suppose that α = ε mod p for some fixed ε ∈ {±1}. Then b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p.
sourceIssues.correction: b_p + εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p (equivalently ε^2 + a_p ε + b_p ≡ 0).
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this on the page images at 130 and 250 dpi. p. 889 prints the characteristic polynomial as "X^4 + a_pX^3 + (2p + b_p)X^2 + pa_pX + p^2", with roots "α, β, α^{-1}p and β^{-1}p". p. 890, case (3), prints "Suppose that α = ε mod p for some fixed ε ∈ {±1}. Then b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p." The "=" instead of "≡" is also as printed.

My computation from the printed polynomial:
- The roots sum to −a_p, so a_p = −(α + β + p/α + p/β).
- The X^2 coefficient is 2p + b_p, so b_p = αβ + p^2/(αβ) + p(α/β + β/α).
- In this case α and β are units at the prime above p. That is forced by the factor αβ in Lemma A.7(2), after using case (1) and the α↔β, β↔p/β relabelling. So mod p we get a_p ≡ −(α + β) and b_p ≡ αβ. Equivalently, the polynomial is ≡ X^2(X^2 + a_pX + b_p) mod p.
- So α ≡ ε gives ε^2 + εa_p + b_p ≡ 0, that is b_p + εa_p + 1 ≡ 0.
- For the printed expression: b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ εβ + (1 + εβ) + 1 = 2(1 + εβ). This is not ≡ 0 unless β ≡ −ε.

Concrete counterexample: p = 7, with polynomial (X^2 − X + 7)(X^2 − 3X + 7) = X^4 − 4X^3 + 17X^2 − 28X + 49. So a_p = −4 and b_p = 3. The unit root α ≡ 1 mod 7, so ε = 1. The printed expression gives 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 ≢ 0 mod 7. The corrected one gives 3 − 4 + 1 = 0.

A script over every product (X^2 − t1X + p)(X^2 − t2X + p) with p = 7, 11, 13 and unit t_i gave these results. The corrected congruence held in all 72 cases with α ≡ ε. The printed one failed in 66 of them.

No convention in the paper rescues the printed sign. The error does not depend on arithmetic versus geometric Frobenius: it is fixed by the printed polynomial, which is invariant under x ↦ p/x. It would be correct only if the cubic coefficient were −a_p, i.e. if a_p were the trace. The paper's remark that a_p^2 is the trace on V⊗V is sign-blind.

The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1 (Lemma 4.1, case (3), p. 9) prints the same "b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p", with the same characteristic polynomial "X^4 + a_pX^3 + (2p+b_p)X^2 + pa_pX + p^2".

sourceIssues.locator: References, entry [33], p. 893
sourceIssues.printed: [33] W. GOLDRING and J.-S. KOSKIVIRTA, Strata Hasse invariants, Hecke algebras and Galois representations, Invent. Math. 217 (2019), no. 3, 137–151. MR 3989256. DOI 10.1007/s00222-019-00882-5. (49)
sourceIssues.correction: Invent. Math. 217 (2019), no. 3, 887–984. The page range should read 887–984; the rest of the entry (volume, issue, year, MR 3989256, DOI) is correct.
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 893 at 130 dpi. The entry reads exactly as quoted, with the page range 137–151 and the back-reference "(49)". I checked the page range against two independent sources, and both give 887–984. First, Crossref for DOI 10.1007/s00222-019-00882-5 gives the title "Strata Hasse invariants, Hecke algebras and Galois representations", authors Wushi Goldring and Jean-Stefan Koskivirta, volume 217, issue 3, pages 887-984, print date 2019-09. Second, the MathSciNet mref BibTeX for MR3989256 has MRNUMBER = {3989256}, VOLUME = {217}, YEAR = {2019}, NUMBER = {3}, PAGES = {887--984}. So the MR number and the DOI in the printed entry are right and only the page range is wrong. The error came in with the published version. The arXiv main-text preprint 1907.08691v1 cites the paper as "[KG15] Jean-Stefan Koskivirta and Wushi Goldring, Strata hasse invariants, hecke algebras and galois representations, preprint, 2015.", with no journal data or page numbers. The appendix preprint 1907.08694v1 does not cite it at all. The only place the paper cites [33] is p. 849 (§7-8 area, before Theorem 8.10). There it says the Hasse invariant h̃ ∈ H^0(S, ω^{⊗(p^2−1)}) "was constructed in unpublished work of the second author with Goldring, but is also constructed in greater generality in [12] and [33]". The facts actually used (extension to the boundary and Hecke equivariance) are cited to [12] (Boxer), so no argument depends on this entry's page range. This is a pure bibliographic misprint with no mathematical consequence.

sourceIssues.locator: Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris, "Bloch–Kato conjectures for automorphic motives"), References, entry [38], p. 893. It is cited twice in the appendix introduction on p. 881: "…compatible families of n-dimensional representations whose existence was only recently proved to exist in [38]" (before Theorem A.1) and "For the families of Galois representations constructed in [38], we prove the following result" (before Theorem A.2). The appendix preprint arXiv:1907.08694v1 (the only version) prints the same entry: "[HLTT] Michael Harris, Kai-Wen Lan, Richard Taylor, and Jack Thorne, Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation." It is cited there at the same two places. The main-text preprint arXiv:1907.08691v1 does not cite this work.
sourceIssues.printed: [38] M. HARRIS, K.-W. LAN, R. TAYLOR, and J. THORNE, Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation. (81)   [the title is in italics; "(81)" is the green back-reference to the citing page]
sourceIssues.correction: [38] M. Harris, K.-W. Lan, R. Taylor, and J. Thorne, On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties, Res. Math. Sci. 3 (2016), Paper No. 37, doi:10.1186/s40687-016-0078-5. It was also on arXiv as arXiv:1411.6717 (25 Nov 2014, "Version of December 2013").
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered p. 893 at 110 dpi, and entry [38] reads exactly as quoted. I also rendered p. 881; the only citations of [38] are the two quoted in the locator. I checked Crossref for doi:10.1186/s40687-016-0078-5. It gives the title "On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties", the authors Michael Harris, Kai-Wen Lan, Richard Taylor and Jack Thorne, the journal Research in the Mathematical Sciences, volume 3, article number 37, published online 26 Oct 2016 and in print Dec 2016. It is the same work. The arXiv abstract of 1411.6717 says: "We construct the compatible system of l-adic representations associated to a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n over a CM (or totally real) field … we impose no self-duality hypothesis". This is exactly the family r_λ(π) that Theorem A.2 uses. So the 2020 paper cites, as "in preparation" and under an old working title, a work that had been on arXiv under its final title since Nov 2014 and in print since 2016. The paper's own wording, "was only recently proved to exist in [38]", also treats the work as finished. The entry does not say where to find the cited work, but the intended reference is clear from the authors and context. That makes it a bibliographic slip ("misprint" in the sense of PROTOCOL §18), not a mathematical error. This matches earlier accepted bibliography misprints such as PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18/E217. No correction exists: Crossref's deposit for doi:10.1215/00127094-2019-0044 (the final issue version, vol. 169, no. 5, 1 Apr 2020) still lists "[38] … Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation." It shows no update-to/erratum. The appendix arXiv preprint has only v1, with the same text. The date arithmetic in the candidate is right (2016 vs 2020, four years). Its correction matches the Crossref record. I added the arXiv number only for completeness.

sourceIssues.printed: A general approach to resolving these questions has been recently found by Pilloni [56], who constructs all the operators used in this paper. More importantly, his method also allows one to give an action of these operators on higher coherent cohomology as well.

sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the rendered p. 860. The description (a recent general construction of the normalized Hecke operators at p, with an action on higher coherent cohomology) is that of [58], as the paper itself says on p. 805: "[58] develops a conceptual method to define (normalized) Hecke operators at p, and in particular establishes the action of these operators on higher cohomology". [56] is Pilloni, "Modularité, formes de Siegel et surfaces abéliennes", J. reine angew. Math. 666 (2012), which is cited for regular-weight modularity lifting and Taylor–Wiles primes for GSp4 on pp. 804, 813, 817 and 818. The back-references of [56] in the bibliography include this page, those of [58] do not. The reader can recover the intended reference, so this is a misprint. Found while checking the prerequisites (not by the section readers or hunts).
